trap: Mostly guessable, but 'talk about X' is usually X no hanashi (o suru), shorter than X ni tsuite hanasu.
why: Very frequent framing (nan no hanashi? = what are you talking about). Low trap risk, so it is a reserve.
freqNote: 話 #96 counts every hanashi use; suru #15.

why: Everyday way to say you listen to someone.

trap: Learners say suki for 'I love it!' about something new; natives say ki ni itta, and iru here conjugates godan (itta), not like iru 'be' (ita).
why: Top-frequency way to say you like a gift, place or purchase (kore ki ni itta); contrasts with ki ni naru and suki.
freqNote: 入る read iru (#63142) survives almost only inside this phrase; the whole expression 気に入る is #889.

trap: 'Have time' takes aru/nai, not motsu.
why: Staple excuse and hurry phrase.

trap: Not junbi desu or redi: 'Are you ready?' is junbi dekita?, where ready means the preparation has come into being.
why: The everyday 'Ready?' / 'I'm ready' before going out, eating or starting something, as in junbi dekitara oshiete.
freqNote: できる #73 is the kana form; 出来る #1313.

trap: English 'disturb/bother' has no matching verb: it is jama (o) suru, and entering someone's home is the set phrase ojama shimasu.
why: Gives jama shinaide, jama? (am I in the way?) and the unguessable ojama shimasu. Close to noun + suru, but it earns a place through the greeting.
freqNote: 邪魔 #566 includes jama da (in the way) and ojama shimasu uses.

trap: Not benri for people and advice: 'useful' or 'helpful' is yaku ni tatsu. Benri means convenient.
why: Used in thanks and self-deprecation (yaku ni tatte yokatta; yaku ni tatanakute gomen).
freqNote: Phrase entry 役に立つ at #1516, the highest-ranked collocation entry missing from the pool. 役に立たない is #6939.

trap: Not uso o hanasu or uso o suru: lies take tsuku (uso tsuite nai yo).
why: Everyday accusation and denial; the verb cannot be guessed, and the learner already knows uso! as an interjection.
freqNote: uso #1544 (kana うそ #2305 counted separately). tsuku: kana つく #355 pools all kana tsuku senses; 吐く read as つく is only #173635, so no clean rank for this sense.

trap: Not hanasu hitsuyou ga aru: 'I need to talk to you' is chotto hanashi ga aru n da kedo.
why: A serious-conversation opener. English 'need to' pushes learners into a grammar construction instead.
freqNote: 話 #96 counts every hanashi use; aru #21.

trap: Not shitsumon o kiku: 'ask a question' is shitsumon (o) suru, and kiku alone means 'ask' without the noun.
why: Comes up in class, at work and everywhere else. It sits near the transparent kango + suru line, but English 'ask' pulls learners toward kiku.

trap: Not jikan o toru: the time a task takes is kakaru (jikan o toru means setting time aside).
why: The everyday way to say how long anything takes (dore gurai kakaru?), and English 'take' points straight at toru.
freqNote: かかる #385 is the kana spelling across all senses; 掛かる #5316.

why: Basic household action.
Everyday stepping outside.

trap: Not itaku naru or kizutsuku: an injury is 'done', kega o suru, even by accident (kega shita?).
why: An unguessable suru pairing that covers any injury; also kega shinai you ni.
freqNote: けが #3721 (怪我 #7111); する #15. No phrase entry.

trap: 'Have time' uses aru, not motsu.
why: Ima jikan aru? asks if someone is free.

trap: Not yume o motsu (that's a life ambition): dreaming in your sleep is yume o miru, 'seeing' a dream.
why: Common morning small talk ('hen na yume mita'), and English 'have' sends learners to motsu. Could also sit under senses.
freqNote: 夢 #351 covers both night dreams and ambitions; 夢見る #4121 is the one-word 'dream of' verb.

trap: Not ki o tsukeru: caring for a pet, child or plant is sewa o suru (inu no sewa).
why: The giving side of osewa ni naru; keep the two together or drop both.

trap: 'Interested' is an adjective in English; Japanese says kyoumi ga aru/nai.
why: Standard way to say you are (not) interested.

trap: English 'take care of' gives no clue: you 'see to the bother' with mendou o miru. Keep it apart from mendokusai (what a hassle).
why: Used for looking after kids, juniors and parents. It competes with sewa o suru, so keep only one if space is short.
freqNote: 面倒 #1114 is mostly the 'hassle' sense; 見る #55.

trap: 'Lucky' is an adjective in English, but Japanese says un ga ii (your luck is good), or rakkii. Unlucky is un ga warui.
why: An everyday reaction (un yokatta ne) that pairs naturally with un ga warui.
freqNote: Phrase entries 運が悪い #10068 and 運がいい #11653.

english: make sense; get what something means
trap: There's no 'make sense' verb: 'that makes no sense' is imi ga wakaranai (imi wakannai), 'the meaning can't be grasped'.
why: Imi wakannai is one of the commonest casual reactions. English 'make sense' gives the learner nothing to translate.
Common for seeing someone in person (kao o mitai).

trap: No 'hungry' adjective: the stomach empties, onaka suita, past tense for the feeling now.
why: Daily need with no English-shaped route; onaka suita is the only natural 'I'm hungry'.
freqNote: おなか #1253 (お腹 #4758). Verb rank is kana すく #2947, the usual spelling here; it can also be 好く, which is rare in speech. Kanji 空く read すく is #47898. Phrase entries: お腹が空く #22626, お腹がすく #27605.

why: One of the most-said requests (shashin totte moraemasu ka?); guessable from English, but it anchors toreru, douga o toru and shashin o ageru.
freqNote: verbRank is the 撮る spelling (photo/film sense); 取る 'take' is #228.

trap: Getting out of bed is okiru; me o samasu is coming awake.
why: Typical set for waking from sleep.

trap: Not tatakau, which means battle: a fight or argument between people is kenka suru (kare to kenka shita, with to).
why: Common in relationship stories. It is a noun + suru, but English 'fight' points to the wrong verb. Pairs with nakanaori.
freqNote: kana けんか #5489 and 喧嘩 #6973 are counted separately, so the true noun frequency is higher than either; suru #15.

why: Raising a hand in class or to signal.

trap: 'Interested' is not an adjective: X ni kyoumi ga aru. Learners say omoshiroi desu, which means 'it's interesting/funny'.
why: Needed constantly when talking about hobbies and plans (kyoumi aru? / kyoumi nai); English leads to the wrong word class.
freqNote: The ga-aru expression has no entry (tokenized apart); 興味ない is #1906 and kyoumi o motsu 興味を持つ #4531.

trap: English 'notice' has no 'mind' word, so learners say miru or wakaru; and it is ki GA TSUKU, not ki o tsukeru (be careful).
why: Everyday 'I didn't notice' (zenzen ki ga tsukanakatta) and the near-homophone of ki o tsukeru, so the pair must be learned apart.
freqNote: Verb rank is 付く; kana つく (#355) mixes several tsuku verbs. The list also holds the whole expression 気が付く #2832 / 気がつく #3139; one-word kizuku 気付く is #1083.

english: feel good, be in a good mood
trap: 'Feel good' is not kanjiru; mood is kibun ga ii, physical comfort kimochi ii.
why: Everyday way to talk about mood and wellbeing.

trap: No single verb for 'ruin'; say dainashi ni suru/naru.
why: Fixed set for spoiling plans or things.
Common workday phrase.

english: get in a car, ride in a car
trap: Takes ni, not o; 'get in' is noru, not hairu.
why: Core transport set.

english: be pleasant, nice (a person or place)
trap: For a pleasant manner or vibe, not yasashii: kanji ga ii, as in kanji no ii hito / kanji warui.
why: The everyday verdict on staff, new acquaintances and shops.

trap: Not kodomo o motte iru or kodomo ga aru: people you 'have' take ga iru (kodomo iru? kyoudai iru? kareshi iru?).
why: The get-to-know-you question. H-iru-exist teaches the sense; this item fixes the family and partner slots (kyoudai, kareshi, kanojo).
freqNote: 子供 #589 (子ども #2264 separate spelling); iru: kana いる #42 (居る #6802).

trap: 'I know how you feel' is sono kimochi wakaru, not shitteru: shiru is for knowing facts.
why: Core empathy line in conversation (wakaru, sono kimochi); English 'know' leads to shiru.
freqNote: No expression entry (tokenized apart); judged from parts.

trap: Not kao o tsukuru: wearing an expression is kao o suru, as in hen na kao shiteru or sonna kao shinaide.
why: The 'X kao o suru' pattern (kanashii, kowai, hen na kao) is how people describe someone's expression, and English 'make' gives the wrong verb.

trap: Not nioi o kagu or nioi da: 'it smells good' is ii nioi ga suru, with suru.
why: Daily reaction (ii nioi suru!, nanka kusai nioi shinai?) built on the unguessable X ga suru frame shared by oto, koe and aji.
freqNote: nounRank is the kana spelling におい; 匂い #2171, 臭い (bad smell) #7168. Expression 匂いがする #7128.

trap: kiru only covers tops and whole-body clothes (shirt, coat, dress, kimono). English 'wear' also covers shoes, trousers, hats and glasses, which each take a different verb.
why: The base wearing verb (nani kiteku? / kore kite mite) that every other wear verb is learned against. shatsu, kooto, seetaa and kimono take it too.
freqNote: Rank is for 着る #754. Kana きる is mostly 切る 'cut' (#546), the same sound. Pairing commonness is judged.

trap: Not kotaeru: picking up the phone is denwa ni deru ('come out to the phone'); kotaeru answers a question.
why: Needed for 'he's not picking up' (denwa ni denai) and 'can you get the phone?' (denwa dete); English 'answer' always points to kotaeru.

trap: 'Call' meaning summon is yobu; denwa suru is only phoning.
why: Set phrase, over-counted by crime films but real.

trap: A voice you just happen to hear is koe ga kikoeru.
why: Common on calls (koe ga kikitakatta).

english: get in touch, stay in contact
trap: Not renraku o morau or tamotsu: making or keeping contact is toru (mada renraku totteru? / renraku ga torenai).
why: Takes the versatility item renraku suru further, to 'still in touch?' and 'can't reach them'. Hearing from someone is renraku ga kuru.

trap: 'Have a question' is aru, not motsu.
why: Fixed classroom and work phrase.

trap: Takes ni, not o.
why: Typical set; particle catches learners.

trap: Not furuku naru (that's for things): people 'take years', toshi o toru (toshi totta naa).
why: Common in self-deprecating chat, and furui for people is a classic learner error.
freqNote: 年 read とし #1354 (the reading ねん is #155); 取る #228. Phrase entries 年を取る #5402 and 年取る #8003 rank high for phrases.

trap: Eyes take tojiru (or tsuburu), not shimeru.
why: Typical body action with a non-English verb.

trap: The place you leave takes o: ie o deru.
why: Daily routine (nanji ni ie o deru?).
Fixed everyday set for being busy.

trap: 'Put back' is moto ni modosu, not oku.
why: Typical tidying and undo phrase.

trap: Not only okiru: waking from sleep is me ga sameru ('eyes wake'); okiru is getting up.
why: Plain, literal way to say 'I woke at 4' or 'I'm wide awake now' (me ga sameta), which okiru can't express. Not a figurative idiom.
freqNote: 覚める #6527; 目覚める #3028 is the one-word narrative/written form.

trap: 'Be helpful' is tasuke ni naru, not tetsudau.
why: Common way to say something helps.

english: wait and see, keep an eye on it
trap: Not matsu: 'let's wait and see' is yousu o miru ('watch how things look').
why: Used by doctors and parents and in plans (ni-san-nichi yousu mimashou).
freqNote: Phrase entry 様子を見る at #3061.

why: Core hobby set.

trap: 'Leave me alone' is hitori ni shite, not oite iku.
why: Set phrase hitori ni shite.

trap: No single everyday verb for 'breathe'; say iki o suru.
why: Standard way to say breathe.

trap: Not tanoshii or ii kanji for a bath, breeze or massage: physical pleasantness is kimochi ii.
why: Constant spoken reaction (aa, kimochi ii; kaze ga kimochi ii ne) that learners have no word for.
freqNote: Usually said without ga: 気持ちいい #2005 vs 気持ちがいい #13062.

trap: Not sumaato (that means slim and stylish): 'smart' is atama ga ii. Kashikoi exists but is less everyday.
why: The everyday word for 'smart', used constantly about kids, colleagues and friends.
freqNote: 頭 #375; いい #24 (良い #1474, よい #120). Its opposite, atama ga warui, is common in casual self-deprecation but rude about others.

why: Literal everyday set (te o hanasanaide).

trap: Not kokoro o kaeru: changing your mind is ki ga kawaru, with ki as the subject (ki ga kawattara itte).
why: The plain, literal way to say you changed your mind about a plan (so not an idiom). Keep it apart from ki ga suru and ki ni naru.

english: wrap up, call it a day
trap: Ending a session is owari ni suru; owaru alone is intransitive.
why: Common for ending work or a task (kyou wa owari ni shiyou).
Basic household action.

trap: 'Talented' is an adjective; Japanese says sainou ga aru.
why: Standard way to call someone talented.
Core daily-routine set.

trap: Not yobu or iu: phoning someone is denwa o kakeru (or simply denwa suru); yobu is summon, iu is call something a name.
why: The core phone verb; English 'call' leads to yobu, and casual speech alternates it with denwa suru (ato de kakeru ne / denwa suru ne).
freqNote: verbRank is kana かける, which pools every sense (call, sit, spend, put on); 掛ける alone is #2742.

trap: Means physically sick or queasy, not 'grumpy' (that is kigen ga warui); kimochi warui is the casual twin.
why: What you say when you might throw up or faint, and it's easy to misuse as 'in a bad mood'.
freqNote: 気分 #804; 悪い #139; phrase entry 気分が悪い #10247. Compare 気持ち悪い #1740 (one word, also 'gross') and 機嫌 #3757.

trap: 'See a doctor' is byouin ni iku (go to the clinic), not isha ni au; byouin covers any clinic.
why: Everyday advice and plans (byouin itta hou ga ii yo); English 'see' and 'hospital' both mislead.
freqNote: 病院 #651; 行く #40. No phrase entry.

trap: Not doa ga akeru: when it opens by itself or is open, use aku (doa aiteru yo); akeru needs someone to do it.
why: The intransitive half of aku/akeru ('the door's open', train doors, shops opening). doa ga shimaru follows the same pattern.
freqNote: 開く read あく #14086 looks low because the tokenizer files much of 開く under ひらく #624; 空く #1498 is the 'free/vacant' aku.

trap: English 'lie down' has no Japanese verb a learner could guess: it's 'become sideways', yoko ni naru. It has nothing to do with the 'lie' of uso o tsuku.
why: Needed whenever you feel unwell (chotto yoko ni naru) and at the doctor's. Learners can't build it from what they know.

trap: Not geemu o asobu: asobu takes no game object, so a game is done with suru or yaru (geemu yatteta).
why: Gaming is a top small-talk topic. The same suru slot covers toranpu o suru and janken o suru.
freqNote: yaru #45 is the common casual alternative (geemu yaru).

english: light the stove or a fire; light a cigarette
trap: English 'light' has no obvious verb; it is tsukeru, the same verb as for lights, and hi o tsukete sounds like ki o tsukete (be careful).
why: The opposite of hi o kesu, which is already in the pool; used for cooking and for cigarettes.
freqNote: 火 #1743 (kana ひ is shared with 日 #209). 393 is kana つける, the usual spelling, which mixes all senses; 付ける #1452, 点ける #52228.

trap: 'Gross/creepy' and 'I feel queasy' are both kimochi warui; learners reach for kirai or byouki.
why: Very frequent reaction word and the other half of kimochi ii; covers both disgust and nausea.
freqNote: Usually said as one word 気持ち悪い #1740; slang clip kimoi キモい #4580.

trap: There is no verb for 'complain': you 'say complaints', as in monku iwanaide (guchi o iu = grumble, vent).
why: Used daily about people and service. guchi o iu is the venting twin.

trap: Not yakusoku o motsu or tamotsu: keeping a promise is mamoru, 'protect' (jikan o mamoru = be on time).
why: A common reminder and reproach (yakusoku mamotte yo), and English 'keep' gives no route to mamoru. jikan o mamoru is folded in here.
freqNote: 守る #303 is likely inflated by its 'protect' sense in drama plots.

why: Fixed set mirroring English; casual talk prefers suki ni naru.

trap: 'I had a scary experience' is kowai omoi o shita, not kowai keiken o motta: the feeling is the object of suru.
why: Native way to recount how something felt (samishii omoi sasete gomen); unguessable suru pairing.
freqNote: Expression 思いをする #2427. Noun rank 思い is shared with 'thought'. Always said with an adjective in front (kowai, tsurai, samishii, ii).

trap: No 'thirsty' adjective: the throat dries, nodo kawaita, past tense for the feeling now.
why: Daily need that mirrors onaka ga suku; teach the two together.
freqNote: 喉 #3552; 渇く #6159 (its homophone 乾く 'dry' is #6556); phrase entry 喉が渇く #14507.

trap: English makes the hearer the subject; Japanese makes the voice the subject with ga kikoeru, not o kiku.
why: Standard way to say a voice can be heard.

trap: Not kuruma o paaku suru: parking is just 'stopping' the car, tomeru (chuusha suru is the word on signs). Not yameru, which means quitting.
why: The transitive half of the tomaru/tomeru pair. doko ni tomeru? is the parking question.
freqNote: Phrase not counted. 止める covers stopping anything, so its rank overstates the parking sense; the parking spelling 停める is #22793.

why: Everyday set: nanika you? / you ga aru kara.
Showing each other photos on a phone is an everyday act; 'kono shashin mite' is heard constantly.

trap: English 'have problems' leads to motsu; Japanese says kakaeru or mondai ga aru.
why: Strongest verb for carrying problems, semi-formal.

english: have no time, money or room to spare
trap: There's no verb for 'afford': 'I can't afford it' and 'I'm swamped' are both yoyuu ga nai (no margin).
why: Covers money, time and mental bandwidth. Yoyuu (de) is also slang for 'easy'.
Daily-routine staple; miru covers watch.

trap: English 'hit' leads to tataku or naguru; bumping your own head is utsu.
why: Standard set for bumping your head in an accident.

trap: English 'have' leads to motsu; experience takes ga aru.
why: Common in jobs and life talk.

trap: Japanese has no verb for 'look forward': you 'make it a pleasure', as in tanoshimi ni shiteru (ne).
why: The versatility list has tanoshimi da, but only the ni suru frame takes an object ('X o tanoshimi ni shiteru'), and it's the closing line of most plans.

trap: English 'grow up' leads to sodatsu; becoming an adult is otona ni naru.
why: Everyday way to say grow up or act mature.

trap: Not kanjiru: 'I feel sick' has no feel verb; the condition is bad, guai ga warui.
why: The general 'I'm not well', and the caring question guai warui no?
freqNote: 具合 #1423; 悪い #139; phrase entry 具合が悪い #5837, high for a phrase.

trap: English 'lock' gives no verb: you kakeru the key, and 'it's locked' is kagi ga kakatteru (kagi o shimeru is also heard).
why: Comes up every time someone leaves the house ('kagi kaketa?'). Unlocking is kagi o akeru, which can sit in this entry's notes.
freqNote: かける #244 is the kana spelling across all senses (掛ける #2742); カギ #9849 is a variant spelling of the noun.

trap: Not kanjiru for 'it feels like...': the everyday form is ~ kanji ga suru (or ~ tte kanji).
why: Common hedge for impressions (natsukashii kanji ga suru); sits between ki ga suru and tte kanji in the versatility list.
freqNote: Expression 感じがする #3120.

why: Basic guessable set; letters less common now.

english: go back to how it was
why: Common set for things or people returning to normal.

trap: English 'smoke' is one verb; Japanese 'inhales' tobacco (tabako o suu). kemuri (smoke) is no help.
why: Asked and answered often (tabako suimasu ka?, sutte mo ii?). The older form tabako o nomu turns up in older speakers' talk.
freqNote: タバコ #4158 is the most frequent spelling (たばこ #7069, 煙草 #28060). 吸う #1684 also counts breathing in.

trap: Not shawaa o toru: you abiru (pour over yourself) a shower.
why: A daily-routine staple ('shawaa abite kuru'), and the verb is impossible to guess from English 'take'.
freqNote: Both parts ranked; abiru is almost only used for showers, sunlight and criticism, so this phrase is where learners meet it.

trap: Not tomodachi o tsukuru: 'make friends with X' is X to tomodachi ni naru, while tomodachi ga dekiru means gaining friends in general.
why: The only one of the two that takes a person, and it's very frequent.

trap: English 'call me' leads to yobu (summon); a phone call is denwa (o) kureru or denwa shite.
why: Everyday request: denwa kurete / denwa chodai.
Top hobby set in small talk.

trap: English 'be interested' is an adjective; Japanese uses the noun kyoumi with motsu or ga aru, and ni for the topic.
why: Standard way to talk about interests.

kana: えいきょうをあたえる
trap: English 'affect' is one verb; Japanese uses the noun eikyou with ataeru (or ukeru for being affected).
why: The fixed verb for influence; semi-formal.

trap: English 'oneself' leads to jibun o mamoru; the set uses mi.
why: Fixed set for self-protection, also in disaster safety talk.

trap: There is no verb for this: 'we get along' is naka ga ii (the relationship is good). This naka is not naka 'inside'.
why: Describes friends, family and coworkers. Its opposite naka ga warui comes free, and it overlaps with the describing domain.
freqNote: 仲 #1305; kana なか #4046 mixes in 中 'inside'. ii: kana いい #24.

why: Constant topic for a learner in Japan.

trap: There is no verb for 'thank': you 'say thanks' with orei o iu (orei also means a thank-you gift).
why: For reporting thanks (orei iwanakya) rather than saying arigatou. rei o iu is the stiffer variant.
freqNote: お礼 #968; bare 礼 #3119, so the o- form is the spoken headword.

trap: Not just renraku dekinai: 'I can't reach him' is renraku ga torenai (or renraku ga tsukanai).
why: Used when worrying about someone or chasing a reply (zenzen renraku torenai). It is the intransitive partner of the pool's renraku o toru.
freqNote: Phrase entries 連絡が取れる #4561 and 連絡がつく #7918. 取れる #631 counts all senses.

trap: English 'I didn't mean it' leads to imi; Japanese says warugi wa nakatta.
why: Common apology and excuse phrase, 93% share.

english: be good at one's job, be capable
trap: Not shigoto ga jouzu: being good at your job is dekiru, usually shigoto ga dekiru hito.
why: The most common praise for a coworker. English 'good at' leads to jouzu, which is wrong here.

trap: Not ame ga ochiru, and English 'it rains' has no Japanese verb of its own: rain and snow fall with furu.
why: The core weather sentence (ame futteru, ame furisou). English pushes learners toward both ochiru and a made-up verb 'to rain'.
freqNote: The whole phrase 雨が降る is also listed as a set expression at #5450. Kana あめ also covers 飴 (candy), and ふる covers 振る (wave/dump), so the kanji ranks are used.

trap: English 'get caught in the rain' points to tsukamaru. Japanese uses the suffering passive of furu with ni: ame ni furareta.
why: The very common way to say you got rained on (kinou ame ni furarechatta). It can't be guessed, and it uses the passive pattern the learner already has.
freqNote: The passive 降られる is not a dictionary form, so it isn't in the list. The rank is for the base 降る.

trap: Not shigoto o deru or a 'get off' verb: you say the work itself ends, shigoto ga owaru (shigoto owatta? nanji ni owaru?).
why: A daily question in making plans. English 'get off / finish work' suggests a person-as-subject verb; Japanese makes the work the subject.
freqNote: 仕事 #134, 終わる #190. Same frame: gakkou ga owaru, jugyou ga owaru.

trap: Not ki o tsukeru (be careful): tsukau means fussing over others, as in ki o tsukawanaide (don't go to any trouble).
why: Comes up constantly between hosts and guests. It nearly rhymes with the versatility item ki o tsukeru, so the two must be learned apart.
freqNote: 気 #315; 使う #171 is the general spelling, but this sense is usually written 遣う (#6992).

trap: Not jikan o tsukau or sugosu: putting time into something is kakeru (jikan kakete tsukutta), the transitive of kakaru.
why: The transitive partner of jikan ga kakaru. okane o kakeru works the same way and is folded in here.
freqNote: かける #244 is the kana form across every sense (call, sit, wear glasses); 掛ける #2742.

trap: Not tsukau, which treats time as a resource you use up. Spending time with people, or spending a weekend, is sugosu (shuumatsu dou sugoshita?).
why: Used in small talk about holidays and weekends, and for "had a good time" (tanoshii jikan o sugoshita). English "spend" leads to tsukau.

trap: Particle is ni, not o; noru covers every vehicle.
why: Guessable vehicle set; boats less frequent than trains.

trap: English 'answer' leads to kotae, which is an answer to a question; replying to a person, message or call is henji (o) suru.
why: Covers message replies (henji shite, henji ga konai). The useful lesson is the henji/kotae split; it overlaps with the media domain.

trap: English 'leave' leads to saru or hanareru; leaving a place is o deru.
why: Everyday movement set with the o-of-departure.

trap: Not meiwaku o suru or tsukuru: you 'hang' trouble on people with kakeru (meiwaku kakete gomen).
why: The core apology frame; the same kakeru also carries shinpai o kakeru and koe o kakeru, so the set is cheap to learn.
freqNote: kakeru: kana かける #244 pools every sense (call, put on, spend); 掛ける #2742 listed separately.

english: blame (someone else), pin it on someone
trap: Not semeru, which means 'criticise, attack'. To pin the blame on someone is X no sei ni suru.
why: 'Hito no sei ni suru na' and 'ore no sei ni shinaide' are stock lines in any argument, and X no sei da ('it's X's fault') comes with them. The dictionary verb for 'blame' (semeru) is too strong, and a learner has no way to guess the noun + ni suru shape.
freqNote: せい #400 is the hiragana 'fault' noun. That count also includes X no sei de ('because of X'). There is no phrase count.

trap: Not joudan o tsukuru or suru: a joke is 'said', and joudan da yo means just kidding.
why: A banter staple. joudan desho? and joudan da yo are the most frequent chunks, and both sit next to uso! as replies.

trap: Not byouki o toru or byouki ga dekiru: illness is something you 'become' (ni naru).
why: The general frame for getting ill. The pool has only specific illnesses and symptoms.
freqNote: Phrase entry 病気になる at #4880.

trap: Not kusuri o toru: medicine is 'drunk', kusuri o nomu, even pills.
why: English 'take' leads straight to toru; nomu covers pills, syrup and powder alike.
freqNote: 薬 #1283; 飲む #229. No phrase entry.

trap: Not 'kare wa takai' or 'nagai': height is se ga takai, and takai alone sounds like 'expensive'.
why: The most-used way to describe someone. English 'tall' has no one-word Japanese equivalent.
freqNote: 背 (せ) #5388, plus 背 (せい) #39147 for the sei ga takai variant. The bare noun ranks low because se almost only occurs inside this phrase.

english: hear a sound, there's a noise
trap: Not oto o kiku: you don't 'hear a noise', the noise 'does' it: nanka oto ga shita.
why: The normal way to report a sound (nanka hen na oto shinai?); English pushes learners to kiku with the speaker as subject.
freqNote: Expression 音がする #5813.

trap: Not himitsu o motsu or tamotsu. You keep a secret with mamoru (protect), the same verb as yakusoku o mamoru.
why: Typical uses are himitsu mamotte ne and zettai mamoru kara. It complements naisho ni suru (make something a secret) in the pool: this one is keeping it, that one is creating it.
Strong, high-share everyday set (lifts, machines, buses).

trap: English 'wear' is one verb; Japanese splits it: kiru for suits and tops, haku for trousers and shoes.
why: Typical clothing set for work life.
Common gossip set, high share.

trap: English 'it smells good' sends learners looking for a verb; Japanese says ii nioi (ga suru).
why: Said constantly about food, people, places.
Standard set at work and in apologies.

trap: Not kakeru (hang): denwa o kakeru makes the call; ending it is kiru ('cut').
why: Every call ends with ja, kiru ne, plus 'she hung up on me' (kirareta); it sounds like kiru 'wear' from the clothes list.
Essential daily phrase.
Daily routine staple.
Guessable but constant (ato de meeru okuru ne); casual speech often shortens it to meeru suru or rain suru.
freqNote: verbRank 送る also counts seeing someone off and sending parcels.

english: make a hole; get (one's ears) pierced
trap: Not ana o tsukuru. Making a hole is akeru, and getting your ears pierced is piasu (no ana) o akeru.
why: The transitive half of ana ga aku, which is in the pool. Its everyday use is piercings (piasu aketa, mimi ni ana aketai).
freqNote: 穴 #2765; 開ける #480 (空ける #3596 is another spelling of the same verb); ピアス #13111

trap: English 'in the sky' leads to de; moving through the sky takes o.
why: Strong typical set; birds, planes, dreams.

trap: Not michi o nakusu or michi o ushinau: getting lost is michi ni mayou ('stray on the road'), or casually just mayotta.
why: The core travel-trouble phrase; English 'lose' leads to nakusu (lose an object).
freqNote: Phrase not counted. mayou alone also means 'can't decide', which raises its rank.

trap: Not onegai o kiku, which means agreeing to a favour: asking one opens with onegai ga aru n da kedo.
why: The standard opener before a request. It sets the asking side (ga aru) against granting (o kiku); tanomi ga aru is the casual twin.
freqNote: お願い #258 mostly counts onegai (shimasu) as 'please'; aru #21.

trap: English 'follow' suggests tsuite iku; instructions take shitagau with ni.
why: Standard work and school set for obeying directions.

trap: English 'too late' leads to osoi; for something past saving it is teokure.
why: Teokure nearly always appears with ni naru, e.g. before an illness gets worse.

english: have something to do, have an errand
trap: Learners say suru koto ga aru or just isogashii. The standard vague excuse is chotto youji ga atte.
why: The default polite way to turn down an invitation or leave early. Learners need it ready to say.

trap: 'I can't explain it' is setsumei ga tsukanai, not a form of setsumei suru.
why: Common way to say something does or doesn't make sense.

trap: Not benri: a time that suits someone is tsugou ga ii (benri is for tools and places). The opposite is tsugou ga warui, 'can't make it'.
why: The tactful way to ask when someone is free (itsu ga tsugou ii?) and to decline (sono hi wa chotto tsugou ga warukute). tsugou ga warui is folded in here.
freqNote: いい #24 is the spoken form; 良い #1474.

trap: 'Tell me your name' uses oshieru, not iu.
why: Everyday request when meeting someone; oshieru for giving info.
Everyday way to say you, a machine or things are going well.

trap: 'Get a chance' is kikai ga aru, not kikai o morau.
why: Fixed in 'kikai ga areba' (if I get the chance).

trap: 'I have a bad feeling about this' is iya na yokan ga suru, not warui kimochi ga aru, which sounds like nausea.
why: Fixed chunk heard in drama and daily talk; English 'have a feeling' leads away from yokan and suru.
freqNote: No expression entry; noun 予感 #2760, 嫌 #304. Almost always with iya na in front.

trap: 'Do my best' is zenryoku o tsukusu or ganbaru, never suru.
why: Strong fixed pairing used in work and sports talk.

trap: 'Pack your things' is matomeru (gather up), not tsumeru.
why: Typical set for packing to leave or move.

trap: 'Get out of the car' is oriru (step down), not deru.
why: Everyday vehicle set; oriru for leaving any vehicle.

trap: English 'close' suggests shimeru; mouths and eyes take tojiru.
why: Literal body action; tojiru is the verb for mouths and eyes.

trap: 'Make a mistake' is not tsukuru; say machigai o okasu or just machigaeru.
why: Standard noun pairing for mistakes; casual speech often uses machigaeru.

trap: Not jikan ga tooru: time passing is tatsu (jikan tatsu no hayai ne), a different tatsu from 'stand'.
why: A common remark (mou ichinen tatta), and English 'pass' leads to tooru. sugiru is possible but more formal.
freqNote: 経つ #3603 is the time sense. The kana たつ is dominated by 立つ #610.

english: speak up; say it out loud
trap: English 'speak up' pushes toward hanasu. Japanese 'puts out the voice': motto koe dashite.
why: Classes, karaoke and sport. Also an audio-first learner's own practice instruction ('say it out loud').
Fixed emergency set; inflated by film but real.

trap: 'I can't breathe' is iki ga dekinai; there is no single verb 'breathe'.
why: Common body set, mostly as iki ga dekinai.
Guessable (sing = utau) and usually said as utau alone (karaoke de utau). It is kept only because the domain brief named it, so the selector can rule on it.

trap: 'I can't imagine' is usually souzou mo tsukanai, not souzou dekinai.
why: Fixed set for being able or unable to picture something.

trap: 'Ask for opinions' uses kiku, not tanomu.
why: Typical meeting and discussion set.
Basic body action set.

trap: 'I have a favor to ask' is tanomi ga aru, not a form of kiku.
why: Everyday opener: tanomi ga aru n da kedo.

trap: 'Take the bus' is noru with ni, not toru.
why: Core transport set.

trap: 'Confident' is an adjective in English, but Japanese has confidence: jishin aru / jishin nai. (Jishin is also 'earthquake', as in jishin ga okiru.)
why: 'Jishin nai' is constant before tests, interviews and dates.
freqNote: 自信 #839 is its own entry, separate from 地震 #7156.

trap: 'Make trouble' is okosu (raise), not tsukuru.
why: Typical set for someone causing problems at school or work.
Daily phone and chat set.

trap: Not e o hiku (that is sen o hiku, draw a line) or e o nuru (paint a wall): drawn or painted, a picture takes kaku.
why: Covers both drawing and painting. It sounds like kaku (write), so it is best heard as one unit with e.
freqNote: 描く is listed under the reading えがく (#1092) and the tokenizer does not split off its かく reading. 書く (かく, write) #233 is the homophone.

why: Strong pairing, a bit formal; casual speech says junbi ga dekita.

trap: Also means to apologize or ask humbly, not just a physical bow.
why: Everyday bowing and apologizing set.

trap: Not namae o ageru: you 'attach' a name (namae o tsukeru).
why: Used for babies, pets and files (neko ni nan te namae tsuketa?).
freqNote: Phrase entries 名前を付ける #14728 and 名前をつける #20826. verbRank is 付ける.

english: be worthwhile, do you good (advice, a book, an experience)
trap: Not yaku ni tatsu for advice or experiences: a tool is yaku ni tatsu, but something that does you good is tame ni naru.
why: Used to praise a talk, book or piece of advice. Kept apart from yaku ni tatsu and from the grammar pattern tame ni (in order to).
freqNote: ため at #203 is mostly the grammar word (tame ni). The phrase ためになる is its own row at #4007.

why: Everyday set for something going wrong.

trap: 'Make way' is akeru (clear), not tsukuru.
why: Fixed set for clearing a path in crowds or traffic.

trap: 'This medicine works' is kouka ga aru or kiku, not hataraku.
why: Typical set for medicine, diets and methods working.
Core daily set.
Everyday set for attending or heading to college.

trap: 'Live a happy life' is jinsei o okuru (send), not ikiru with jinsei.
why: Fixed pairing for describing the life someone leads.
Daily media set; also nyuusu de miru (saw it on the news).

trap: 'Can you hear me?' is kikoeru?, not kiku: kiku is deliberate listening, and the thing heard takes ga.
why: Phone and video-call staple (kikoeru? kikoenai); the kiku/kikoeru split is invisible to English speakers.
freqNote: No expression entry for 音が聞こえる; noun and verb ranked separately. The same frame takes koe (koe ga kikoenai).

trap: Not keikaku o tsukuru: plans are tateru, 'stand up'. yotei o tateru works the same way.
why: How people talk about planning a trip or a budget, where English 'make' leads to tsukuru. yotei o tateru is folded in here.
freqNote: The rank is for 計画; yotei (予定 #843) also takes tateru.

trap: 'I don't remember that' is often kioku ga nai, not only oboete inai.
why: Common set, also as kioku ni nai (I don't recall).

trap: 'Look around' needs mawari (surroundings) as the object; there is no 'around' particle.
why: Everyday perceiving set, literal and 'consider others'.

trap: 'I have no money' is okane ga nai, not motte inai.
why: Very common everyday complaint.
Literal body set, heard at the dentist and doctor.
Fixed noun + adjective for describing people's manners.

trap: yakusoku isn't only 'promise': it means any arrangement to meet, so kyou wa yakusoku ga aru = I'm meeting someone today.
why: Goes beside yotei ga aru: yakusoku is plans with a person, yotei is anything scheduled. Learners only know yakusoku as 'promise'.

trap: 'Take responsibility' is sekinin o motsu or toru, not ukeru.
why: Typical work and family set.

trap: 'Leave a message' is nokosu, not deru or saru.
why: Phone and voicemail set.

kana: びょういんにつれていく
trap: 'Take someone' is tsurete iku; motte iku is only for things.
why: Everyday set for illness and family care.
Natural literal set; not a daily activity.

trap: English 'go up and talk to' leads to hanasu; approaching someone is koe o kakeru (koe o dasu just means make a sound).
why: Starting contact and 'give me a shout' (nanka attara koe kakete); also used for being approached or hit on. Same kakeru as meiwaku o kakeru.
freqNote: kakeru: kana かける #244 pools all senses.

trap: 'Bleed' is one verb in English; Japanese says blood comes out, chi ga deru (chi deteru yo).
why: The only everyday way to say 'bleed'; it joins the ga deru symptom set.
freqNote: 血 #1261; 出る #81. No phrase entry.

trap: 'I'm not sure I can' is jishin ga nai, not wakaranai.
why: Very common way to express self-doubt.

trap: 'I have no experience' is keiken ga nai, not motte inai.
why: Common set for jobs and trying new things.

trap: Not yotei o motsu: having plans is aru (yotei aru kara = I've got plans).
why: The standard reason for turning down an invitation, and the opener for asking about one (konshuumatsu yotei aru?).

english: be off, not feel right; (a machine) act up
trap: Not just genki ja nai: choushi ga warui covers being off form, a bad stomach, or a phone or PC that's acting up.
why: One phrase for 'something's off' with your body, your form or a device (pasokon no choushi ga warui). Choushi ga ii is the positive. It is broader than the pool's guai ga warui.
freqNote: Phrase entries 調子が悪い #8863 and 調子がいい #16780.

ja: お悔やみを申し上げる
kana: おくやみをもうしあげる
trap: 'I'm sorry for your loss' is okuyami moushiagemasu, not sumimasen.
why: Fixed humble formula at funerals and on hearing of a death.

trap: Not kekka o morau: results 'come out' (kekka ga deru). Getting good results yourself is kekka o dasu.
why: Used for exams, medical tests and job applications (kensa no kekka ga deta).
freqNote: 結果を出す (produce results) is a phrase entry at #8074.

why: Everyday drink order and small talk.

trap: "Are you hurt?" is kega wa nai?, not itai desu ka.
why: What you ask after someone falls or bumps into something.
Standard opener: chotto ohanashi ga arun desu ga.

trap: "Get some fresh air" is soto no kuuki o suu; suu (inhale) does the work of 'breathe'.
why: Common when stepping outside or in nature.

trap: "Give me your number" is bangou oshiete (teach/tell), not ageru or kudasai.
why: Swapping numbers and contacts is everyday.

trap: No adjective for 'confident'; say jishin o motsu or jishin ga aru.
why: Common encouragement: jishin o motte!

trap: There is no English equivalent: thanks for someone's help is osewa ni narimashita (you 'became' the one cared for), not sewa o shite kurete arigatou.
why: The set thanks to hosts, teachers and colleagues (osewa ni natte imasu). Mostly said in the polite form, and casual osewa ni natta also exists.
freqNote: お世話 #3633 (bare 世話 #2302); naru: kana なる #29.

trap: There's no verb for 'cheer up': you say genki dashite ('put out your energy').
why: The standard thing to say to comfort someone. Genki ga deru (feel better, get a lift) is its intransitive partner, and the pool already has genki ga nai.
freqNote: Phrase entries 元気が出る #8964 and 元気を出す #13529.

why: hitokoto itte kureba / hitokoto mo iwanai are everyday.

trap: 'Take responsibility' is sekinin o toru; ou means carry it on your back.
why: Formal work/news set; real but not daily chat.

english: step away (from one's desk or the table)
trap: Not seki o deru. Stepping away for a moment is hazusu ('remove'), as in the phone line tadaima seki o hazushite orimasu.
why: The standard way to excuse yourself from a meeting or table (chotto seki hazushimasu), and what you hear when you phone an office.

trap: 'Panic' is a verb in English, so learners say panikku suru; natives say panikku ni naru.
why: Common for any flustered moment.
Work-life staple; yasumi o toru is the casual twin.

trap: No 'look' verb: 'looks familiar' is mioboe ga aru (have a memory of seeing).
why: Said about faces, places and objects.

trap: 'Sit on' takes ni, not ue ni or de.
why: Basic daily action.

english: be shocked, be hurt (by news, a remark)
trap: Not shokku suru: you receive a shock, so shokku uketa. Shokku datta is the other natural way.
why: Reacting to bad news, a breakup or a harsh comment.

trap: 'Smell this!' is kaide mite: actively smelling is kagu, not nioi o suru or kiku.
why: Active partner to nioi ga suru, so the two smell verbs are learned together. Reserve.
freqNote: No expression entry; nounRank is the kana spelling におい (匂い #2171).

trap: 'Have a party' is suru (or hiraku), not motsu.
why: Birthday and home parties are everyday talk.

trap: 'Get lost' is maigo ni naru (become a lost child), even for adults.
why: Common for kids, stations and new neighbourhoods.

trap: 'Rely on' is not shinrai suru (trust); it is tayori ni suru.
why: tayori ni shiteru yo is warm everyday praise.
Common drink order and dinner talk.

trap: Not kaze o toru or tsukamu: you 'pull' a cold, kaze o hiku (kaze hiichatta).
why: The textbook unguessable pairing and the everyday excuse: kaze hiita.
freqNote: 風邪 #2666 (kana かぜ #1532 is mostly 風 'wind'); 引く #1039. Phrase entries also exist: 風邪ひく #3998, 風邪をひく #10899, 風邪を引く #27734. These are partial counts because the tokenizer usually splits; the particle-dropped form ranking highest supports the casual drop.

trap: The pairing itself is guessable; the risk is transitivity, mado o akeru (you do it) vs mado ga aiteru (it's open).
why: The transitive half of the aku/akeru pair. It's frequent ('mado akete ii?') but low-trap, so it's mainly here to keep the pair complete.

trap: 'Have a heart attack' uses okosu (set off), not motsu.
why: Standard medical set; film over-counts it.

trap: English passive leads to eikyou sareru; natives say eikyou o ukeru (receive influence).
why: Common when talking about idols, parents, hobbies.

trap: Not fuku o toru: every garment comes off with nugu, whichever verb put it on.
why: Covers uwagi nuide ii? and atsui kara nuida. It is the clothes half of nugu, a reserve if kutsu o nugu already carries the verb.
freqNote: Ranks are for 服 #1051 and 脱ぐ #2074. Pairing commonness is judged.

why: Core money set.
Strongest food pair in the corpus; daily talk about drinking.
Real set, though jikka ni kaeru is the everyday version.

trap: Not kakkou o kiru: 'dressed like that' is sonna kakkou shite. Kakkou means outfit or look.
why: Comments on outfits: 'sono kakkou de iku no?', 'kawaii kakkou shiteru'.

trap: 'Take an interest' uses motsu (hold), not toru.
why: Standard set, a step more formal than kyoumi ga aru.

trap: English 'wave' is one verb; Japanese shakes the hand, te o furu.
why: A plain, literal everyday action with no single-verb equivalent. It sounds the same as the furu of ame ga furu.
freqNote: 手 #259; 振る #1638 (homophone 降る #2179, as in ame ga furu).

english: have a complaint, got a problem
trap: 'Complain' is monku o iu; nanka monku aru? is 'got a problem?'
why: Everyday grumbling and teasing.

trap: Not kirei na tenki or yasashii tenki for 'a beautiful/nice day': good weather is just ii, and bad weather is warui.
why: The default small-talk opener (ii tenki da ne). The trap is low, but the learner says it all the time, and tenki ga warui covers bad weather.
freqNote: いい is #24 (the spelling 良い is #1474). The attributive form ii tenki is used just as often.

trap: Not sumaho o kesu: devices are powered off with dengen o kiru ('cut the power'). Kesu is for lights and TVs.
why: Heard in announcements at cinemas, on planes and in exams, and used when restarting a phone (ichido dengen kitte mite).
freqNote: Phrase entry 電源を切る at #16226.

trap: 'Wear' splits by body part: kiru for dresses and tops, haku for skirts and trousers.
why: Typical clothing pair; dresses less daily than shirts.

trap: 'Any idea where it went?' is kokoroatari aru?, not aidia.
why: Used for lost items and mysteries; detective plots inflate it.

trap: English 'it's locked' has no noun in it, so learners can't guess kagi ga kakatteru. It's the intransitive partner of kagi o kakeru.
why: 'Is it locked?' (kagi kakatteru?) is the half of the lock pair that you hear and have to answer. It also keeps kakaru, 'take time / cost', apart from the lock sense.
freqNote: かかる #385 is the kana entry, shared with jikan ga kakaru and okane ga kakaru. Kanji 掛かる alone is #5316.

trap: There is no phrasal verb for 'make up': it is nakanaori suru ('mending the relationship'), never tsukuru.
why: The second half of kenka o suru, and it shares naka with naka ga ii. This is the weakest reserve.
freqNote: 仲直り #3219; suru #15.

trap: 'Do your best' is not besuto o suru; it is besuto o tsukusu (or ganbaru).
why: Common before exams, matches and interviews.

trap: Not te o motsu: holding hands is 'linking' them with tsunagu, the same verb as netto ni tsunagu.
why: Comes up with children, couples and crowds. English 'hold' gives motsu.
freqNote: Kana つなぐ is #1886 and 繋ぐ is #10471; the higher one is recorded.

trap: 'Are you serious?' is honki de itteru?, not majime (earnest by nature).
why: Constant reaction line in casual talk.

trap: Not raido o ageru: giving a lift uses noseru ('put on board'), the transitive of noru. To ask for one: nosete kureru?
why: Asking for or offering a ride is common. It's the transitive half of the pool's densha ni noru.

trap: Not me o shimeru: shimeru is for doors and windows. Eyes take tsuburu (casual) or tojiru (neutral).
why: Me tsubutte ('close your eyes') is everyday: surprises, eye drops, photos. The pool's open/close items all teach shimeru.
freqNote: Kana つぶる is #8069 and つむる is #42175. 閉じる #3880 also covers books and apps. The phrase also has a figurative 'turn a blind eye' sense, but the literal one comes first.

trap: Not oto o tsukuru: 'make a noise' is oto o tateru ('raise' a sound).
why: Oto tatenaide (don't make noise) comes up in shared homes, at night and with kids.
freqNote: Phrase entry 音を立てる at #18077.

why: Standard way to say keep your hopes up.

trap: Not hazukashii ni naru: making a fool of yourself is haji o kaku, with the same kaku as ase o kaku and ibiki o kaku.
why: The action that goes with hazukashii (minna no mae de haji kaita).
freqNote: verbRank is hiragana かく, the form used for sweat, snoring and shame. Phrase entry 恥をかく at #6752.

english: have time or money to spare; be relaxed about it
trap: English 'can afford' or 'have time to spare' has no single verb here; Japanese uses yoyuu ga aru / nai for time, money and calm.
why: A high-frequency noun with one fixed partner, and it covers 'afford', 'spare' and 'composure'.

trap: 'Raise your voice' tempts ageru; Japanese puts out (dasu) a big voice.
why: Heard constantly: oogoe dasanai de.
Everyday reaction to bad luck.

trap: 'Lead/live a life' uses okuru (send), not michibiku.
why: The standard verb for living a kind of life.

english: drive (someone), offer to take the car
trap: Not unten suru when offering a lift: 'I'll drive' is kuruma dasu yo ('take the car out').
why: How lifts get offered and arranged among friends and family.
Said at every counter and form.

english: be expecting, have a baby on the way
trap: Not kodomo o motsu: 'we're having a baby' is kodomo ga dekita. Kodomo ga iru means you already have children.
why: Life news among friends, and the clearest contrast with the pool's kodomo ga iru.

trap: 'Have courage' is aru/nai, not motsu.
why: Common way to admit you can't bring yourself to.

trap: 'Throw/have a party': Japanese opens (hiraku) it.
why: The set verb for hosting any party.

trap: 'Lose' is ushinau here, not nakusu.
why: The standard phrase for passing out.

trap: 'Get treatment' tempts morau; Japanese receives it with ukeru.
why: Doctor and dentist talk.

trap: 'Take action' is not toru; Japanese raises (okosu) it.
why: Fixed pairing for actually doing something.

english: work up the courage, be brave
trap: Not yuuki o motsu or mitsukeru: you 'put out' courage, yuuki o dasu (yuuki dashite itta), as in genki o dasu.
why: Used for confessing, asking someone out or speaking up. It pairs with genki o dasu, which is already in the pool.

trap: Not yakusoku o kowasu: breaking a promise is yaburu, 'tear'.
why: The opposite of yakusoku o mamoru, mostly heard as a complaint (yakusoku yabutta jan).

trap: Not kutsu o kiru: anything on the feet or legs takes haku.
why: Said at every doorway (kutsu haite, hayaku). The haku/kiru split is the core of the wearing system.
freqNote: Rank is for 履く #3474. Kana はく is mostly 吐く 'throw up' (#1739), so the kana count was not used. Pairing commonness is judged.

kana: じょうほうをあつめる
why: Standard pairing at work, school and trip planning.

trap: 'I'm not free/busy' maps to tsugou ga warui, not hima ja nai.
why: The polite everyday way to say a time doesn't work.
Iroiro jijou ga atte: everyday excuse.

trap: Sounds like naru 'become', but this is 鳴る 'ring': keitai natteru yo = 'your phone's ringing'.
why: A short household alert (keitai natteru yo!); the same verb works for alarms and doorbells, which the home list can reuse.
freqNote: verbRank is 鳴る only; kana なる (#29) is almost all 'become'.

trap: 'Distracted/distracting' has no adjective in Japanese: ki ga chiru (urusakute ki ga chiru); learners only manage shuuchuu dekinai.
why: The plain way to say you can't focus (borderline rule: IN); useful at home, work and study.
freqNote: Expression 気が散る #11908.

english: be reliable, dependable (someone you can count on)
trap: There is no plain adjective for 'reliable': a dependable person 'becomes a support', tayori ni naru. Tayori ni suru means 'rely on someone'.
why: Common praise for friends, partners and colleagues ('tayori ni naru ne', 'tayori ni shiteru yo'). English 'reliable' or 'count on' leads a learner to shinrai or kazoeru. It is literal, not a body-part or metaphor idiom, like seikaku ga ii in the pool.
freqNote: 頼り #4701 is the 'reliance' word. The homophone 便り ('news, letter') is counted separately (#11999).

trap: 'Have a meeting' is kaigi ga aru, not motsu.
why: Daily office schedule talk.
Basic music talk.

trap: 'Have a baby' is umu (give birth), not motsu.
why: Family-life topic.

trap: 'Have a headache' is zutsuu ga suru, not motsu or aru.
why: Core symptom phrase.

trap: 'Wear' splits by body part: kiru for tops, haku for bottoms.
why: Daily dressing.

trap: 'Wear' a mask is tsukeru (or suru), not kiru.
why: Masks are routine in Japan; corpus undercounts.

trap: 'Make a mistake' is not tsukuru; okasu, or casually misu suru.
why: Set verb for mistakes; casual speech prefers misu suru.

trap: Toggles take on ni suru; tsukeru is for lights and TVs.
why: Everyday phrase for switching phone and app settings on.

trap: oboeru is memorise/keep in mind; recalling on the spot is omoidasu.
why: Meeting people constantly.

trap: Sit takes ni (into the seat), not o.
why: Trains, restaurants, classrooms.
Phone-photo sharing is constant.
Kaado tsukaemasu ka at every register.

trap: 'Fasten/buckle' is shimeru (tighten), not tsukeru.
why: Belts and seatbelts (shiitoberuto o shimete).
Classic daily routine pairing.

trap: 'Morning comes' is asa ni naru (becomes), not kuru.
why: Asa ni nattara: everyday time talk.

trap: 'Sweat' is a verb in English; Japanese 'scratches out' sweat: ase o kaku, not ase suru.
why: Daily summer and gym talk (ase kaichatta), and the verb can't be guessed.
freqNote: 汗 #2650. Verb rank is kana かく #11889, the spelling used here, which mixes 掻く with kana-written 書く/描く. Kanji 掻く is #51963. Phrase entry 汗をかく #13368.

trap: Not te ga yakeru or moeru: burning your skin is the noun yakedo + suru, like kega o suru.
why: The kitchen counterpart of kega o suru. The brief allows noun + suru when the pairing can't be guessed, and here 'burn' leads to yakeru or moeru.
freqNote: Kana やけど is #5364 and kanji 火傷 is #20901; the higher one is recorded.

why: Rough everyday 'eat'; polite version is gohan o tabemasu.

trap: 'Turn around' is muku (face), not mawaru (spin).
why: Basic body direction phrase.

trap: Not boushi o kiru: anything pulled over the head (hat, cap, helmet, hood) takes kaburu.
why: Hats, caps and helmets are everyday, and the partner verb can't be guessed.
freqNote: Rank is for kana かぶる #1926, the usual spelling; the kanji 被る is #7902. The kana count also includes the casual 'clash/overlap' sense (yotei ga kaburu), so it overstates the wearing sense.

english: have a baby (a child is born)
trap: Not kodomo o motsu or kodomo ga aru: 'we had a baby' is kodomo ga umareta (or akachan ga umareta), with the child as subject.
why: Core life news. English 'have' gives aru or motsu. It pairs with the pool's kodomo ga iru.
freqNote: 赤ちゃん #2204 is the common alternative noun.

trap: 'Ask out' is sasou with ni, not kiku (ask a question).
why: Standard way to say you invited someone on a date.

trap: Settings and toggles take ofu ni suru; kesu is for lights and TVs.
why: Everyday phrase for toggling sound, Wi-Fi, notifications off.

trap: No single verb for 'be ruined'; it is dainashi ni naru (dainashi ni suru to ruin it).
why: Fixed set for plans, clothes or a day getting spoiled.

trap: Not jiko o shita or jiko o motta: being in an accident is jiko ni au, the same sound as meeting someone. A driver who causes one jiko o okosu.
why: English 'have' or 'get in' gives no clue. The same ni au frame gives ame ni au (get caught in the rain).
freqNote: Phrase not counted. 遭う is ranked apart from 会う (#110), though they sound the same.

trap: There's no single verb for 'feed': you give the food (esa o yaru or ageru), with the same yaru as mizu o yaru.
why: Comes up with pets and kids, and pairs with the pool's mizu o yaru. Many speakers now say esa o ageru.
freqNote: やる #45 is mostly the 'do' sense. This 'give' sense is a small share of it.

trap: With tabi the verb is deru (go out), not iku.
why: Typical set for heading off on a trip.

trap: 'Take pride' uses motsu (hold), not toru.
why: Standard set for pride in work or self.
Fully guessable and very common (ongaku kiki nagara); it earns a place only as the listener's side of ongaku o kakeru.
freqNote: verbRank is 聞く (also hear/ask); 聴く is #1930.

trap: 'I heard someone's voice' is koe ga shita (suru) when it just reaches you, not koe o kiita.
why: Completes the X ga suru perception set with oto and nioi (tonari kara koe ga suru).
freqNote: Expression 声がする #10808.

trap: Not kibun ga warui, which means feeling sick: a bad mood is kigen ga warui. A good mood is kigen ga ii or gokigen.
why: It's what learners mean when they say kibun ga warui and get misread as feeling ill. The pool already has kibun ga warui, so the two should be taught as a pair.
freqNote: Same sound as kigen 期限 'deadline' (see kigen ga kireru).

why: Core everyday set for travel plans.

trap: English 'taste' is a verb; Japanese says the flavour 'does': ichigo no aji ga suru, not ichigo o ajiwau.
why: The everyday way to describe any flavour (hen na aji suru, nanimo aji shinai); same shape as oto ga suru / nioi ga suru in senses.
freqNote: Ranks are for the parts only; suru's #15 covers every use of suru. How often the phrase itself comes up is my judgement.

trap: Not yume ga hontou ni naru: dreams are 'granted' (kanau).
why: Common in talk about goals, weddings and travel. The pool's yume o miru is the sleeping sense.
freqNote: verbRank is 叶う. Hiragana かなう (#935) also counts kanawanai ('no match for').

ja: トラブルに巻き込まれる
kana: トラブルにまきこまれる
trap: 'Get into trouble' is the passive makikomareru with ni, not hairu.
why: Typical set for being dragged into a problem.

trap: 'Next to' is tonari; tsugi means next in order.
why: Everyday set on trains, in class, at dinner.

trap: 'Have tea' is nomu; motsu would mean holding it.
why: Core daily-life set.
Everyday media set.

trap: 'In bed' takes de (place of action), not naka.
why: Everyday home routine set.

trap: Dreams are seen (miru), not had (motsu).
why: Standard set for bad dreams.

trap: 'I feel well' is guai ga ii, not kanjiru.
why: Everyday health check set (pair of guai ga warui).

trap: 'Wear' splits by body part; uniforms take kiru.
why: School and work uniforms are everyday life in Japan.
Natural set for farewells.

trap: Rules are broken with yaburu (tear), not kowasu.
why: Typical set for school and work rules.

trap: 'Check email' is usually just miru.
why: Everyday phone and inbox set.

trap: Not takushii o kakeru: kakeru goes with denwa (the phone call), while the taxi you summon is yobu.
why: The easy half of the taxi set (hirou to hail one, yobu to call one); a reserve.
freqNote: Phrase not counted.

trap: Intransitive shimaru (it closes) vs transitive shimeru (close it).
why: Daily set, heard in every train announcement.
Fixed pairing for the distant past.

trap: Screams are raised (ageru), not dasu.
why: Fixed set; also used for a body 'screaming' from strain.
Everyday complaint about messages or a knock unanswered.

trap: Not eru, and usually not morau: 'I got a message' is meeru kita ('a message came').
why: The message is the subject in every channel: rain kita, denwa ga kita, henji ga konai (no reply yet), renraku ga kuru.

english: get a haircut, cut one's hair
trap: Not kami o kitte morau or a 'haircut' noun: Japanese says kami kitta even when a hairdresser did the cutting.
why: Kami kitta? is the standard way to notice someone's new look, and English 'get a haircut' pushes learners to the -te morau form.
freqNote: 10-list-nouns #14 kami means 'paper' (a homophone), so it isn't cross-referenced.

trap: 'Put pressure' is kakeru, not oku.
why: Strong fixed set at work and in relationships.

english: be informative; learn a lot (from it)
trap: Not benkyou shita: 'that's really useful to know' is benkyou ni naru (benkyou ni narimashita), and nobody is studying.
why: One of the most common polite reactions when someone explains something. Learners reach for wakarimashita or benkyou shimashita instead.
freqNote: The whole phrase 勉強になる has its own entry in the drama list at #4175.

trap: Not koe ga takai, which means high-pitched, and not just urusai: a loud voice is ookii (big).
why: A frequent remark about people, and the ookii/takai split for voices is a real confusion.
freqNote: 声 #327; 大きい #536. Koe ga chiisai (quiet voice) is the everyday opposite.

trap: 'Flush' has no Japanese verb of its own: you make the water flow, as in toire no mizu nagashite.
why: Household and kids' talk, plus signs in toilets.
Everyday news and web reading set.

trap: 'Carry bags' is motsu; hakobu is moving them somewhere.
why: Everyday offer: nimotsu motsu yo.
Natural seasons talk, like haru ga kuru.

trap: 'Have a phone (on you)' is motte iru, not aru.
why: Everyday: keitai motteru?

trap: Not inu o motsu or inu ga aru: pets are 'kept' (kau, which sounds like 'buy'). You can also say inu ga iru.
why: One of the first questions about someone's life (petto katteru?). The verb sounds the same as 'buy', so learners need to hear the two apart.

trap: 'Make coffee' is ireru, not tsukuru.
why: Daily home routine set.

trap: Consciousness returns (modoru) on its own; there is no 'regain' verb.
why: Standard set for waking after fainting or surgery.
Typical set for turning furniture, a screen, or yourself.

trap: Quoted words take to: noo to iu.
why: Set phrase, often noo to ienai (can't say no).

trap: 'Have plans' is yotei ga aru, not motsu.
why: Everyday when making plans: kyou yotei nai?
Shopping lists, to-do lists; plain everyday set.

trap: Not kao ga aoi or kao ga shiroi: 'you look pale' is kaoiro ga warui (your complexion is bad).
why: Said to anyone who looks ill (kaoiro warui yo, daijoubu?). Going through 'pale' gives aoi or shiroi, which sound wrong here.
freqNote: Phrase entry 顔色が悪い is in the drama list at #13422.

why: Daily-routine staple; asa nanji ni okiru?

trap: 'Break' suggests kowasu; rules and promises are yaburu (tear).
why: Common at school, home and games; pairs with ruuru o mamoru.

trap: English says 'I start early'; Japanese makes the morning the subject.
why: Ashita asa hayai kara: everyday excuse to leave or sleep early.

trap: English 'slow down' has no noun; Japanese drops (otosu) the speed.
why: Driving and cycling staple; strong association.

trap: 'Save' suggests setsuyaku or tameru; effort is cut out with habuku.
why: Tema ga habuketa: common about shortcuts at home and work.

trap: No English verb matches: the day 'closes', hi ga kureru (casually kuraku naru). This kureru is unrelated to kureru 'give me'.
why: Common in 'hi ga kureru mae ni kaerou'. Nothing in English points to it, and it has to be kept apart from kureru 'give'.
freqNote: The phrase 日が暮れる is listed as a set expression at #7770, which ranks higher than the bare verb 暮れる (#14744). 日 #209 mixes the 'day' and 'sun' senses. Kana くれる (#565) is mostly 'give'.

trap: On the stove you 'put out the fire' (hi keshita?), not gasu o shimeru. Turning it on is hi o tsukeru.
why: Cooking and leaving the house: 'hi keshita kke?'

english: hear from someone (they get in touch)
trap: Not X kara kiku, which means you heard some news from X. "Did he get in touch?" is renraku kita?
why: Comes up constantly when making plans or dating (mada renraku konai, renraku kitara oshiete). It is the receiving side of renraku suru in the versatility list.
freqNote: 連絡 #326; 来る #52 counts all coming

trap: English 'I have no idea' tempts aidia ga nai or wakaranai; for 'no idea who or what it could be' Japanese uses kokoroatari ga nai.
why: Standard reply when asked about a missing thing, a strange call or an unexplained bill.

trap: Not a 'have' sentence: the head hurts, atama ga itai; zutsuu is the written word.
why: Body part + ga itai is the pattern for every pain, and head is the most said.
freqNote: 頭 #375; 痛い #336; phrase entry 頭が痛い #8807. That count is partial and includes the figurative 'it's a headache' sense.

trap: Keep it apart from shigoto o sagasu (look for one) and shigoto ga mitsukaru (one turns up): mitsukeru is the transitive 'find'.
why: The transitive half of a pair the pool has only one side of.

trap: 'Start' suggests hajimeru; engines are kakeru.
why: Everyday driving set with a non-obvious verb.
Everyday home routine; in casual talk people often say bangohan (o) tsukuru, with the same verb.

trap: 'Miss' has no single verb; chances are nogasu, trains noriokureru.
why: Strong set; chansu o nogasu is the casual twin.

trap: English says 'I can't feel'; Japanese says there is no sensation.
why: Cold hands, numb legs, at the doctor's.

trap: Not ha o burashi suru or haku: teeth are migaku'd (polished).
why: Core routine phrase, and English 'brush' gives no route to migaku.
freqNote: 歯磨き #16183 (hamigaki suru) is the competing noun form, worth noting as a partner.

trap: The bridge takes o as the route crossed, not ni.
why: Directions and walks; strong association.

trap: Not ofuro o toru: you 'enter' the bath, so it's ofuro ni hairu.
why: The nightly routine in Japanese homes ('ofuro haitta?'), and its particle and verb both differ from English.
freqNote: お風呂 #1921 (plain 風呂 #2586); 入る #115 counts every sense of hairu.

trap: Not okane o sugosu: money is spent with tsukau, 'use'; sugosu is only for spending time.
why: A common phrase (okane tsukaisugita), and 'spend' sends learners to sugosu.

trap: English 'glad' tempts ureshii; relief that someone is safe is yokatta.
why: What people say after an accident, earthquake or late arrival home; almost always in the past form yokatta.

trap: English 'have guests'; Japanese says the guests come.
why: Home and shop talk; usually okyaku-san ga kuru.
Doctor's checkups and calming down; iki o sutte.

trap: 'Make a fire' suggests tsukuru; fires are okosu (raise).
why: Camping and barbecues; strong set.
Common retort: joudan wa yamete.

trap: Not shujutsu o suru, which is what the surgeon does. The patient 'receives' it: shujutsu o ukeru.
why: Comes up constantly in talk about family health. The same ukeru frame gives kensa o ukeru (get a checkup).
freqNote: Phrase entry 手術を受ける at #9903.

trap: The stairs take o as the route, not ni.
why: Stations and homes; strong association.

trap: Gohan means a meal here, not only rice.
why: Gohan tabeta? is one of the most common daily questions.

trap: Takes ni, not o; ruuru o mamoru is the more casual choice.
why: Strong set, a little formal next to ruuru o mamoru.

trap: No 'live up'; you answer (kotaeru) expectations, with ni.
why: Common about school, sport and work pressure.

trap: Not masuku o kiru: small worn items (mask, watch, scarf, tie) just take suru, as in masuku shiteru. masuku o tsukeru is the announcement register.
why: Masks are routine in Japan (colds, pollen). masuku shiteru and masuku hazushite ii? are everyday phrases.
freqNote: Ranks are for マスク #5039 and する #15. The drama corpus is partly older than 2020, so マスク may rank lower than it is used today. That is a judgement; the rank was not adjusted.

trap: 'Look in' suggests ni; the mirror takes o.
why: Morning routine; kagami mite! when someone has something on their face.

trap: 'Turn' suggests mawaru; at corners it is magaru.
why: Directions and taxis; very strong association.
Choudo ii taimingu: common when someone arrives right on cue.

trap: English 'side with' is a verb; Japanese says 'become an ally'
why: Standard way to say you're on someone's side.

trap: 'make' is not tsukuru; decisions are handed down (kudasu)
why: Set verb for weighty decisions.
Common self-deprecating or critical remark.
Checking whether someone is conscious.

trap: 'play' is not asobu; roles are fulfilled (hatasu)
why: Set verb for roles and duties.

trap: Not popyuraa da: 'popular' is ninki ga aru ('has popularity'), and ninki nai for unpopular.
why: The everyday 'popular' for people, shops and shows. The noun + aru shape is not guessable.
freqNote: 人気 #1303; ある #21. Ninkimono (#5320, 'a popular person') is a related noun, noted only.

trap: No 'dizzy' adjective: dizziness 'does', memai ga suru.
why: Same ga suru frame as samuke and hakike; a set of three learned together.
freqNote: Kana めまい #8617 (kanji 目眩 #67709 is rare); する #15. No phrase entry.

why: Standard phone and office phrase.
Emergency phrase for someone passed out.

trap: Not naisho o mamoru: 'keep it secret' is ni suru, as in kore naisho ni shite ne (himitsu ni suru is the more neutral twin).
why: A high-use request between friends, and it teaches the X ni suru 'make it X' frame.
freqNote: 内緒 #2414; kana ないしょ #4442 counted separately; suru #15.

trap: Not ai kontakuto o suru: eyes 'meet' with au 合う (fit), not au 会う (meet a person).
why: A literal, storytelling staple (me ga atta). It overlaps with the body and senses domains.
freqNote: 目 #216; 合う #563 (会う 'meet' #110 is a different verb).

trap: 'Healthy' sends learners to kenkou. For food and habits Japanese says karada ni ii ('good for the body'), and karada ni warui for the opposite.
why: Part of daily talk about food, sleep and smoking, and it brings karada ni warui with it.
freqNote: Phrase entries 体にいい #11815 and 体に悪い #13606.

trap: Saying thanks is orei o iu; orei o suru means repaying with a gift or favour
why: Common promise to return a favour.

kana: じゅうしょをおしえる
trap: Telling someone an address is oshieru, not iu
why: Everyday request for contact details.

trap: English 'it costs a lot' has no verb to copy: money kakaru, the same verb as time (kekkou kakatta).
why: The usual way to talk about overall costs (a trip, a car), and it uses the same verb as jikan ga kakaru.
freqNote: お金 #422. The casual 金 (kane, #670) sounds rougher. かかる #385 is the kana form across all senses.

trap: Not ocha o tsukuru: tea and coffee are 'put in' (ireru), not made.
why: A daily offer and request (ocha ireru ne, koohii irete). koohii o ireru works the same way. The versatility list's ireru gloss mentions 'make (tea)', and this entry makes the pairing a unit.
freqNote: #222 is 入れる and counts every sense of ireru (put in, include, switch on). The tea-only spelling 淹れる sits at #19863 because of how it is written, not because the phrase is rare.

trap: Not yuki ga ochiru: snow falls with furu, the same verb as rain.
why: Same verb as ame ga furu. Learning the two together ties furu to things falling from the sky. The selector could fold it into the ame entry.
freqNote: Kana ゆき also covers place names and 行き, so the kanji rank is used.

trap: Not terebi ni iru: a person on TV terebi ni deru ('comes out on'); a programme is terebi de yaru.
why: Celebrity and news talk (kinou terebi ni deteta); it uses the same deru as denwa ni deru.

trap: English 'shave' needs no object, but Japanese names what comes off: hige o soru (face), ashi no ke o soru (legs).
why: A daily grooming action that pairs with hige o hayasu (grow a beard).
freqNote: nounRank is the katakana spelling ヒゲ (#9045); ひげ is #10683 and 髭 #35748.

trap: Money received from someone is morau, not eru.
why: Everyday set for pay, pocket money, gifts.
Typical remark at a window or viewpoint.

trap: 'face' is not mukau here; you look at (miru) reality
why: Common blunt advice: genjitsu o mite.
Typical weather verb for storms.
Set verb for sunrise.

trap: Not kanashii or daun: 'you seem down' is genki nai ne. Genki ja nai sounds more like 'not healthy'.
why: The stock way to notice someone seems low ('genki nai ne, doushita no?'). It treats genki as a noun, not the versatility adjective.

trap: Not chigai o iu or oshieru: here 'tell' is wakaru, and the difference is the subject. It is usually heard as chigai ga wakaranai.
why: It comes up when tasting, shopping and comparing ('zenzen chigai ga wakannai'). English 'tell' pushes a learner toward iu or oshieru. It is a third everyday X ga wakaru, next to imi ga wakaru and kimochi ga wakaru in the pool.

trap: Crossing takes o, not ni
why: Set verb for crossing water or roads.

trap: Activity as purpose takes ni, no -ing form
why: Common leisure plan.

trap: Crossing takes o, not ni
why: Set phrase for going overseas.
Praise for manners; gyougi yoku shite = behave.

trap: One verb in English; Japanese needs noun + haku
why: Only way to say spit.

trap: Not megane o kiru or tsukeru: glasses 'hang' on the face, so the verb is kakeru.
why: Used for routines and for describing people (megane kaketeru hito). Builds on the 'put on' sense of versatility kakeru.
freqNote: Ranks are for 眼鏡 #4549 (the katakana spelling メガネ is listed separately at #6067) and the kanji 掛ける #2742. Kana かける (#244) also counts the call, sit and spend senses.

trap: Not inu o aruku, because aruku can't take the dog as its object. You go on the dog's walk: inu no sanpo ni iku, or inu o sanpo ni tsureteku.
why: A daily routine for any dog owner and a standard small-talk line. The pool has inu o kau and esa o yaru for pets, but not the walk. English 'walk' is transitive here and Japanese aruku is not.

trap: Forms are put out (dasu), not 'filed'
why: Police reports, leave, marriage registration.

trap: 'put on' splits by body part; coats take kiru
why: Everyday clothing verb.
Everyday time phrase, often yoru osoku made.

trap: Hearing ability is kikoeru, not kiku
why: Standard for hearing ability, often negative.
Set phrase for steeling oneself.

trap: You enter (hairu) the main topic
why: Common meeting and conversation phrase.

trap: Impression is received (ukeru), no passive needed
why: Fixed verb for being moved.

trap: Granting a favour is kiku (listen), not suru
why: Everyday favour-asking set.
The usual way to call someone generous.
Guessable everyday set.

trap: Not keshou o tsukeru or kiru: makeup takes suru. Many speakers say okeshou suru, and younger ones meiku suru.
why: Part of the daily routine. 'Put on' leads English speakers to a wear verb, but makeup is something you do.
freqNote: Ranks are for 化粧 #4597 and する #15. The younger alternative メイク is #5468.

trap: Not okane o tsukuru: 'make money' is kasegu, 'earn'. Okane o tsukuru sounds like printing it or raising funds.
why: Jobs, side work and part-time work (baito de kasegu) are core small-talk topics. 'Make' gives exactly the wrong verb.

trap: Following rules is shitagau with ni, not tsuite iku
why: Formal set; ruuru o mamoru is the casual one.

trap: Transitive akeru, not aku
why: Everyday guessable set.
Set phrase for joining a family or team (kazoku no ichiin).

trap: English 'comfortable' about a place or group is igokochi ga ii, not just raku or kaiteki.
why: High-share fixed pairing for how a place or company feels.

trap: English 'take' works here. The trap is the contrast: a day off sick is shigoto o yasumu, while a planned break is yasumi o toru.
why: Needed for talking about holidays. It is kept with shigoto o yasumu so the two 'time off' frames don't blur.
freqNote: 休み #1322, 取る #228 (撮る, take a photo, is counted separately at #649). At work, 有給 yuukyuu o toru (take paid leave, #13555) uses the same frame.

trap: 'Get an education' uses ukeru (receive), not morau.
why: Standard verb for receiving schooling or training.

trap: 'Have an attitude' is not motsu; Japanese takes toru.
why: Common in complaints about behaviour (sonna taido toranaide).

trap: 'Dissatisfied' is a noun + aru; complaining aloud is monku o iu.
why: Common (nani ka fuman ga aru no?).

trap: Emergency 'taken to hospital' is hakobareru, not tsurete ikareru.
why: Usual way to report accidents (byouin ni hakobareta).

trap: The adjective 'considerate' is noun + aru in Japanese.
why: Standard way to describe a kind, thoughtful person.

trap: 'I'm hungry' is a past-tense verb in Japanese: onaka ga hetta.
why: Everyday hunger set; hara ga heru is the rougher male form.

trap: Personal habits and quirks are kuse, not shuukan.
why: Common for describing someone's habits.

kana: ちゅうもくをあつめる
trap: 'Attract' attention is atsumeru (gather), not hiku.
why: Fixed set used for trends and people in the news.

trap: The path takes o (kaidan o oriru), and 'go down' is one verb, not iku.
why: Typical everyday movement pairing.

trap: 'Have' a meal is toru or taberu, never motsu.
why: Polite/neutral meal set; casual speech says bangohan o taberu.
Everyday talk about concerts, films and trips (chiketto katta?). For train fares, kippu o kau is the classic version, and the list already has chiketto o toru.
Used for 'shows no sign of' (okiru kehai ga nai) and empty places.

trap: Not kutsu o toru: shoes and clothes come off with nugu, and toru sounds like picking them up.
why: Heard or said at every Japanese doorway, and the model take-off verb for anything worn with kiru or haku.
freqNote: Ranks are for 靴 #1818 and 脱ぐ #2074. Pairing commonness is judged; kutsu o nuide kudasai is heard at Japanese entrances every day.

trap: Not adobaisu o ageru: to listen to someone's problem you 'ride on' it, soudan ni noru (to ask for advice is soudan suru).
why: Asking for or offering support between friends (soudan notte kurenai?). It is the plain way to say this, not a metaphor for character.
freqNote: 乗る #439 (載る #2368 is a different verb).

trap: Not tsuri o iku or tsuri suru ni iku: an activity noun takes ni iku directly (tsuri ni itta).
why: Model for English 'go -ing' with activity nouns (sukii, kyanpu, sanpo, karaoke ni iku). It is the noun twin of the versatility pattern -ni iku.
freqNote: Also sukii #11454, kyanpu #5473, sanpo #2304 ni iku.

english: get tested, have a (medical) check or test
trap: Not kensa o suru, which is what the doctor does: the patient 'receives' a test, kensa o ukeru, as in shujutsu o ukeru.
why: Blood tests, check-ups and screenings come up constantly. Kenshin o ukeru (annual health check) works the same way.

trap: Lower-body clothing takes haku, not kiru; pantsu usually means underwear.
why: Core clothing verb split learners must get right.

trap: 'Use violence' is furuu (wield), not tsukau.
why: The fixed verb for violence, used in news and abuse talk.
Common talk about getting jobs through connections.
Typical for memorable things (kioku ni nokotte iru).

trap: Helpful advice is sankou ni naru, not tasukeru.
why: Everyday thanks for advice (sankou ni narimashita).
High-share set, often negative (nagusame ni mo naranai).

english: appear in a dream; dream about (someone)
trap: English 'I dreamt about you' leads to translating 'about'. Japanese says the person came out in the dream: yume ni kimi ga dete kita.
why: Telling someone about last night's dream nearly always uses this (kinou yume ni dete kita yo). It uses the 'appear' sense of deru, like terebi ni deru.
freqNote: nounRank is 夢 and verbRank is 出る. The list has no phrase counts.

trap: 'Be away' from home is rusu ni suru, not just inai.
why: Everyday for leaving the house empty (shibaraku uchi o rusu ni suru).

trap: 'Right decision' is usually handan, not kettei.
why: Typical adjective-noun pairing for judgement calls.
Core everyday money pairing.

trap: 'Smash to pieces' is konagona ni suru, not a single verb.
why: Fixed set for shattered things (pair with konagona ni naru).

trap: 'Turn' at a corner is magaru, not mawaru.
why: Core directions phrase.

trap: Means making unreasonable demands, not saying 'impossible'.
why: Common in requests and refusals (muri itte gomen).
A basic daily-routine set. In casual speech bangohan or yuuhan tabeta? is more usual, and yuushoku is the neutral word for the same thing.

trap: Not densha o noru or densha o toru: you ride on a vehicle with ni noru, and 'take' is never toru here.
why: One frame for every vehicle; English 'take' and the habit of using o both push learners wrong.
freqNote: Phrase not counted, so noun and verb are ranked separately. The same frame covers basu (#2466), takushii (#1987), hikouki (#3222) and jitensha (#2927) ni noru.

trap: Not netsu o motteru: a fever 'exists', netsu ga aru (netsu aru mitai).
why: The basic sick-day report built on aru, paired with netsu ga deru for the onset.
freqNote: 熱 #1641; ある #21. No phrase entry.

trap: English 'come out/open' points to deru or hiraku. Flowers bloom with saku, and petals fall with chiru, not ochiru.
why: Spring talk is dominated by 'sakura saita / mou chitchatta', and saku and chiru are the two verbs it needs. Hana here is the flower, not hana 'nose' (#37 in the noun list).
freqNote: 花 #1169. Kana はな is mixed with 鼻 (nose). 桜 is #3953, and its partner 散る is #5348. 花見 is #10548.

trap: Personal bad habits are kuse, not shuukan.
why: Common self-description (warui kuse da).

trap: Means a tasteless joke or 'this can't be real', not an unfunny one.
why: Set reaction phrase (warui joudan wa yamete).

trap: 'Cause' trouble is okosu, not tsukuru.
why: Typical set (sawagi o okosanaide).
Typical object for nageru.

trap: 'Watch' a game is just miru.
why: Everyday sports talk.
Set for prospects or a promising person (mikomi ga nai = hopeless).

trap: Accessories take suru (or hameru), not kiru.
why: Everyday accessory verb English speakers get wrong.

trap: 'Mark' is noun + tsukeru; there is no single verb.
why: Everyday for marking maps, calendars and lists.

trap: Not kado ni magaru: the corner takes o and the direction takes ni (tsugi no kado o migi ni magaru). 'Turn' is not mawaru (spin).
why: The backbone of giving and following directions, with two particles in one phrase.
freqNote: Phrase not counted. Both words rank mid-list because drama dialogue rarely gives directions.

trap: 'I go to a Japanese school' as a routine is kayotteru, not itteru: iku is one trip, kayou is regular attendance.
why: A learner will describe their own language school or classes. English 'go to' hides the iku/kayou split.
