freqNote: 学校 #661, 通う #1026. The same frame is used for gyms, classes and hospitals (jimu ni kayotteru).

trap: English 'shed' has no match: tears are made to flow (nagasu).
why: Standard set for crying in stories and news; in chat naku is more usual.

trap: No 'to': kiku takes the radio directly with o.
why: Everyday habit in the car or at work; guessable.

english: wait for someone to come home
trap: 'Wait for' takes o, not ni.
why: Family talk: uchi de kaeri o matteru.

trap: Dressing someone else is kiseru; kiru is only dressing yourself.
why: Parents and carers say it daily (kodomo ni fuku o kiseru).
Everyday adult money talk; fully guessable.

trap: Not beruto o kiru: belts, watches and ties take suru.
why: Daily dressing, and the verb can't be guessed from English.
Set verb for interest and appetite, often passive (kyoumi o sosorareru).

trap: English 'it smells' has no verb match: the scent 'does' (ga suru).
why: Said of food, flowers, shampoo: ii kaori ga suru.

english: make one's dream come true, achieve a dream
trap: English 'achieve / realise a dream' pushes to tassei suru or jitsugen suru. The everyday verb is kanaeru, the transitive half of yume ga kanau.
why: You hear it when people talk about goals and ambitions (yume o kanaeru tame ni ganbaru). It completes the transitive/intransitive pair with yume ga kanau.
freqNote: verbRank is for the kana spelling かなえる (#2619). The kanji spelling 叶える ranks #6190 separately, because subtitles split the spellings.

why: Fixed compliment for someone who works quickly and neatly.

trap: Usually ni, not a bare object like English 'climb'.
why: Hiking is a common weekend topic.

kana: きゅうりょうをもらう
trap: 'Get paid' is not a passive: you receive (morau) the salary.
why: Everyday work and money talk.

trap: Not takushii o toru: vehicles take noru with ni.
why: Everyday travel, and English 'take' misleads.
Common conversation move; guessable.
How people describe swearing (kitanai kotoba o tsukau).

kana: ちょうしょくをたべる
why: Guessable; choushoku is hotel/formal, in speech people say asagohan o taberu.

trap: Careful planning 'kneads' (neru) the plan; tsukuru sounds flat.
why: Set verb for drafting plans carefully, trips included.

trap: English 'whistle' is one verb; Japanese blows (fuku) a noun.
why: The only way to say whistle; the shape isn't guessable.

trap: Not michi o iu or michi o hanasu: telling someone the way is oshieru ('teach'), as in eki made no michi oshiete kuremasen ka?
why: How the learner asks for directions; the partner of michi o kiku.
freqNote: Phrase not counted.

trap: Used with suru (tsurai omoi o suru = go through a hard time); omoi here is not 'thought'.
why: Common in comforting talk (tsurai omoi o saseta ne).

trap: Not eigo o wakaru: wakaru takes ga.
why: Learners and travellers ask and answer it constantly.

trap: Takes ni, not a bare object like English 'climb'.
why: Kids and pets talk; guessable verb.

trap: Accidents 'arise' (okiru/okoru); being in one is jiko ni au.
why: News and daily talk about road and train accidents.

trap: You 'put out' (dasu) a conclusion, not reach it.
why: Meetings and decisions; verb not guessable.

trap: Not zubon o kiru: trousers, skirts, socks and tights take haku, like shoes (anything you step into).
why: A worse trap than shoes, because trousers count as clothes, so learners reach for kiru. sukaato o haku and kutsushita o haku go in its notes.
freqNote: Ranks are for ズボン #6081 and 履く #3474. sukaato (#6710) and kutsushita (#5748) take the same verb.

trap: Lights and the TV take tsukeru, but powering up a phone or PC is dengen o ireru ('put the power in').
why: Device trouble talk: 'dengen ireta?' The negative dengen ga hairanai means 'it won't turn on'.
Everyday remark; guessable.

trap: okashii here means 'odd', not 'funny'.
why: Common when someone seems off (kare no yousu ga okashii).
Gardening and kids at the beach; guessable.

trap: Intransitive naru with ga; ringing it yourself is narasu.
why: School and alarm bells; at home chaimu is more usual.

trap: Not tomodachi o tsukuru as the default: friends 'come into being' with ga dekiru (tomodachi dekita).
why: A core life-update phrase; the same frame gives kareshi / kanojo ga dekiru.
freqNote: dekiru: kana できる #73 (出来る #1313 separate).

trap: Not shinpai suru, which means you are the one worrying: worrying someone else is shinpai o kakeru (shinpai kakete gomen).
why: A twin of meiwaku o kakeru, set against D-shinpai and shinpai shinaide.
freqNote: 心配 #210 counts every shinpai use (shinpai da, shinpai suru); kakeru kana #244 pools all senses.

trap: Not ruuru ni tsuite iku: following rules is mamoru ('protect'), like promises and time. Ruuru ni shitagau is stiffer.
why: Comes up with kids, sharehouses, rubbish sorting, sport and work. Kimari o mamoru is the same pairing.
Said of time, battery, money; particle usually dropped.

trap: Effort is 'hung' (kakeru), not taken (toru).
why: Cooking with care and apologising for trouble (tema o kakesete gomen).

trap: Events are 'opened' (hiraku), not held (motsu).
why: Parties and meetings, usually compounds like nomikai o hiraku.

trap: Lights and devices take tsukeru, not mawasu or ireru.
why: Car lights and torches; for room lights denki o tsukeru is more usual.

trap: Not hima o motsu: free time 'exists' (ga aru).
why: Everyday for plans and invitations (ima hima aru?).

trap: Not denki o tomeru or shimeru: lights, TVs and heaters go off with kesu (put out).
why: The other half of tsukeru, used just as often. terebi o kesu and eakon o kesu use the same verb, so they don't need their own entries.
freqNote: 消す #964 also covers erase and delete.

trap: English has no verb to translate: a hole 'opens' (ana ga aku). Making one is ana o akeru.
why: Said of socks, clothes and walls (kutsushita ni ana aiteru).
freqNote: Phrase entries 穴が開く #9696 and 穴があく #24499. verbRank is 空く; 開く read as aku is #14086.

english: make fun of, look down on
trap: Not warau or anything with tsukuru: 'make fun of' is baka ni suru, literally 'treat as a fool'.
why: A stock line in teasing and complaints ('baka ni shinaide yo', 'baka ni sareta'), and the passive is as common as the active. English 'make fun of / mock' gives no route to it, and warau ('laugh at') covers only part of the meaning. It is the plain literal phrase, not a metaphor idiom.
freqNote: nounRank is the katakana spelling バカ (#433). ばか is #2695 and 馬鹿 #6994. There is no phrase count.

trap: English 'attractive' is an adjective; Japanese says the person has charm.
why: Standard everyday way to call someone or something appealing.

trap: 'Come true' is the single verb kanau, not hontou ni naru.
why: Fixed pairing; wishes and dreams kanau.

trap: Switches and power are cut (kiru), not erased (kesu) like lights.
why: Everyday device action with a specific verb.

trap: 'Finish' suggests owaru; for errands and business Japanese says you ga sumu.
why: Everyday set: you ga sundara kaeru.
Core everyday media pairing.

trap: Chuudoku also means poisoning; addiction to games etc. uses ni naru.
why: Common in talk about games, phones, coffee.

trap: Kaori is for pleasant scents; nioi is neutral, kusai is bad.
why: Everyday exclamation: ii kaori!

trap: Not kusuri ga hataraku: medicine 'takes effect', kusuri ga kiku, a homophone of kiku 'listen'.
why: Asked after every pill (kusuri kiita?); this kiku has to be kept apart from kiku 'listen'.
freqNote: 薬 #1283; 効く #1822; phrase entry 薬が効く #19852.

trap: Not seki o mamoru or tameru: saving a seat is 'taking' it, seki o toru. Totte oku means keeping it for later.
why: Comes up in cafés, trains and events (seki totte oku ne). 'Save' and 'keep' give the wrong verbs.

trap: Okuru isn't the default here: posting a letter or card is tegami o dasu ('put it out'); the same goes for nengajou.
why: Fewer letters now, but the pairing carries over to cards, forms and parcels at the post office.

trap: English 'unlock' is one verb; Japanese 'opens the key', kagi o akeru, the opposite of kagi o kakeru.
why: Needed every day (kagi akete), and the missing half of the pool's lock items.

english: have things to talk about, click in conversation
trap: Here au means 'fit', not 'meet'. People whose conversation fits are hanashi ga au; ki ga au is the separate idiom.
why: The literal way to say you get on with someone (kare to wa hanashi ga au). Its link to H-au-meet keeps the two meanings of au apart.

trap: Bones snap (oru), not break like objects (kowasu); also means take pains.
why: The standard way to say you broke a bone.
Typical driving pairing; supiido o ageru in casual talk.

trap: Not sayonara o iu; people say (o)wakare o iu.
why: Fixed way to say a farewell.

trap: 'Get a message' is not morau here; a passed-on message is heard (kiku).
why: Typical pairing for passed-on or voicemail messages.

trap: 'Take' tempts toru; risks are usually borne (ou), though risuku o toru exists.
why: Typical set in work and money talk.
Fixed set, as in hitome mitai.

trap: English 'water' is a verb; Japanese 'gives' water, (hana ni) mizu o yaru, or politely ageru.
why: A household chore with a giving-verb no learner would guess. It reuses yaru/ageru from the versatility list in a new sense.
freqNote: やる #45 counts every sense (do, give); 水やり #28613 is the noun form.

trap: Not gitaa o suru: guitar takes hiku like the piano (gitaa hikeru? = can you play guitar?).
why: Second anchor for hiku. It shows the verb covers strings as well as keyboards.
freqNote: バイオリン #12637 takes the same verb.

trap: Not shokuyoku o motte inai: an appetite ga aru or ga nai.
why: Doctors and friends ask about it whenever you're ill, and a learner has to answer.
freqNote: 食欲 #3504; ない #43 also counts the negative ending.

why: Common set for unfounded claims or hunches.
Everyday routine set people talk about often.

trap: 'Make a good impression' is ii inshou o ataeru, not tsukuru.
why: Typical set; also inshou ga ii.
Literal, typical pairing.
Typical praise for work or results; also deki ga ii.

trap: 'I have a bad feeling' is warui yokan ga suru, not motsu.
why: Fixed set; also iya na yokan.

trap: 'Miss' is not sabishii or noriokureru; chances are let slip (nogasu).
why: Typical set; nogasu is the verb for chances.

trap: 'Carry' tempts hakobu; carrying a bag is motsu.
why: Everyday pairing, as in baggu o omochi shimasu ka.

trap: Not denki o mawasu or akeru: lights are tsukeru'd, and denki here means the light itself.
why: Said every evening ('denki tsukete'). It sets up tsukeru for the TV and air conditioner, and starts a four-way transitive/intransitive set.
freqNote: つける #393 is the kana spelling across all senses (付ける #1452, 点ける #52228); 電気 also counts 'electricity'.

trap: 'Make trouble' is not tsukuru; trouble is raised (okosu).
why: Typical set with a non-obvious verb.

trap: English 'motivated' is an adjective; Japanese has (or lacks) yaruki.
why: Very common everyday set, often as yaruki ga nai.
Typical music pairing; kyoku o tsukuru also used.

english: become the talk of the town
trap: English passive 'be talked about' becomes X ga wadai ni naru.
why: Common for trending shows, shops, news.

trap: Not jikan o korosu: killing time is tsubusu, 'crush' (kafe de jikan tsubushiteta).
why: The natural phrase when you're early for a meeting; a literal translation of 'kill' gives the wrong verb. The noun hima tsubushi is also common.
freqNote: 潰す #2027 also covers 'crush' and 'ruin'. The kana つぶす is #4184.

trap: Not chiimu o sanka suru: you 'enter' a team, club or circle with ni hairu (saakuru ni haitta).
why: 'Join' has no single Japanese verb. For teams, bukatsu and university circles it is ni hairu, building on H-hairu.
freqNote: 部活 (school club) #4867, サークル #5842 and クラブ #3027 take the same verb.

why: Plain physical set, 腕を掴まれた is a normal report.

trap: English 'cause a fuss' makes learners want a transitive verb; Japanese says the situation becomes a fuss.
why: Common way to report that something blew up into a commotion.

trap: English 'be honest' points to shoujiki; for speaking your true feelings people say honne o iu.
why: Everyday phrase, especially 本音を言うと to open a frank admission.

trap: English 'get water' suggests toru or morau; scooping water up from a source or tap into a container is kumu.
why: The fixed verb for fetching water; still used for filling buckets and jugs.

trap: English 'everyone is here' leads to zenin iru; for a group that has all gathered people say zenin sorotta.
why: Standard line when a group has assembled, at meetings, dinners, classes.

kana: いんしょうをあたえる
trap: English 'give' suggests ageru; with impressions Japanese uses ataeru.
why: Fixed verb for impressions, used for how someone or something comes across.

trap: The stairs take o (the path you move along), not ni.
why: Basic movement set at home, stations and shops.

trap: English 'shatter' has no single verb here; Japanese says it becomes pieces.
why: Normal way to say a plate or glass smashed to bits.

trap: English 'close' suggests shimeru; holes and gaps are blocked with fusagu.
why: Fixed verb for blocking holes and gaps around the house.

english: has a nice ring to it
trap: English 'sounds good' leads to yosasou; for how a name or word sounds people say ii hibiki.
why: Common reaction to a name or phrase: ii hibiki da ne.

trap: English 'mean' has no direct adjective; Japanese says the disposition is bad (also ijiwaru).
why: Fixed set for spiteful people, often contracted to ijiwaru.

trap: English 'come and cheer' leads to kite ouen suru; Japanese puts the purpose noun with ni kuru.
why: Usual for friends and family coming to games, sports days and shows.

trap: English 'agree' points to sansei suru; for two people sharing views Japanese says opinions match.
why: Common in talk about friends, couples and colleagues getting along.

trap: English 'kneel' has no single verb; Japanese puts the knee down with tsuku.
why: The physical set for kneeling, also for collapsing to one's knees.

trap: Dictionaries give i for 'stomach', but an everyday tummy ache is onaka ga itai, not i ga itai.
why: Second most-said pain; reuses the onaka of onaka ga suku.
freqNote: おなか #1253 (お腹 #4758); 痛い #336. No phrase entry.

trap: Not okane o harau: paying back a loan is kaesu, 'give back' (ashita kaesu ne).
why: The third verb of the lending set, where 'pay back' tempts learners toward harau. Keep it apart from kaeru (go home).

trap: English 'buy/get insurance' leads to kau; Japanese enters insurance with ni hairu.
why: Standard set for health, car and travel insurance.

trap: English 'it costs' has the thing as subject; Japanese makes the expense the subject with ga kakaru.
why: Typical way to talk about expenses for moves, repairs, school.

trap: English 'reach a conclusion' suggests tsuku; Japanese says the conclusion comes out (ga deru, or o dasu).
why: Usual for meetings and decisions: mada ketsuron ga denai.

trap: English 'get sleep' suggests eru or morau; Japanese takes sleep with toru.
why: Standard health advice phrase: chanto suimin o totte.

trap: English 'tell apart' is something you do; Japanese says the distinction attaches (ga tsuku), mostly in the negative.
why: Common for twins, similar things: kubetsu ga tsukanai.

trap: Transitive narasu for ringing it yourself; naru is the bell ringing on its own.
why: Fixed verb for bells; doorbells are often chaimu or pinpon.
Common for friends coming over to help with moving, events, chores.

trap: English 'uncomfortable' points to physical discomfort; for an awkward place or situation it's igokochi ga warui.
why: Everyday phrase for awkward rooms, gatherings, atmospheres.
Normal for driving and work pace.

trap: English 'on the sofa' leads to no ue ni; the place of sleeping takes de.
why: Common home situation: dozing off on the sofa.

trap: Not atama o tataku (that's hitting on purpose): banging your head into something is butsukeru, as in tana ni atama butsuketa.
why: A common small injury. The same verb works for knees, toes and cars.

english: can make it, can fit it in
trap: Not tsugou ga dekiru: an arrangement 'attaches' (tsuku). Example: tsugou tsuitara renraku shite.
why: The other everyday tsugou pairing besides tsugou ga ii. tsugou ga tsukanai is the soft way to decline.

trap: English 'short-staffed' has no direct word; Japanese says hands are not enough.
why: Constant complaint at shops, restaurants, workplaces.

trap: The person you ask takes ni, not o (honnin ni kiku), and kiku is also 'listen'.
why: Everyday advice line: honnin ni kiite yo / honnin ni kikanai to wakaranai.
Recording video with phones; douga o toru is also common.

trap: English 'form/make a team' leads to tsukuru; teams and pairs are put together with kumu.
why: Usual for projects, sports and games.

kana: きゅうりょうをはらう
why: Typical set from the employer side; kyuuryou o morau is the worker side.
Classic adjective + noun pair for fine weather.

trap: English 'take advice' leads to toru; Japanese listens to advice with kiku.
why: Fixed verb for heeding warnings; adobaisu o kiku is the casual twin.

trap: 'Gain' is not eru here; experience is piled up (tsumu).
why: Default way to say you are building up experience at work or study.

trap: 'Take off' clothes is nugu, not toru.
why: Clothes come off with nugu, and shirts are the commonest case.

trap: English 'I have news' pushes toward motsu; Japanese says oshirase ga aru.

trap: 'Sign' a contract is musubu 'tie', not sain suru.

trap: 'Adopt' has no single verb; you make the child your youshi (youshi ni suru).

trap: 'Follow' rules is mamoru 'protect/keep', not a verb of following.
why: Formal twin of ruuru o mamoru, used at school and work.

trap: 'Stand in line' is just narabu; no tatsu.

trap: Going on stage is agaru 'go up', not iku.
why: Typical for concerts, karaoke events and performances.

trap: English 'tea' usually means koucha; ocha means green tea by default in Japan.

english: get through (on the phone), reach someone

trap: 'Make' an appointment is toru 'take', not tsukuru.

trap: 'Get' cancer is naru 'become', not motsu or toru.
why: Standard way to talk about someone getting cancer, like byouki ni naru.

trap: 'Ask' someone to dinner is sasou with ni, not kiku.
why: Typical invitation set; casual speech uses gohan ni sasou.

trap: 'Panic' as a verb is panikku o okosu or panikku ni naru, not panikku suru.

trap: 'Put up for sale' is uri ni dasu 'put out to selling', not just uru.

trap: 'Have symptoms' is shoujou ga deru 'come out', not motsu.
why: Said at clinics and about colds, allergies and covid.

trap: 'Go out for dinner' is just gohan (ni) iku; no taberu needed.
why: Top invitation in Japan; casually gohan ikou with no particle.

trap: English 'windy' is one adjective. Japanese says the wind is strong: kaze ga tsuyoi, not kaze ga ooi.

trap: Not terebi o akeru or on ni suru: screens, like lights, are tsukeru'd, and off is kesu.

why: Said of scars, bruises, stains and marks that will not go away.

trap: 'Live a ... life' is ~na kurashi o suru, not ikiru.
why: Used with an adjective: ii kurashi, shizuka na kurashi o suru.

trap: ashi covers both foot and leg; 'my feet hurt' is still ashi ga itai.
why: Said after walking, standing or exercise every day.

trap: 'Get' a tattoo is ireru 'put in', not morau or suru.
why: The set verb for tattoos; matters at onsen and gyms.

kana: あかちゃんがうまれる
trap: 'Have a baby' is akachan ga umareru 'is born', not motsu.
why: How births are announced among friends and family.

trap: naosu is curing it; 'I got better' is byouki ga naotta.
why: Common with 'hayaku byouki o naoshite' wishes and doctors.

trap: 'Turn off' a light is kesu 'erase/put out', not ofu ni suru.

Common way to praise or tease someone for being bold.
Common when judging whether to walk; also emotional distance.

trap: seki is a noun; to cough is seki o suru (or seki ga deru).
why: Everyday illness talk, like kushami o suru.
Stiffer twin of monku o iu.

trap: 'Achieve' results is ageru 'raise', not eru or tsukuru.
why: Standard office set for delivering results.

trap: Not hoteru ni iru or sutei suru: staying the night is tomaru, the same sound as a car stopping.
why: Used for every trip and sleepover (doko ni tomaru?, tomodachi no ie ni tomaru). The transitive tomeru means to put someone up (tomete!).
freqNote: Phrase not counted. 泊まる is ranked apart from 止まる (#776).

trap: Easy to guess once fuku is known. The risk is the homophones: kaze means wind or a cold, and fuku means blow or wipe. Keep it apart from kaze o hiku (catch a cold).
why: The pairing is literal, but it anchors the kaze ga fuku / kaze o hiku contrast with the body domain that the plan calls for.
freqNote: Kana ふく is dominated by 服 and 拭く, so the kanji 吹く is used.

trap: Not piano o suru or asobu: keyboard and string instruments take hiku (piano hiiteru).
why: The model for every keyboard or string instrument (gitaa, baiorin). It sounds the same as hiku in kaze o hiku, so it needs a fixed anchor.
freqNote: 弾く (ひく) #5832. The kana ひく #2982 and 引く #1039 are the homophone hiku (pull; kaze o hiku), counted separately.

trap: Not denwa o morau: an incoming call 'hangs' on you (denwa ga kakatte kuru). It is the intransitive of denwa o kakeru.
why: As in sakki haha kara denwa kakatte kita. It is the other half of the pool's denwa o kakeru.
freqNote: Phrase entries 電話がかかる #10203 and 電話がかかってくる #32857.

trap: 'Something came up at work' is shigoto ga haitchatta (work 'entered' the schedule), not okiru or kuru.
why: The standard reason for cancelling or turning down plans (gomen, kyuu ni shigoto haitchatta). English gives no hint that hairu works here.
freqNote: 入る #115. The same frame for plans in general (yotei ga hairu) belongs to time-money.

kana: でんわがかかってくる
trap: Not denwa o morau: a call comes in, so it's denwa ga kakatte kita (casually just denwa kita).
why: The receiving half of denwa o kakeru: 'okaasan kara denwa kakatte kita'.
freqNote: verbRank is kana かかる, all senses together.

why: Everyday for phones, keys and wallets.
The usual verb for holding a doubt or question; formal register.

trap: "Break in" is not kowasu; a burglar simply 'enters' (hairu), and dorobou ni hairareta = we got burgled.
why: The everyday way to report a burglary at home.
Everyday set for carrying or holding a bag (kaban motou ka?).
Typical way to say a gap or difference exists between two things.

trap: "Have a headache" is not motsu; the headache is the subject: zutsuu ga hidoi / zutsuu ga suru.
why: How people describe a severe headache to friends or a doctor.
Common praise for grit and perseverance (konjou aru na).

trap: "Put on" is not kiru or tsukeru; switching a call mode is X ni suru.
why: Everyday phone talk: switch the call to speaker.
Typical set for costumes at events, Halloween, performances.
Very common casual judgement of someone's taste or knack.

trap: "Cover" is not kabuseru or oou; ears are blocked: fusagu.
why: Standard body action against noise or unwanted words.

trap: "Take off" is not nugu; masks, glasses and accessories are hazusu.
why: Everyday in Japan, where masks are worn often.

trap: "Leave" is not deru or oite iku; a note left for someone is nokosu.
why: Common household and office set for leaving a message.

trap: "Make" is not tsukuru; errors are okasu (casually just machigaeru).
why: Fixed formal set for committing an error.

trap: No dekiru needed; mostly heard negative: yosou ga tsukanai = can't tell what will happen.
why: Fixed set for whether something can be guessed in advance.

trap: "Come back" is not kaeru or modoru; memories revive: yomigaeru.
why: Typical set for memories flooding back.

trap: Not yoyaku o tsukuru: you 'take' a booking (yoyaku toreta? = did you get one?). Plain yoyaku suru also works.
why: Used for restaurants, salons and doctors, and toreta / torenakatta is how people say whether they got in.
freqNote: 取る #228. The potential 取れる (#631) is the form heard most (toreta, torenakatta).

trap: "Win" is not katsu; prizes are taken: shou o toru (or morau).
why: Everyday set for winning awards in contests or school.

trap: "Close" is not chikai (physically near); close friends are shitashii.
why: The standard way to say a close friend, a bit formal with yuujin.
Fixed set heard in work and news talk.

trap: "Appear" is not arawareru; being printed is noru (載る).
why: Typical set for being printed in the paper.
Common description of a pleasant, sociable person or shop clerk.

trap: "Cold" is not samui (weather); cold to the touch or drink is tsumetai.
why: Everyday request and description of drinks and water.
Usual set for saying someone or something has a weakness.

trap: "Take" is not toru here; attending a class is ukeru (toru means signing up).
why: Core school-life set.

trap: "Keep" is not motsu; distance is maintained: tamotsu (or kyori o oku).
why: Typical set for physical or social distance.

trap: No passive verb needed; being expelled is taigaku ni naru.
why: Standard school-life set for expulsion.
Fixed set for carrying out one's duty or role.

trap: "Turn off" pulls toward kesu (lights); engines are kiru.
why: Everyday driving set.

trap: "Rise" pulls toward agaru; the sun noboru (casually hi ga noboru).
why: The standard sky set for sunrise.

trap: "Have" is not motsu; body marks use ga aru.
why: Typical way to mention a scar on the body.
Extremely common everyday complaint about motivation.

trap: "Have" is not motsu; the attack itself occurs: hossa ga okiru.
why: Standard set for asthma, panic or other attacks.

trap: "Take off" is not nugu; belts and seatbelts are hazusu.
why: Everyday for belts and seatbelts (shiitoberuto o hazusu).

trap: Not hone ga kowareru: bones, sticks and umbrellas 'snap' (oreru). Kowareru is for machines.
why: The literal injury phrase (ashi no hone ga oreta). The transitive hone o oru is mostly the idiom 'take pains', which is out of scope.
freqNote: Phrase entry 骨が折れる at #17817. That count includes the figurative sense 'be hard work'.

trap: "Keep" is not motsu; balance is toru.
why: Common for physical balance and balancing life or diet.

trap: "Arrive" pulls toward tsuku; mail and parcels todoku.
why: Everyday set for receiving mail.

trap: Doraibu means a leisure drive, not driving itself (unten suru).
why: Very common weekend and dating plan.

trap: Not se ga mijikai: short in height is hikui (low). Mijikai is only for length.
why: The other half of se ga takai, and the textbook trap for 'short' (hikui, not mijikai).
freqNote: 背 (せ) #5388; 低い #1747. Casual speech also uses chiisai for a short person.

trap: Swapped with kariru: kashite = lend me; karite ii? = can I borrow?
why: Completes the kasu / kariru / kaesu set. The verb is already H-kasu, so this mostly adds the money pairing.

english: be expecting a baby, get pregnant
trap: Not akachan o motsu: 'we're having a baby' is akachan ga dekita (a baby 'came into being').
why: Big life news. It contrasts with the pool's kodomo ga iru (have children) and teaches dekiru as 'come into being'.

trap: Japanese has no word for 'flush': you make the toilet 'flow' (nagasu), as in toire nagashite or mizu o nagasu.
why: Everyone needs it, and nothing in English points to nagasu.

trap: English says 'likely'; Japanese says the probability is high.
why: Typical way to say chances are high, e.g. rain chances.

trap: English uses a verb (don't get along); Japanese says the relationship is bad.
why: Everyday way to describe people who don't get along.

trap: Approach takes ni, not o.
why: Common way to say something is nearly over.
Typical hair description; kami ga kuroi also common.
Standard work phrase for accepting a commissioned job.

english: be immune; be used to it
trap: English uses an adjective; Japanese says you 'have immunity'.
why: Used for illness and, jokingly, for being used to something.

trap: kippu is a train ticket; concert tickets are chiketto.
why: Basic travel phrase at stations.

trap: baiku means motorbike, not bicycle; noru takes ni.
why: Everyday transport phrase.

trap: Japanese 'heads toward' the goal, usually mokuhyou ni mukatte ganbaru.
why: Common motivational phrase at school and work.

trap: English 'goes off'; Japanese says the alarm rings (naru).
why: Daily morning-routine phrase.

trap: Drums are hit (tataku), not hiku like other instruments.
why: Instrument-specific verb learners get wrong.

trap: Not shiken ni shippai suru: failing an exam is 'falling', ochiru with ni (ukatta / ochita).

freqNote: 落ちる #490 counts every 'fall' sense; the exam sense rests on native judgement. Also used for interviews and schools: mensetsu ni ochita.

english: the call drops, get cut off
trap: Not denwa ga ochiru: a dropped call is denwa ga kireta, the intransitive half of denwa o kiru.
why: Everyday phone trouble: 'gomen, denwa kireta'.

trap: 'Tear up' has no verb to copy: tears come out, so namida deta. Naku is crying outright.
why: Movies, onions, yawning and laughing: 'waraisugite namida deta'.

trap: 'Put in' is ni ireru, not oku.
why: Heard at every till: fukuro ni iremasu ka.

trap: English uses one adjective; Japanese says the will is strong.
why: Common personality description; ishi ga yowai is the opposite.
Bedtime routine phrase.

trap: 'Pull' here is nuku, not hiku.
why: Standard dentist phrase.

trap: Errands 'get settled' (sumu); owaru is less typical.
why: Everyday: youji ga sundara kaeru.

trap: Casual grumbling is monku o iu; kujou is a formal complaint.
why: Complaining to neighbours, shops or landlords.
Constant topic for learners; eigo de shaberu also common.

trap: Heavy breathing is 'rough breath' (arai), not omoi.
why: Said of someone panting after effort or illness.
Fixed time phrase; chikai uchi ni is more casual.

trap: Speed is 'put out' (dasu), not raised or made.
why: Common in driving talk: supiido dashisugi.

trap: In speech people just say seikou suru.
why: Strong set but mostly news and formal writing.

trap: Not netsu o morau or eru: a fever 'comes out', netsu ga deru (netsu deta).
why: The onset partner of netsu ga aru, and the model for seki, hanamizu and chi ga deru.
freqNote: 熱 #1641; 出る #81. No phrase entry.

trap: Not shigoto o toru or shigoto ni ikanai: missing work is yasumu ('rest') with o, the same for school (gakkou o yasumu).
why: The everyday way to say you're off sick or skipping work or school. English speakers know yasumu only as 'rest' and wouldn't put it with o.
freqNote: 仕事 #134, 休む #584. Same frame with gakkou (#661) and kaisha (#474): kyou gakkou yasunda.

trap: Not boushi o hazusu: hats come off with toru (boushi o nugu also works), not with the accessory verb hazusu.
why: Completes the kaburu pair. Low trap risk because English 'take off' leads to toru, which is correct.

trap: Not kyanseru sareru for events: rained-off matches and cancelled events chuushi ni naru. Postponed is enki ni naru.
why: Comes up in talk about weather and plans (ame de chuushi ni natta). Enki ni naru uses the same frame.
freqNote: 延期 (postponement) is #6376, and 延期になる is a phrase entry at #20128.

english: how much it comes to (in total)
trap: A total isn't 'is' but 'becomes': zenbu de ikura ni naru? asks the total, and every cashier says sen-en ni narimasu.
why: Shopping and paying: asking for the total and understanding the till's X-en ni narimasu, heard at every purchase. It contrasts with ikura suru, which asks one item's price.

trap: Not ame ga tomaru or owaru, and not yameru (a person quitting): rain stops with intransitive yamu.
why: The everyday follow-up to talking about rain (ame yanda?, yamu made matou). Its look-alike yameru (quit) is already in the learner's list, so the two have to be told apart.
freqNote: Rank is for the kanji 止む. Kana やむ (#3517) is how the word is usually written, but that count mixes in 病む and yamu o enai, so it isn't used.

trap: Not me ga yowai or 'warui me ga aru': poor eyesight is me ga warui (shiryoku is the formal word).
why: The standard way to explain glasses or contacts, or why you can't read something.
freqNote: 目 #216; 悪い #139. The opposite, me ga ii, is rarer and can also mean 'has a good eye' (taste).

trap: Not sutoresu ni naru: stress 'piles up' (tamaru).
why: Comes up in talk about work and life (sutoresu tamatteru). Same tamaru as the pool's okane ga tamaru.
freqNote: verbRank is hiragana たまる, the usual spelling (溜まる is #16850).

trap: English uses one verb; Japanese needs ibiki + kaku, the same kaku as ase o kaku (sweat).
why: Common family and travel-room talk, and the verb is unguessable. It shares kaku with the body domain's ase o kaku.
freqNote: かく #11889 is the kana form this phrase uses (掻く #51963); 書く 'write' #233 is a different word.

trap: Landing a job is usually intransitive, shigoto ga mitsukatta (a job turned up). English 'I found' pushes toward shigoto o mitsuketa, which sounds less natural.
why: Common news to share or ask about (atarashii shigoto mitsukatta?). It teaches the ga-intransitive habit on a high-need noun.
freqNote: 見つかる #445. shigoto o sagasu (look for a job) is the guessable lead-in.

trap: Scores are 'taken', not received: hyakuten totta, ii ten toreta (not ten o morau).
why: How everyone reports test results. 'Get' tempts morau, and toru is the fixed partner.
freqNote: 点 #1137 also covers 'point, dot'. It is usually fused with a number (hyakuten, gojutten). 点数 tensuu (#6480) is the noun for 'score'. The same verb scores points in sport.

english: get the hang of it, get the knack
trap: The set phrase is kotsu o tsukamu ('grab the knack'). Kotsu ga wakaru is also heard, but kotsu o toru is not.
why: How you talk about improving at any skill, sport or job (yatto kotsu tsukanda).

trap: Not menkyo o morau: you 'take' a licence by earning it (menkyo totta). The same goes for qualifications: shikaku o toru.
why: A common life milestone. It covers the whole 'earn a credential = toru' frame (driving licence, certificates).
freqNote: 免許 #5824 is mid-frequency, but the pairing is near-fixed. 資格 shikaku (#1671, qualification) takes the same verb and is folded in here.

trap: Not 'hayai rannaa': a fast runner is ashi ga hayai ('legs are fast'). Ashi ga osoi is slow.
why: Common about kids, school sports and friends. It frames speed through the legs, not 'runner'.
freqNote: 足 #707; 速い #2346 (speed). 早い #396 is 'early' and shares the kana はやい #396, so the kana rank overstates this sense.

trap: Not takarakuji ni katsu: you don't beat a lottery. The ticket 'hits' with ataru, and the lottery is the subject. The same goes for raffles and prize draws (kuji ga ataru).
why: 'What would you do if you won the lottery?' (takarakuji atattara nani suru?) is a classic small-talk question. It's the luck-based counterpart to shiai ni katsu.

trap: English 'graduate' leads to sotsugyou suru (fine but stiff). In conversation people say daigaku deta ('left university').
why: Self-introductions and background chat: 'daigaku dete kara...'

trap: Not takarakuji ni katsu: you don't beat a lottery, it hits you. 'Takarakuji atattara...' (also ga ataru).
why: A favourite 'what if' topic, and the same verb covers prize draws and raffles.

english: there are a lot of them
why: Typical way to say the number of something is large.

trap: Not asobu: playing music from a speaker is ongaku o kakeru; asobu is play as in have fun, hiku is play an instrument.
why: 'Can I put some music on?' (ongaku kakete ii?) comes up daily; nagasu is the alternative in shops and at events, and kiku is the listener's side.
freqNote: verbRank is kana かける pooling all senses; 掛ける alone is #2742.

trap: Not shiken o toru: you 'receive' an exam, ukeru (also tesuto o ukeru, mensetsu o ukeru, and daigaku o ukeru for sitting a university's entrance exam).
why: The core exam verb (think JLPT). English 'take' leads straight to toru, which is wrong here; contrast jugyou o toru (take a class), where toru works.
freqNote: 試験 #3067, 受ける #356. Everyday school tests are more often tesuto (#2539), with the same verb. 面接 mensetsu (#3050, interview) takes ukeru too.

trap: Not tsuku: a dead phone that 'won't turn on' is dengen ga hairanai.
why: Used when troubleshooting (sumaho no dengen ga hairanai). Pairs with dengen o kiru and dengen o ireru.
freqNote: Phrase entry 電源が入る at #9986.

trap: Learners swap kariru (borrow) and kasu (lend). The lender takes ni or kara (tomodachi ni karita).
why: Comes up every day (karite ii?), and mixing up which way kasu and kariru go is a classic learner error.

trap: Not 'nagai kami ga aru' for 'she has long hair': say kanojo wa kami ga nagai.
why: Basic appearance description. It drills the 'person wa X ga ADJ' frame instead of English 'has'.
freqNote: 髪 #1752; 長い #467. The kana かみ is shared with 神 #1988 and 紙 #2672.

trap: Not se ga sodatsu: 'you've grown!' is se nobita ne (or ookiku natta ne).
why: The stock remark to kids, nieces and nephews. Nobiru also feeds kami ga nobiru.

trap: Not jugyou o nuku or tobasu: skipping class or work is saboru (from 'sabotage'), while skipping a meal is nuku.
why: Very common in school and uni talk, and it splits English 'skip' from asagohan o nuku.
freqNote: verbRank is the katakana spelling サボる (#3137), the usual one.

trap: Not gasorin o kau or morau: fuel is 'put in' (ireru), as in gasorin irete kara iku.
why: A routine driving line, and English 'get' leads to the wrong verb.

trap: English 'fit' has no one-word verb: say saizu ga au / awanai. This au means 'match' and sounds the same as au 'meet'.
why: The phrase for trying clothes on in a shop (saizu awanai, chotto ookii). The learner has to say it, not just hear it.
freqNote: Rank is for 合う #563. Kana あう is mostly 会う 'meet' (#110). Pairing commonness is judged.

trap: Not okane o tasukeru or setsuyaku suru: saving up is tameru, 'pile up' (setsuyaku means cutting back).
why: How people talk about saving for a trip or a purchase, and English 'save' leads to the wrong verb. It pairs with okane ga tamaru.
freqNote: 貯める #10930 is the money spelling. The kana ためる #3410 covers every sense.

trap: Not yotei ga kuru or deru: a plan that gets booked 'enters' (sono hi yotei haitteru = I've got something that day).
why: The standard way to say a day is taken or that something came up. It pairs with yotei o ireru.

trap: There's no adjective for 'motivated': motivation 'comes out' (yaruki ga deru, or yaruki ga denai).
why: Yaruki denai is one of the most common everyday complaints. Yaruki ga aru (be keen) is the stative version.

trap: Learners reach for hagu or toru. Peeling the skin off fruit or vegetables is muku, as in mikan no kawa o muku.
why: Everyday kitchen and fruit-sharing talk (ringo muite ageru). The verb can't be guessed.
freqNote: 剥く #30971 is the kanji entry. The kana むく entry is #6799 but is shared with 向く written in kana.

trap: Not mimi ga kikoenai: the plain, polite way is 'far ears' (mimi ga tooi), the mirror of me ga warui.
why: The plain, literal description of hearing ability, a sibling of me ga warui. It's often said about grandparents.

english: not be in the mood, not feel like it
trap: Nothing in 'I don't feel like it' leads to noru (ride). The plain way to say it is ki ga noranai.
why: A soft way to turn down plans (ima ki ga noranai). Without it, learners say yaritakunai, which sounds blunter.
freqNote: 気が乗らない is not a phrase row in the list. The positive ki ga noru is rare, so the headword keeps the negative, like genki ga nai.

trap: Mostly guessable from yameru = quit. The catch is that you quit the company or the job (kaisha/shigoto o yameru), and 辞める sounds identical to 止める 'stop'.
why: Common life talk. It is low-trap but high-need, and it is built directly on the versatility yameru.
freqNote: 辞める #604 (resign) is counted apart from kana やめる #117, which mixes both senses.

trap: Not shumi o motsu in speech: having a hobby is ga aru (nanka shumi aru?), like jikan ga aru.
why: The opener for hobby talk, alongside shumi wa nan desu ka. Its trap is mild, since shumi o motsu exists in writing.

trap: Not kami o migaku: teeth are brushed with migaku, hair with tokasu.
why: English 'brush' gives the wrong verb, and it fits between ha o migaku and kami o kawakasu.
freqNote: 梳かす is almost always written in kana, and kana とかす (#46719) also covers 溶かす (melt), so the kanji row is a floor, not a real count.

english: get hit / run over by a car
trap: Not kuruma ni utareru: being run over is hikareru, the passive of hiku, which sounds the same as the hiku in kaze o hiku.
why: Shouted as a warning and used in near-miss stories ('hikaresou ni natta').
freqNote: 轢く is often written in kana, and kana ひく (#2982) mixes 引く and 弾く.

trap: No English pairing to copy. 'Do you like the food here?' is asked as nihon no tabemono, kuchi ni au? Here au means 'fit', not 'meet'.
why: This is the stock question put to foreigners (kuchi ni au?) and the polite hedge when serving food (okuchi ni au ka wakaranai kedo). Natives hear it as the plain, literal way to say 'suits my palate', not as a character metaphor, so it passes the borderline rule.

trap: Not hataraku or ugoku: 'the Wi-Fi isn't working' is netto ga tsunagaranai ('doesn't connect').
why: A daily complaint (netto tsunagaranai); the same verb covers a call going through (denwa ga tsunagaranai). This is the intransitive half of the tsunagu pair.
freqNote: verbRank is kana つながる (繋がる #6342) and also counts people or things being linked.

trap: Not kareshi o eru or morau: a partner 'comes into being' with ga dekiru (kanojo dekita!).
why: Classic catch-up news. It uses the same frame as tomodachi ga dekiru, so kanojo swaps straight into the slot.
freqNote: 彼氏 #1230; kanojo (彼女) #273 is inflated by its 'she' sense.

english: have good taste / a good eye (style)
trap: English 'good taste' leads to aji (flavour). Taste in clothes, music or gifts is sensu ga ii; shumi ga ii is also used.
why: Sensu ii ne is a stock compliment. The pool's aji ga suru and aji o miru train learners toward aji.

english: get some exercise, move your body
trap: Not only undou suru: the casual 'I need some exercise' is karada o ugokasu.
why: How people actually talk about exercise (tamani wa karada ugokasanai to).
freqNote: Phrase entry 体を動かす at #13082.

trap: Not gomi o toru or motte iku: taking out the trash is gomi o dasu (put it out).
why: The chore everyone has to mention, and English 'take' points to toru.
freqNote: ゴミ #2709 (ごみ #8915); ゴミ出し #17427 is the noun form.

trap: Not yubiwa o kiru: things you push a finger or hand into (rings, gloves) take hameru. yubiwa shiteru is also common for wearing one.
why: Covers rings and gloves; tebukuro o hamete is the everyday winter use and goes in the notes.
freqNote: Rank is for kana はめる #2952, which also counts the drama-heavy 'set someone up' sense. 手袋 'gloves' is #6640.

trap: English 'the snow is sticking/settling' has no match: snow piles up, tsumoru, not tsuku or nokoru.
why: An unguessable verb for snow that stays on the ground. Mostly winter and snow-region talk (sugoi tsumotteru).
freqNote: Ranks are for the parts only. How common the phrase is depends on region (frequent in snowy areas), which is a judgement call.

trap: Not netsu ga oriru or heru: a fever 'drops', netsu ga sagaru (netsu sagatta?).
why: The recovery check that follows netsu ga deru; agaru/sagaru is the fever's up-down pair.
freqNote: 熱 #1641; 下がる #1064 (上がる #503, for a rising fever). No phrase entry.

trap: Attending a class is deru with ni. jugyou o deru would mean walking out of it, and shusseki suru is the formal word.
why: Students say it constantly (kyou jugyou deru?). It shares one ni-deru frame with kaigi ni deru, and the o/ni switch flips the meaning.
freqNote: 授業 #2326, 出る #81. The deru count covers all its senses; the attend sense rests on judgement.

trap: Not shiai o suru for 'play in the game': taking part is deru (nichiyou shiai deru), and so is taikai ni deru (enter a tournament).
why: 'Are you playing Sunday?' is shiai deru no? It is the same deru as terebi ni deru (be on TV), so the 'appear in' sense is worth fixing.
freqNote: 大会 (tournament) #2691 takes the same verb.

trap: Not fue o hiku or suru: wind instruments are blown with fuku, the verb of kaze ga fuku (the wind blows).
why: Completes the instrument set, and also covers toranpetto/sakkusu o fuku and kuchibue o fuku (whistle).
freqNote: フルート #31008 and トランペット #33519 take the same verb. The 吹く rank #2962 includes the wind sense.

trap: False friend: sutairu ga ii means a good figure (slim, well-proportioned), not good fashion sense. Fashion is oshare.
why: A very common compliment, and an English speaker will misread or misuse it.
freqNote: スタイル #3954 covers both senses of the loanword, so it is not a count of this phrase.

trap: Not kopii o tsukuru: copies are 'taken' with toru. Kopii suru is also used.
why: A routine office and school request. It joins the pool's toru set (shashin, menkyo, ten, yasumi o toru).

trap: Not youji ga kuru: 'something came up' is kyuu ni youji ga dekita. Youji ga aru means 'I have things to do'.
why: The standard polite excuse for cancelling plans.

trap: Not hige o sodateru or nobasu: facial hair is 'made to sprout' (hayasu), the transitive of haeru. hige haeteru hito = a man with a beard.
why: The standard way to describe facial hair. It pairs with kabi ga haeru and hige o soru.
freqNote: nounRank is the katakana spelling ヒゲ (#9045).

english: be compatible, go well together (people, also food pairings)
trap: 'We're compatible' has no Japanese verb to copy. You say the match is good, aishou ga ii (also wain to chiizu wa aishou ga ii).
why: Everyday talk about couples, friends, coworkers and food pairings. It is the plain, literal word, not the idiom ki ga au.

english: do someone a favour (agree to a request)
trap: Not onegai o suru, which means making the request. Doing the favour is onegai o kiku (chotto onegai kiite kureru?).
why: This is the usual way to ask "can you do me a favour?" and to agree to one. English "do" leads to suru, which reverses who is asking.
freqNote: お願い #258 includes the onegai (shimasu) phrase; 聞く #67 counts all listen/hear/ask uses

english: run a shop, bar or restaurant
trap: Not hashiru or motsu. Running a shop is yaru (oya ga izakaya yatteru); keiei suru is formal.
why: Comes up when talking about family and jobs (jikka de pan'ya yatteru). English "run" gives no route to yaru.
freqNote: 店 #440 (みせ reading; てん #3482 counted separately); やる #45 counts every casual 'do'

trap: Not toire o tsukau: asking to use someone's toilet is 'borrowing' it (toire karite mo ii?).
why: A learner needs it at friends' homes, cafes and shops, and the natural verb can't be guessed from 'use'.

trap: 'Silent mode' is the made-in-Japan manaa moodo ('manner mode') with ni suru, not sairento ni oku.
why: A Japan-made loanword with a fixed frame, needed in cinemas, on trains and in meetings.
freqNote: Rare in drama subtitles but heard daily in train and venue announcements; commonness is judged.

trap: The candidate ukeru (receives) the interview, like shiken o ukeru; mensetsu o suru means you are the one interviewing.
why: Job hunting and part-time job interviews are common talk, and English 'have' leads the wrong way.

english: hot water comes out / runs (tap, shower)
trap: 'There's no hot water' is oyu ga denai, not oyu ga nai. This is the intransitive of mizu o dasu / oyu o dasu.
why: What you tell a landlord or hotel front desk (shawaa no oyu ga denai). It is the other half of mizu o dasu in the pool.

trap: 'Work for X' is not X no tame ni hataraku: say X ni tsutometeru (or X de hataraiteru), with ni and almost always in the -te iru form.
why: The self-introduction line about one's job. Neither the verb nor the particle can be guessed from English.
freqNote: 会社 #474, 勤める #2170. Homophones 務める (#2501, serve as) and 努める (#8888, strive) are counted separately. 働く hataraku #361 is the general partner (kaisha de hataraku).

english: a shop opens (for the day), is open
trap: Not mise ga akeru or hiraku: 'is it open?' is aiteru? or nanji made aiteru?. Mise o hiraku means opening a new shop.
why: Opening hours (nanji made aiteru?) are one of the most common shopping and plan-making questions.
freqNote: 開く read as aku shows #14086, but the tokenizer probably files most 開いてる under 開く read as hiraku (#624), so the real spoken rank of aku 'open' is higher. 空く #1498 is a different word.

trap: Not takushii o toru or takushii o tsukamu: hailing one in the street is hirou ('pick up'). tsukamaeru also works; phoning for one is yobu.
why: A verb nobody could guess; part of a set with takushii o yobu and takushii ni noru.
freqNote: Phrase not counted. hirou's rank mostly counts picking things up.

trap: Not seki o ageru: offering your seat to someone is yuzuru ('hand over').
why: A verb nobody could guess and a common train situation, though it's more often heard or told about than said.
freqNote: Phrase not counted.

trap: English 'an earthquake hit/struck' has no matching verb. Say jishin ga okiru (casually jishin ga atta / kita). The shaking itself is yureru.
why: Earthquakes are routine conversation in Japan, and okiru 'happen' is already in the versatility list.
freqNote: Rank is for the kanji 地震, because kana じしん is dominated by 自信 and 自身. 揺れる (shake) is #3717.

trap: Not samui kaze by default: wind you feel on your skin is tsumetai (cold to the touch). Samui describes the air or how you feel.
why: Shows the tsumetai vs samui split on wind. The split itself mostly belongs to senses/food (tsumetai mizu), so this is a reserve.
freqNote: 冷たい #1084 and 寒い #1214 rank close together. The split between them is a judgement call (samui kaze is also heard).

trap: English 'clean your room' leads to souji suru, which means scrubbing and vacuuming. Putting things away is katazukeru.
why: It's the most common household nag (heya katazukenasai) and the everyday word for tidying up. 'Clean' sends learners to the wrong verb.
freqNote: The 片づける spelling is #2251 and 片付ける is #2543; the higher one is recorded.

trap: Not uso ga mitsukaru: lies and secrets 'come out' with bareru (casual), as in uso bareta.
why: Pairs with uso o tsuku in the pool. bareru is very frequent in speech.
freqNote: nounRank is katakana ウソ (#1168); 嘘 is #1544. verbRank is katakana バレる.

english: put something off, deal with it later
trap: 'Put off' has no Japanese verb to copy. You turn the task into 'later', atomawashi ni suru.
why: Used for chores, homework and replies you keep putting off (sore wa atomawashi ni shiyou).

trap: Not kaigi o deru (= leave the meeting room) or kaigi ni sanka suru in casual speech: attending is ni deru.
why: The office twin of jugyou ni deru. English 'attend' has no obvious Japanese partner, and deru is the one natives use.
freqNote: 会議 #1612, 出る #81. The other everyday frame is ima kaigi chuu (in a meeting now).

trap: Not michi ni wataru or kurosu suru: what you cross takes o (michi, hashi, shingou o wataru).
why: Used in directions and warnings to children; the o for the path crossed is the only trap.
freqNote: Phrase not counted.

trap: There is no word for 'seconds' or 'refill' to translate; it is the noun okawari, used with suru or on its own (okawari kudasai).
why: A staple at restaurants and at home (okawari jiyuu, okawari suru?). Borderline under the noun+suru rule: the hard part is the noun, and suru is guessable.
freqNote: お代わり #3640 and the kana おかわり #4023 are counted separately, so the noun is more frequent than either rank shows.

trap: English 'it thunders' is one verb. Japanese makes the thunder sound: kaminari ga naru (鳴る 'ring', a homophone of naru 'become').
why: The standard way to say it's thundering (kaminari natteru). It separates naru 'sound' from naru 'become'. Same verb as denwa ga naru (media).
freqNote: The phrase 雷が鳴る is listed at #42945. Rank is for the kanji 鳴る, because kana なる (#29) is almost all 'become'.

trap: Not samui alone: chills 'do', samuke ga suru; samui means the room is cold.
why: Early fever sign on the sensation + ga suru frame, which English never predicts.
freqNote: 寒気 read さむけ #15754; する #15. No phrase entry.

trap: Shots are 'hit', chuusha o utsu; as the patient say chuusha utte moratta or utareta.
why: Clinic and vaccine talk; the patient side needs morau, so it's a reserve.
freqNote: 注射 #6757 (homophone 駐車 'parking' #18495); 打つ #1103; phrase entry 注射を打つ #36338.

english: expire, go past the use-by date
trap: There's no verb for 'expire': the deadline 'snaps' with kireru. For food, people say shoumi kigen ga kireteru. Passports and cards just say kigen ga kireta.
why: Fridge talk and expired cards or passports. It uses the same kireru as the pool's juuden ga kireru.
freqNote: 賞味期限 'best-before' is #12993. Kigen 期限 sounds the same as kigen 機嫌 'mood'.

trap: Not nimotsu ga tsuku: deliveries 'reach' you, so nimotsu todoita. Tsuku is for people and vehicles arriving.
why: Online orders arrive daily. Messages and letters use the same verb.

english: be a good person, have a nice personality
trap: 'He's nice' is usually seikaku ga ii or yasashii; seikaku ga warui means mean or nasty.
why: The literal personality description (not a metaphor), used constantly when describing people.

trap: Not juutai de tomaru: you 'fall into' traffic (hamaru), the same verb as geemu ni hamaru (get hooked).
why: The standard excuse for being late, and it pairs with geemu ni hamaru in the pool.
freqNote: verbRank is kana はまる (#3789), which also counts the 'get hooked' sense.

trap: A bruise dekiru (forms), not tsuku; usually aza dekichatta.
why: A common minor injury. It joins kega o suru, yakedo o suru and hone ga oreru.
freqNote: Kana あざ #10267 may include the clipped slang あざっす (thanks); アザ #11029, 痣 #34510.

trap: Not tokei o kiru: a watch takes suru (tokei shiteru). tsukeru also works but sounds stiffer.
why: Comes up in everyday talk ('no watch on today'). The clearest example of the suru-for-accessories rule.
freqNote: 時計 #3262 also counts clocks; 腕時計 'wristwatch' is #10342. Pairing commonness is judged.

trap: English 'iron' is a verb; Japanese says airon o kakeru, not airon suru.
why: A strong trap and part of the kakeru family, but ironing comes up less often than the other chores, so it's a reserve.
freqNote: かける #244 counts every sense of kakeru.

trap: Not ichinichi ga nagai, which means 'it was a long day': daylight hours are hi ga nagai / hi ga mijikai.
why: Seasonal small talk (hi ga nagaku natta ne, hi ga mijikaku natta). The catch is which 'day' noun to use.
freqNote: 日 #209 mixes the 'day' and 'sun' senses. Its partner 短い is #1621. The phrase itself isn't listed.

trap: No 'sore' adjective: the throat hurts, nodo ga itai.
why: Top cold symptom, and it shares nodo with nodo ga kawaku, so the two sit side by side.
freqNote: 喉 #3552; 痛い #336. No phrase entry.

trap: Not shingou: phone signal is denpa ('radio waves'); shingou is a traffic light.
why: Explains dropped calls and slow loading (koko denpa warui ne); denpa ga nai or kengai covers no signal at all.

trap: Not petto ga aru or petto o motsu: you keep an animal with kau (飼う), which sounds exactly like kau, 'buy'.
why: 'Do you have any pets?' (petto katteru?) is a staple of small talk. English 'have' pushes learners to aru or motsu, and the right verb sounds like 'buy'.
freqNote: 飼う #2759 is the kanji entry. Kana かう is dominated by 買う 'buy' (#238).

trap: 'Punctual' is an adjective in English, but Japanese 'protects the time': jikan mamotte ne.
why: Workplace and friend expectations. The same mamoru is used with ruuru and shimekiri.

trap: Like kami o kiru, you say you dyed your hair even when the salon did it. kinpatsu ni someru = go blond.
why: A common appearance change to describe, and it goes with kami o kiru.

english: be in a photo, appear in a picture
trap: Not shashin ni iru or haitte iru: appearing in a photo is utsuru, as in kono shashin ni utsutteru no dare?
why: Common when looking through photos together. English 'be in' leads to iru.

trap: Not koe ga fukai: a deep voice is low, hikui. A high-pitched one is koe ga takai.
why: How people describe a voice (on the phone, a singer, someone they like). Koe ga takai is its pair, and koe ga ookii (loud) is already in the pool.

trap: Not seki ga furii or seki ga hima: a free seat is aiteru ('open'), as in koko aitemasu ka?
why: Asked whenever you sit next to a stranger. Kept apart from suku (empty), though both are written 空く.
freqNote: Phrase not counted. 空く (aku) is ranked separately from 開く (#14086, a door opening).

trap: Not ikura kakaru for a price tag: what an item costs takes suru (kore ikura shita? = how much was this?); kakaru is for running costs of a trip or service.
why: People ask and give prices all the time (sore ikura shita?), and nothing in English suggests suru for 'cost'.
freqNote: いくら #553 counts all uses, including 'no matter how'. The shape is price + suru, so it takes amounts in place of ikura.

trap: Not suupu o taberu: soup and miso soup are drunk (nomu), even with a spoon.
why: English 'eat soup' pushes learners to taberu, and misoshiru o nomu is said at home every day. Thick, chunky soups and stews can take taberu.
freqNote: For miso soup: 味噌汁 #9117, みそ汁 #8272. 飲む #229 counts all drinking.

english: get an upset stomach, get diarrhoea
trap: English 'have an upset stomach' gives no usable verb. Japanese 'breaks' the stomach with kowasu, transitive, with the speaker as subject: onaka kowashita.
why: One of the most common reasons for calling in sick or skipping food. It's the polite everyday stand-in for diarrhoea.
freqNote: Kana おなか is #1253 and お腹 is #4758; the higher one is recorded.

trap: False friend: tenshon means excitement or energy, not stress. 'I'm excited' is tenshon agaru, and tenshon takai means hyper.
why: Constant in casual speech, especially among younger speakers, and the English word 'tension' points the opposite way.
freqNote: Phrase entry テンションが上がる at #30223. The tokenizer usually splits it.

trap: Not denki ga kesu: the intransitive is kieru, and 'the light is off' is denki kieteru.
why: Completes the four-way tsukeru/kesu/tsuku/kieru set, and covers power cuts and lights that are off.

trap: Not hana o fuku: fuku is for blowing air, wind or a flute. You blow your nose with kamu, which sounds like kamu, 'bite'.
why: The pool's kaze ga fuku and fue o fuku actively push learners toward hana o fuku. The cold cluster also needs this action.
freqNote: かむ #4775 is the kana entry, which mixes 擤む 'blow (nose)' with 噛む 'bite' (#6347). 擤む itself is not in the list.

trap: No 'addictive' adjective is used for snacks: you say kuse ni naru ('it becomes a habit').
why: Common when reacting to food and music (kono aji kuse ni naru). It also has the plain meaning 'become a habit'.
freqNote: Phrase entries 癖になる #14210 and クセになる #22463.

trap: Not okane o tsukau when you mean putting money into something: fuku ni okane o kakeru. It's the transitive half of okane ga kakaru.
why: For talking about where money goes: hobbies, looks, travel.
freqNote: verbRank is kana かける (#244), all senses; 掛ける alone is #2742.

english: get dirt or a stain off, clean it off
trap: English 'get off' or 'remove' suggests toru; the usual verb is otosu (drop), as in keshou o otosu.
why: The transitive half you use when you are the one cleaning (kono yogore otosenai).

trap: Not pakku suru or nimotsu o ireru: packing a bag is tsumeru, 'cram in' (mou nimotsu tsumeta?). nimotsu o matomeru means 'get your stuff together'.
why: Every trip starts with this. The same verb is used for bentou o tsumeru.
freqNote: nounRank is 荷物 and verbRank is 詰める.

trap: Not jiyuu: being free is aku, 'to open up' (ashita aiteru? = are you free tomorrow?).
why: The everyday way to ask about and offer availability, usually said as aiteru with jikan dropped.
freqNote: 空く (あく) #1498. The kana あく #3508 mixes senses, and 開く (a door opens) is ranked separately.

trap: Not warui kaze: a bad cold is hidoi kaze; warui means wrong or at fault.
why: Adjective + noun trap on the most common illness word (hidoi kaze hiichatta).
freqNote: 風邪 #2666; ひどい #444 (酷い #15387). No phrase entry.

trap: Not mizu o kesu: kesu is for lights, the TV and fire. Water and gas are stopped with tomeru. To turn the tap on: mizu o dasu.
why: The pool teaches denki o kesu, so learners will carry kesu over to taps. This is the needed contrast.
freqNote: 止める #545. Kana とめる is a separate entry and also covers 泊める.

trap: Japanese has no verb for 'sober up': being drunk 'wears off' (sameru), the same verb as me ga sameru.
why: Completes the drinking set (osake ni you, osake ga tsuyoi) and links the three sameru items in the pool.
freqNote: Also written 醒める (#51825); 覚める is the commoner spelling.

english: send (something) for repair, get it fixed
trap: English 'get it fixed' has no verb to translate; Japanese sends it out: sumaho o shuuri ni dasu.
why: The follow-up to the pool's broken-device items: a learner needs to say they're getting the phone fixed.

english: get a bonus (a bonus is paid out)
trap: The usual line is that the bonus deru (comes out): boonasu deta? Boonasu o morau is also fine.
why: A standard Japanese work topic twice a year. It pairs with the pool's kyuuryou ga hairu.

trap: Not kami ga ochiru: hair coming out (in the shower, from stress, with age) is nukeru. Ochiteru is only for a hair lying on the floor.
why: Common talk about stress, ageing, pets shedding and the shower drain. English 'fall out' pushes learners to ochiru.
freqNote: かみ is ambiguous (神 #1988, 紙 #2672), so 髪 #1752 is used.

trap: Not kaminari ga utsu: lightning falls (ochita). Kaminari ga naru is the thunder you hear.
why: Summer storm talk (ima ochita!, chikaku ni ochita). It pairs with kaminari ga naru in the pool, and English 'strike' sends learners to utsu.

trap: Not nikki o motsu or tamotsu: keeping a diary or any record is tsukeru, as in kakeibo o tsukeru (keep household accounts).
why: This is the textbook 'keep' trap: English 'keep' leads to motsu or tamotsu. It is also the only record-keeping sense of tsukeru, which elsewhere in the pool means 'turn on' or 'wear'. It is lower frequency in speech, so include it for trap value only if there is room.
freqNote: つける #393 covers every sense of tsukeru (turn on, attach, keep a record). 付ける alone is #1452.

trap: Not megane o nugu: nugu is only for clothes and shoes. Glasses, watches, masks, rings and earrings come off with hazusu.
why: One take-off verb covers every accessory (masuku, tokei, yubiwa o hazusu). It undoes kakeru, suru, hameru and tsukeru.
freqNote: Rank is for 外す #1043, which also counts 'miss' and 'step away (seki o hazusu)'. Pairing commonness is judged.

trap: Not sakkaa o asobu: asobu means playing around, so sports take suru (casually yaru: sakkaa yatteru).
why: Stands for every sport + suru/yaru (tenisu, yakyuu, gorufu). Learners reach for asobu here before anywhere else.
freqNote: suru #15; yaru #45 is the casual partner for sports. tenisu #9450 and yakyuu #3911 take the same verb.

trap: Not shiai o katsu: English 'win the game' is transitive, but Japanese wins at it with ni (geemu ni katta).
why: Comes up constantly in sport and game talk. The ni carries over to aite ni katsu (beat someone).
freqNote: 勝負 (contest) #1203 takes the same ni katsu.

trap: Not ka ni kamareru: mosquitoes and bees 'sting' with sasu, used in the passive. Kamu is for dogs and snakes.
why: A summer staple (ka ni sasareta, kayui). English 'bite' gives the wrong verb.
freqNote: The rank is for the dictionary form 刺す. The passive 刺される has no entry of its own.

trap: Not denpa o morau: having signal is denpa ga hairu, and 'no signal' is denpa hairanai.
why: 'Koko denpa hairanai' is said more often than denpa ga warui and is harder to guess.

trap: Not michi ga isogashii (busy is for people) or kuruma ga ooi: crowded roads, trains and shops are konderu.
why: One verb for crowded roads, trains and shops (densha konderu, mise ga konderu); English 'busy' leads to isogashii.
freqNote: Phrase not counted. komu is written 混む or 込む, and the list splits them (#5984 / #10624).

trap: Not jikan o jiyuu ni suru: clearing time for someone is akeru (ashita akete oku ne).
why: The transitive half of jikan ga aku. Less frequent, but the natural way to promise to keep a slot free.
freqNote: 空ける #3596. The kana あける is dominated by 開ける #480 (open a door).

trap: 'Get wet' is the single verb nureru, with no 'get' or naru added. The rain takes ni (ame de nureta is also heard).
why: Needed to say you got soaked (nurechatta, bishonure). Japanese uses one verb where English uses get + adjective.
freqNote: The kana spelling ぬれる (#5139) is unambiguous and outranks 濡れる (#6660), so it is used. びしょ濡れ (soaked) is about #26971–34709.

why: Fully guessable from English, and speech more often uses netsu ga takai; keep only as a weak reserve.
freqNote: 熱 #1641; 高い #421. No phrase entry.

trap: English 'connect' covers both: you tsunagu a device (waifai ni tsunaide), but the net tsunagaru on its own.
why: The transitive half of the pair, for hooking up a laptop or joining Wi-Fi (waifai ni tsunagu); setsuzoku suru is the formal word.
freqNote: verbRank is kana つなぐ (繋ぐ #10471) and also counts holding hands (te o tsunagu).

trap: Handing in is dasu ('put out'), not ageru or teishutsu suru in speech. When a teacher says it, dasu means 'set homework'.
why: Both school senses of dasu (submit / assign) on one noun. The versatility list glosses dasu as 'hand in', so this is the item that carries that sense.
freqNote: 宿題 #3935, 出す #163. The same verb is used for reports and forms: repooto o dasu, shorui o dasu.

trap: Not torihada o morau or ga deru: goosebumps 'stand up' with tatsu, and the noun is the subject. It covers cold, fear and being moved.
why: It's the literal, plain word for goosebumps (not an idiom), and a frequent reaction phrase. English 'get' gives the wrong verb.
freqNote: 鳥肌 is only #19017 in drama scripts. Calling it more common in real talk (torihada tatta! after a song or a scary story) is a judgement, not data.

trap: English gives no hint of kuzusu ('crumble'). Learners say byouki ni naru, which sounds like a real illness rather than being run down.
why: The standard way to say you got run down or caught something minor (taichou kuzushichatte). It comes up all the time in work and school excuses.
freqNote: Phrase entry 体調を崩す at #9388.

trap: Not tamago o kowasu: eggs, glasses and plates 'split' (waru).
why: Basic cooking. Waru is the transitive partner of the pool's gamen ga wareru.

english: visit someone in hospital, visit a sick person
trap: Not byouin o tazuneru or houmon suru: visiting a sick person is omimai ni iku.
why: Part of family and work life. English uses one verb where Japanese needs this noun phrase.
freqNote: The bare form 見舞い is #5796.

trap: Not chiketto o morau: securing tickets is chiketto o toru, and toreta! means 'I got them'.
why: Used for concerts, flights and trains (raibu no chiketto toreta!). Same toru as the pool's yoyaku o toru.

trap: Not hi o morau: sunlight 'hits', so a sunny room is hi ga ataru heya.
why: Housing talk, plants and laundry: 'kono heya, hi ga ataranai'.
freqNote: 日 #209 also counts 'day'.

trap: 'Empty' has no verb form; say kara ni suru (make empty).
why: Emptying bins, glasses, pockets and rooms.

trap: Not koeru: the cold itself 'heals', kaze ga naoru (kaze naotta?); you cure it with kaze o naosu.
why: How people ask and answer after an illness; naosu ('hayaku naoshite ne') is the transitive partner.
freqNote: 風邪 #2666; 治る #1604 (transitive 治す #2761; 直る 'be fixed' #4537 is a homophone). No phrase entry.

trap: Not terebi ni aru: 'the film is on TV tonight' is konban terebi de yaru ('TV is doing it'); ni deru is for people.
why: For asking or saying what's on (ima terebi de nani yatteru?); it contrasts with terebi ni deru, where a person appears.
freqNote: verbRank is やる across all senses.

trap: There's no English verb to translate: breath 'runs out' (kireru), the same verb as juuden ga kireru.
why: Said after stairs, running or sport (iki kireta). Paired with the pool's juuden ga kireru, it shows that kireru means 'run out'.
freqNote: Phrase entry 息が切れる at #37126. 息をする (breathe) is at #11944.

english: the conversation gets lively, have a great chat
trap: No English verb fits: talk and parties 'swell up' (moriagaru), as in sugoi moriagatta ne.
why: The usual way to say a chat, party or event went well. The verb is frequent and can't be guessed.

trap: English 'take' leads to motte iku; natives say dasu (send out), the same pattern as shuuri ni dasu.
why: A routine errand (suutsu o kuriiningu ni dasu). It teaches dasu as 'send out for a service'.
freqNote: クリーニング #7486; 出す #163.

trap: Not hanashi ga kawaru or hanareru: a conversation that drifts 'veers off' (soreru), and hanashi o modosu brings it back.
why: Managing a conversation: hanashi soreta kedo... or gomen, hanashi sorechatta. Useful for a learner keeping a chat going.
freqNote: verbRank uses the kana spelling それる (#17987); the kanji 逸れる is #64636.

trap: 'Sigh' is a verb in English. Japanese uses a noun with tsuku, the same verb as uso o tsuku.
why: Tameiki tsukanai de and tameiki bakkari are everyday remarks. Learners have no other way to say 'sigh'.
freqNote: つく at #355 lumps all its kana senses together. The 吐く (つく) reading alone is #173635.

english: black out; one's memory goes blank (from drinking)
trap: Not kioku o nakusu (amnesia, formal): blacking out from drink is kioku ga tobu (nomisugite kioku tonda).
why: The usual casual way to say you can't remember last night. It must be kept apart from plain oboete nai.
freqNote: nounRank is 記憶 and verbRank is 飛ぶ. The list has no phrase counts.

trap: 'Fall' asleep is tsuku (or just nemuru), not ochiru.
why: Fixed set, slightly narrative; casual speech says nechau.

trap: There's no separate verb for 'tan' or 'burn': the skin is 'grilled by the sun', hi ni yakeru, the same yakeru as niku ga yakeru.
why: Summer small talk (yaketa ne!). It links to the pool's niku ga yakeru and hizashi ga tsuyoi.
freqNote: 日 #209 counts every 'day / sun' use. The compound noun hiyake 日焼け is #11984.

english: take / drop someone to the station, see someone off
trap: Not just eki made tsurete iku: walking or driving someone somewhere is okuru (the 'send' verb), as in okutte iku yo.
why: The end of most evenings. okuru (escort) and mukae (pick-up) form a pair.

trap: Not eki o tsuku or eki ni kita for 'I'm here': arriving is tsuku with ni, as in ima eki tsuita.
why: The most-said travel update on the phone. Low trap because tsuku is already on the versatility list; only the ni is new.
freqNote: Phrase not counted. 着く is ranked apart from the kana spelling つく (#355).

trap: English splits grill, roast, bake, toast and fry; Japanese uses yaku for all dry-heat cooking (pan o yaku = make toast).
why: Yakiniku and barbecue talk (niku yaite, yakisugi). The one verb also covers pan o yaku and tamago o yaku. Its intransitive pair is niku ga yakeru.
freqNote: 焼く #1576 also counts burning things.

trap: Not kami ga sodatsu: hair grows = nobiru. 'Your hair's grown' is kami nobita ne.
why: The intransitive half of the nobiru/nobasu pair on the same noun. A common catch-up remark.

trap: Not tsumoru (that's for snow): work, chores and laundry pile up with tamaru.
why: A common reason to be busy: 'shigoto tamatteru'. The same frame works for sentakumono.
freqNote: verbRank is kana たまる.

english: ruin one's health, make oneself ill (from overwork)
trap: English 'ruin your health' gives no verb; Japanese breaks the body: muri suru to karada kowasu yo.
why: The everyday warning and explanation (karada kowashite yameta). The pool's taichou o kuzusu is the formal version.

trap: A smell clinging to clothes tsuku (sticks), like shimi ga tsuku: yakiniku no nioi ga fuku ni tsuita.
why: Comes up after every yakiniku, smoky bar or cooking session. It sounds the same as tsuku 'arrive'.
freqNote: Kana におい #1940 (匂い #2171, 臭い as におい #7168); 1570 is 付く (kana つく #355 mixes in 着く 'arrive').

trap: Not suibun o nomu: you 'take in' fluids, suibun o toru, just as you say eiyou o toru for nutrition.
why: What everyone says to someone who is ill, or in summer heat: chanto suibun totte ne.

english: stick in one's mind, be memorable
trap: Not oboeyasui or kioku suru: 'the most memorable part was…' is ichiban inshou ni nokotta no wa…
why: The stock way to say what stood out about a trip, film or person, asked and answered constantly (nani ga ichiban inshou ni nokotta?).

kana: きゅうりょうがあがる
trap: Not kyuuryou o morau, which is just 'get paid': a raise is the salary going up, kyuuryou agatta.
why: A staple of work small talk and complaints about prices. It pairs with kyuuryou ga hairu in the pool.
freqNote: 上がる #503; kana あがる #3514 is listed separately.

trap: Not deeta o nakusu: files and photos disappear, kieru (shashin zenbu kiechatta). Kesu is deleting them yourself.
why: The phone-disaster sentence after a reset or a broken phone. It is the intransitive partner of shashin o kesu.

trap: Not taijuu o tsukeru or eru: weight is the subject and it increases, taijuu ga fueru. To lose weight is taijuu ga heru, or simply yaseru.
why: It comes up in health, diet and holiday-eating talk ('shougatsu de taijuu fuechatta'). English 'put on / gain' leads to tsukeru or eru. The single verbs futoru and yaseru are more common, so this item earns its place as the 'put on' trap rather than on frequency.

trap: Not densha ga osoi: osoi means slow, and a train running late is okureteru. Switching ga to ni flips it to 'I missed the train'.
why: The standard excuse (densha okurete...); learned with densha ni okureru, where the subject changes.
freqNote: Phrase not counted. okureru's rank also covers people being late.

trap: Not densha o misu shita or densha o nakushita: missing a train is ni okureru (casually also nogashita or noriokureta).
why: English 'miss' has no direct verb. Must be kept apart from densha ga okureru (the train is late).
freqNote: Phrase not counted. Alternatives natives use: nogasu (#2510) and the single verb noriokureru (#13876).

trap: Not kuruma de byouki ni naru: motion sickness uses you, the verb for getting drunk (kuruma yoi, fune ni you).
why: Common on bus and car trips and impossible to guess; the noun form kuruma yoi (suru) is just as frequent.
freqNote: Phrase not counted. you's rank is mostly about drunkenness.

trap: Same tsukeru as lights, and eakon o kakeru (run it) is equally natural; not on ni suru or mawasu.
why: Said all summer and winter ('eakon tsukete ii?'). Notes can cover the kakeru variant and danbou o ireru.
freqNote: 暖房 #15369 and 冷房 #25132 take the same verbs (also ireru); つける #393 counts every sense.

trap: Not taiko o hiku or suru: drums are hit, tataku, and a drum kit works the same way (doramu o tataku).
why: Third verb of the instrument set (hiku / fuku / tataku). The selector may prefer doramu as the headword for band talk.
freqNote: ドラム (drum kit) #14894 takes the same verb. The kana spelling たたく #1900 is counted apart from 叩く, so tataku is commoner than #5024 suggests.

trap: Not 'sugu byouki ni naru hito' as the default: 'gets sick a lot' is karada ga yowai. Karada ga joubu is the sturdy opposite.
why: The plain way to describe a delicate constitution in yourself, kids or parents. It is the opposite of genki.
freqNote: 体 (からだ) #371, separate from 体 (たい) #47884; 弱い #970. Joubu #6353 for the opposite.

trap: Not kabi ni naru: mould 'grows' the way hair does (haeru).
why: Comes up with bread, bathrooms and the rainy season (pan ni kabi haeteru). Haeru also gives hige ga haeru.
freqNote: Phrase entry カビが生える at #39241. カビ ranks low in dramas but is a fixture of rainy-season home talk.

trap: There's no adjective for 'fit': stamina is something you have or lack (tairyoku aru, tairyoku nai).
why: Comes up in talk about ageing, sport and work. Mou tairyoku nai is the most common form.

trap: Not just yotei ga ippai: a full schedule is 'stuffed' (tsumaru), like a blocked nose. Example: raishuu wa yotei ga tsumatteru.
why: Used to decline or reschedule, and it links to hana ga tsumaru in the pool.

english: have the same tastes, share interests
trap: English 'we share hobbies' points to a sharing verb, but Japanese says your tastes 'match' (au), as in saizu ga au.
why: Meeting people and saying why you get on (shumi ga au hito ga ii). It's a literal way to say it, unlike the idiom ki ga au, which is out of scope.

english: be perceptive, quick to catch on, have good instincts
trap: English 'sharp' leads to atama ga ii, which means clever. Picking up on things is kan ga ii.
why: A frequent remark when someone guesses right (kan ii ne!). It is literal (intuition is good), not a character idiom.

english: run a fever, come down with a fever (of a person, often a child)
trap: Not netsu o morau: with the person as subject it is netsu o dashita (musuko ga netsu dashite). Netsu ga deta is the same event from the fever's side.
why: The standard way to say someone came down with a fever, the commonest reason for cancelling plans or missing work.

trap: English uses the adjective 'stiff'; Japanese uses the verb koru: kata ga kotteru.
why: A national complaint in Japan, said constantly, and koru can't be guessed.
freqNote: 肩 #1811; 凝る #6722 (kana こる #4566); phrase entry 肩が凝る #35013; the noun 肩こり is #33119 and 肩凝り #32224.

trap: Not kaze o ageru: you 'transfer' a cold, kaze o utsusu (kaze utsushichatta, gomen).
why: The transitive half of the pair, used in apologies and in 'dareka ni utsusareta'.
freqNote: 風邪 #2666; 移す #3371 (kana うつす #12396). No phrase entry.

trap: Not shiai o nakusu: losing a contest is makeru (losing an object is nakusu), and it takes ni, never o (shiai ni maketa).
why: Pairs with shiai ni katsu. English 'lose' splits in two here, and the same form gives aite ni makeru (lose to someone).

trap: Not piano o benkyou suru or ressun o toru: lessons with a teacher are narau (kodomo no koro piano naratteta).
why: Childhood lessons are a standard getting-to-know-you topic. narau is the lessons verb for piano, eigo, karate and ryouri alike, and it is not in the versatility list.
freqNote: 習い事 (lessons taken as a hobby) #15541.

trap: Not tebukuro o kiru: gloves 'fit on' (hameru), like rings; tebukuro o suru is also everyday.
why: Gloves are the commonest hameru item in daily life, more so than rings.
freqNote: verbRank is the kana spelling はめる (#2952), the usual one.

trap: Not michi o tanomu or michi o shitsumon suru: asking the way is kiku, the verb for listening.
why: For telling the story of a trip (michi kiitara...); the other half of michi o oshieru.
freqNote: Phrase not counted.

trap: Not jikan ni tsuku or dekiru: making it in time is maniau, with ni on the deadline or train (densha ni maniatta).
why: Said constantly when running late. Its opposite, jikan ni okureru, is H-okureru, and ni marks what you catch.
freqNote: 間に合う #904 counts the whole verb, which also means 'be enough' (mou maniatteru = I'm fine, thanks).

trap: Not mizu o niru: you boil 'hot water' (oyu), and the verb is wakasu; niru is for cooking food.
why: Needed for kettle, tea and instant noodles. The trap is double: both the noun and the verb differ from English. It sits on the food boundary.
freqNote: 沸く #6780 is the intransitive (oyu ga waku = the water's boiled).

trap: Intransitive half: 'the kettle's boiled' is oyu ga waita, not oyu ga wakashita.
why: Completes the pair: oyu waita yo is what you say when the kettle clicks off. ofuro ga waita (home domain) works the same way.
freqNote: The kana わく also matches 湧く (#3148, well up), so the rank used is for 沸く (#6780).

trap: Not taiyou ga tsuyoi or taiyou ga atsui: strong sun is hizashi (sunlight) ga tsuyoi.
why: A common summer remark. The trap is the noun (sunlight, not sun). Groups with kaze ga tsuyoi and ame ga tsuyoi as the 'tsuyoi' weather set.
