freqNote: 日差し is #16499. The spellings 日ざし (#26917) and 陽射し (#82664) are counted separately, so the real frequency of the noun is higher than the rank shows.

trap: No 'stuffy' adjective: the nose clogs, hana ga tsumaru (hana tsumatteru).
why: Cold and hay-fever symptom that sits next to hanamizu ga deru.
freqNote: 鼻 #2627; 詰まる #2789; phrase entry 鼻が詰まる #98306.

trap: A topic that's on the test 'comes out' in it, kore tesuto ni deru?, not shiken ni aru.
why: A classic student question. It sits apart from shiken o ukeru and from jugyou ni deru (attend), which share the noun or the verb.
freqNote: Students mostly say tesuto ni deru (テスト #2539). 出る #81 counts all senses.

trap: Not kami ga hikui: hair length is mijikai. Hikui is only for height (se ga hikui).
why: Completes the hair pair and is the direct contrast to se ga hikui (two kinds of 'short').

trap: Not mezamashi ga deru or ga iku: alarms, phones and bells ring with naru (鳴る), which sounds like naru, 'become'.
why: 'My alarm didn't go off' (mezamashi naranakatta) is the classic excuse for being late. It pairs with mezamashi o kakeru.
freqNote: 目覚まし #15035 counts only the short form; mezamashi tokei is a separate compound. 鳴る #2069 is a different entry from なる 'become' (#29).

english: a stain or dirt comes out
trap: Not yogore ga deru: stains 'fall off', so kono shimi ochinai. Removing them is yogore o otosu.
why: Laundry and cleaning talk. It's the intransitive model behind the pool's keshou o otosu.

trap: Not shimi o morau: a stain 'attaches', so shimi tsuichatta. Getting it out uses ochiru.
why: Spilled coffee and curry on clothes. The frame also covers nioi ga tsuku and kizu ga tsuku.
freqNote: Noun is katakana シミ (#9793); 染み is #13129. Verb is kana つく (#355), which also counts 'arrive'; 付く is #1570.

trap: Not just atatakai fuku o kiru: 'wrap up warm' is one noun, atsugi ('thick wearing'), plus suru.
why: Parents and friends say it every winter, and the suru pairing on a native noun can't be guessed.
freqNote: atsugi is seasonal and rare in drama subtitles; commonness is judged from winter talk.

trap: The stomach rings: naru (鳴る), the verb for a phone or alarm, not the naru that means 'become'.
why: Common and slightly embarrassing moment (onaka natchatta). It links the ringing naru of denwa ga naru to the body.
freqNote: Kana おなか #1253 (お腹 #4758); 2069 is 鳴る. Kana なる #29 is almost all 'become'.

english: get a belly, have a paunch
trap: English 'get a gut' or 'put on weight' gives no clue: the belly deru (sticks out), usually onaka dete kita.
why: The everyday way to talk about middle-age weight, about yourself or someone else.

trap: Not botan o shimeru or kakeru: buttons are tomeru (fasten); undoing them is hazusu.
why: The only fastening item for clothes, with an unguessable verb. It is one of the weaker additions.
freqNote: ボタン #3688 also counts push-buttons. 10553 is 留める; kana とめる #9778 and 止める #545 are the same sound, often written that way.

english: a queue forms, there's a line
trap: Not gyouretsu ga aru: a queue 'comes into being', gyouretsu ga dekiteru. Joining it is narabu.
why: Used for popular ramen shops, sales and attractions (itsumo gyouretsu ga dekiteru mise).

trap: Not kinniku o tsukuru. Muscle is 'attached' with tsukeru, the transitive half of kinniku ga tsuku.
why: It is common in gym and fitness talk (kinniku tsuketai) and is said about yourself, which is where speakNeed comes from. It completes the transitive/intransitive pair with kinniku ga tsuku.
freqNote: verbRank is for 付ける. The kana つける (#393) lumps every sense together (turn on, attach, wear), so it is not used here.

english: join a company, start working at a company
trap: English 'join a company' pushes to sanka suru (take part). Joining a firm, school or club is hairu: kaisha ni haitte sannen.
why: This is a self-introduction staple (kono kaisha ni haitte go-nen desu). The same pattern gives daigaku ni hairu (get into university), so the item also covers school entry.

trap: Not okane o toru: cash from the bank or ATM is orosu, 'bring down' (dasu also works casually).
why: A weekly errand phrase (chotto okane oroshite kuru), and no English verb leads to orosu.
freqNote: 下ろす #2775 covers all senses, including lowering things. 降ろす #4786 is letting people off.

trap: Not omoi ame: heavy rain is strong rain, ame ga tsuyoi / tsuyoi ame (or ame ga hidoi). Omoi is only for weight.
why: English speakers almost always fall into the 'heavy' → omoi trap. 'Ame tsuyoku natte kita' is a staple. Pairs with kaze ga tsuyoi.
freqNote: The attributive tsuyoi ame is the same pairing. The single nouns 大雨 (#11181) and 土砂降り/どしゃ降り (#30415–32931) are alternatives, not collocations.

trap: Not shiken o pasu suru: passing is a verb English gives no hint of, ukaru, and the exam takes ni, not o (also daigaku ni ukatta).
why: Pairs with ochiru as the two outcomes. The verb is unguessable and the particle is counter-intuitive. Learners need it for their own test results.
freqNote: 受かる #3494 is the spoken verb. 合格 goukaku (#2357) is the formal noun (goukaku suru).

trap: Not hirou or toru: you pick a person up by going 'to meet' them, mukae ni iku. When they come for you: mukae ni kuru.
why: Learners need to say this constantly, and the pool's takushii o hirou will teach them hirou for 'pick up'.
freqNote: 迎え #8575 is the noun on its own. Calling it common is a judgement: pick-ups are daily family and friend logistics (eki made mukae ni iku ne).

english: reply to a message or email
trap: Not meeru ni kotaeru: replying to a text is kaesu, 'send back' (LINE kaeshite, henji kaesu). kotaeru is for answering questions.
why: The most common messaging verb after okuru (gomen, kaesu no wasureteta). The pool's henji o suru is the general 'reply' and doesn't give the messaging verb. Keep apart from kaeru (go home).
freqNote: nounRank is メール and verbRank is 返す. The same verb goes with LINE / henji.

trap: Not keshou o nugu or toru: makeup is 'dropped' with otosu, the same verb used for dirt and stains.
why: The take-off half of keshou o suru, done daily by people who wear makeup. The partner verb can't be guessed.
freqNote: Rank is for 落とす #923, which is mostly the 'drop' sense. Pairing commonness is judged.

trap: Not michi ga karappo or michi ga hima: an uncrowded road or train is suiteru, the same suku as in onaka ga suku.
why: The opposite of michi ga komu, learned with it; densha suiteta is just as common.
freqNote: Phrase not counted. The list files nearly all 空く under the aku reading (#1498), so suku's #47898 comes from how the list splits words, not real rarity.

trap: When the money is the subject the verb is tamaru (okane tamattara = once I've saved up), not transitive tameru.
why: The intransitive half of okane o tameru, the form heard when people talk about plans (okane tamattara ikitai).
freqNote: 貯まる #24870 is the money spelling. The kana たまる #1650 is mostly other senses (tamaranai).

trap: Not yotei o tsukuru or oku: you 'put in' a plan (raishuu ni ireta = I put it in for next week).
why: The transitive half of yotei ga hairu, used when booking things into a calendar.

trap: Not kami o kawaku or fuku: drying it yourself is the transitive kawakasu, while kami ga kawaku means it dries.
why: A routine after the bath ('kami kawakashite kara neru'). The trap is mainly the kawaku/kawakasu split, so it's a reserve.
freqNote: かみ #1752 is 髪; 紙 #2672 and 神 #1988 are homophones (the existing lists hold kami = paper).

why: Guessable (up = agaru) and forecast-flavoured. A weak reserve; kion ga sagaru belongs in the same entry.
freqNote: Its partner 下がる (fall) is #1064. Kion sounds like a forecast word; in conversation people mostly say atsuku naru / samuku naru.

trap: 'Cough' is a verb in English; in Japanese the cough comes out, seki ga deru (seki ga tomaranai).
why: Core cold symptom on the ga deru frame; seki o suru is a near-synonym.
freqNote: 咳 #21022 is the kanji only. Kana せき #11682 probably holds most spoken uses but can't be told apart from kana 席/関, so it is not used. 出る #81; phrase entry 咳が出る #70272.

trap: Not hana ga hashiru: 'nose water comes out', hanamizu ga deru.
why: Cold and hay-fever symptom on the same ga deru frame as seki and netsu.
freqNote: 鼻水 #12653; 出る #81. No phrase entry.

trap: Not kami o sodateru: growing your hair out is nobasu ('lengthen'), e.g. ima kami nobashiteru.
why: The transitive half of the pair. Learners need it to talk about their own look ('nobashiteru tochuu').

english: sleep lightly, be a light sleeper
trap: Not karui nemuri: sleep is 'shallow', asai. Deep sleep is nemuri ga fukai.
why: Sleep complaints are common in conversation. English 'light' and 'heavy' push learners to karui and omoi, which are wrong here.

trap: Not senaka ga itai: 'bad back' pain sits in the koshi (lower back and hips). Senaka is the upper back.
why: Probably the most common adult aches-and-pains line. Here the noun is the trap, not the adjective.

trap: Not tsukare ga naoru: tiredness 'comes off' (toreru). It isn't cured.
why: Comes up in everyday talk about sleep, baths and holidays (nete mo tsukare torenai), and the verb can't be guessed.
freqNote: 取れる #631 counts all its senses (come off, can get, be taken). 疲れを取る is a phrase entry at #62068.

trap: There's no verb for 'scratch': a scratch 'attaches' (kizu ga tsuku).
why: Said of phones, cars and floors (sumaho ni kizu tsuita). Pairs with the pool's gamen ga wareru.
freqNote: Phrase entries 傷がつく #8777 and 傷が付く #17905. verbRank is 付く.

trap: Not only nakusu: losing a wallet or phone while out is usually otosu ('drop'), and the police ask where you dropped it.
why: The standard way to report a lost item (saifu otoshichatta). Otosu is also what lost-and-found staff will say back.

trap: Not isha o miru (that means looking at the doctor): to see a doctor is isha ni kakaru, or isha ni mite morau.
why: Common advice, 'isha ni kakatta hou ga ii yo', and English 'see' leads straight to miru.
freqNote: verbRank is kana かかる, all senses together.

trap: Not sakujo suru in speech: 'delete that photo!' is sono shashin keshite. Kesu means erase as well as switch off.
why: Constant in casual phone talk. The same verb covers deleting messages and apps.

trap: Not mise ga aku (that's opening for the day): a shop that has just opened is atarashii mise ga dekita.
why: Neighbourhood small talk: 'eki no mae ni atarashii kafe dekita yo'.

trap: Not kusuri o nomu or tsukeru: creams, ointment and sunscreen are 'spread' on (nuru); nomu is only for swallowing.
why: Contrasts directly with kusuri o nomu (in the pool) on the same noun. It also covers hiyakedome o nuru (sunscreen).

trap: English 'unplug' is one verb; Japanese pulls out the konsento (plug/socket). Plugging in is konsento ni sasu.
why: Household instruction (konsento nuite) with a loanword that is a false friend and a verb English never suggests.
freqNote: コンセント #20298, a low rank for a word used daily, because it is a household word rather than drama dialogue; 抜く #1432.

english: a bug turns up (in the house)
trap: Not mushi ga iru for the moment of seeing it: pests (and ghosts) 'come out', gokiburi ga deta!
why: Gokiburi deta! is the classic household cry. Deru for things appearing is not obvious.

english: have a meal now, make it mealtime
trap: English 'let's eat' pushes to gohan o tabeyou. At home people say sorosoro gohan ni shiyou (let's switch to the meal), and ofuro ni suru? gohan ni suru? asks which comes first.
why: This is a constant household phrase. The same frame gives ohiru ni suru (let's have lunch). It fits next to warikan ni suru, naisho ni suru and manaa moodo ni suru in the pool.
ippai nomi ni ikou is the after-work invitation.

trap: Not densha o tsukamaeru or densha o toru: making a train in time is ni maniau ('be in time for').
why: Said daily (maniau? / maniawanai! / maniatta), and English 'catch' has no matching Japanese verb.
freqNote: Phrase not counted. maniau ranks high because it covers any deadline.

trap: Not mezamashi o oku or setto suru: alarms are kakeru'd, like locks and vacuum cleaners.
why: Needed for every 'I set it for six' exchange. The noun is rare on its own, so the phrase is the useful unit.
freqNote: 目覚まし #15035 is the everyday short form; アラーム #12854 competes (araamu o kakeru / setto suru). かける #244 counts every sense.

trap: Not denki o tsukeru when nobody's doing it: 'the light is on' is denki ga tsuiteru.
why: Intransitive half of the pair, and how you say 'you left the light on' (denki tsuitteru yo). It sounds the same as tsuku 'arrive'.
freqNote: つく #355 is the kana spelling across senses (付く #1570, 点く #45903); 着く 'arrive' is ranked separately at #957.

trap: Not kasa o tsukau, hiraku or motsu: holding an umbrella over yourself is sasu. Kasa o hiraku only means opening it, and kasa o motsu means carrying it.
why: The verb for a daily action can't be guessed, and it is the umbrella's own verb (kasa sashinasai, kasa sasanakute ii?).
freqNote: Rank is for 差す. Kana さす (#3059) mixes 刺す, 指す and the causative -sasu, so it isn't used. Usually written 傘をさす.

trap: Not shinu: the plain way to say a dead phone is juuden kireta ('the charge ran out'); sumaho shinda is only a joke.
why: The everyday excuse for a missed call (juuden kirechatta); charging is the plain verb juuden suru, and juuden ga nai covers 'low battery'.
freqNote: juuden ranks low overall, but nearly all its uses are this phrase and juuden suru; batterii is #9633.

trap: Not nekutai o kiru: a tie is 'tightened' with shimeru, which sounds like shimeru 'close'. Wearing one is just nekutai shiteru.
why: For talk about work clothes. beruto o shimeru (belt) uses the same verb and goes in the notes.
freqNote: Rank is for 締める #4630. Kana しめる is mostly 閉める 'close' (#1764).

trap: Not densha ga yameru: yameru is quitting. A train stopping (at a station, or halted) is tomaru.
why: Two daily uses: kono densha Shibuya ni tomaru? and densha tomatteru (service halted). The intransitive half of kuruma o tomeru.
freqNote: Phrase not counted.

trap: Checking the seasoning is aji o miru ('look at the taste') or ajimi suru; ajiwau means savour.
why: Kitchen talk (chotto aji mite). Worth more for listening than speaking, because tabete miru is an acceptable fallback.
freqNote: The compound most people use, 味見 (ajimi suru), is #5952. How often the phrase itself comes up is my judgement.

trap: Not netsu o toru: you 'measure' a fever, netsu o hakaru (netsu hakatta?).
why: Routine at home and at clinics, and English 'take' misleads again.
freqNote: 熱 #1641; 測る #5009 (計る #10638 is also used for this); phrase entry 熱を測る #89256.

trap: Not ashi ga neru or nemuru: a numb, tingling foot is shibireru.
why: Sitting on the floor and in seiza makes this frequent in Japan, and the English image of 'asleep' is wrong.
freqNote: Kana しびれる is #6477 and 痺れる is #37594; the higher one is recorded.

english: the AC is working (cooling or heating properly)
trap: Not ugoku: for an AC that is running but not cooling, Japanese says it doesn't kiku (take effect), as in kusuri ga kiku. Usually eakon kiitenai.
why: A daily complaint in summer and winter. It reuses the 'take effect' kiku from kusuri ga kiku.
freqNote: エアコン #9318; 効く #1822 (homophone 聞く #67).

english: be online, be posted on the internet
trap: Not netto ni aru: being posted or listed is noru (載る), the same sound as getting on a train. Usually netto ni notteru.
why: Common when pointing someone to information (netto ni notteta yo). The same verb covers 'it's on the menu' (menyuu ni notteru).

english: feel heavy and run-down, feel sluggish
trap: Not just tsukareta: the heavy, achy feeling of a cold coming on is karada ga darui.
why: One of the first things you say at the doctor's or when calling in sick.

trap: Not oru, which is for paper or snapping something. Clothes, laundry, futons and umbrellas are tatamu.
why: Folding laundry is a daily chore, and learners can't guess the verb. The same verb closes an umbrella (kasa o tatamu) and puts the futon away (futon o tatamu), both next to pool items.
freqNote: 服 #1051; 畳む #6592 (kana たたむ #20410 counted separately)

trap: English 'rest up / recover' has no noun. Japanese 'takes off' the tiredness: onsen de tsukare o toru, yukkuri yasunde tsukare totte ne.
why: This is the transitive half of tsukare ga toreru, which is in the pool. You hear it in caring phrases and in talk about baths and holidays.

english: a typhoon is coming, a typhoon hits
trap: English 'a typhoon hits' pushes to ataru or utsu. Japanese says the typhoon comes: ashita taifuu kuru rashii yo.
why: From August to October this is daily small talk and planning ('will the trains run?'). The weather set should not leave it out.
freqNote: 台風 ranks #8171 because drama subtitles under-count weather talk. In a Japanese late summer it is daily small talk, so commonness is a judgement.

trap: Not paama o suru or morau: a perm takes kakeru, like an iron (airon o kakeru). At the salon it is paama o kakete morau.
why: It completes the hair set already in the pool (kami o kiru, kami o someru, kami o nobasu). Of these, it is the only one whose verb can't be guessed: English 'get' gives morau or toru. Include it if the hair set goes in as a group.
freqNote: The noun is rare in dramas (#16625), so commonness rests on judgement of hair-salon and appearance talk.

english: the alcohol kicks in; start to feel drunk
trap: English 'it's hitting me' has no verb a learner could map. Feeling the drink kick in is yoi ga mawaru, also osake ga mawaru.
why: Common at nomikai (kyou wa mawaru no hayai na). It contrasts with yoi ga sameru (sobering up), which is already in the pool.
freqNote: nounRank is 酔い and verbRank is 回る. The list has no phrase counts.

trap: Not densha kara deru or densha ni oriru: getting off is oriru, with the vehicle marked by o (or kara).
why: The partner of ni noru; the particle switch (ni to get on, o to get off) is the classic slip.
freqNote: Phrase not counted. In speech the noun usually drops: tsugi de oriru.

trap: Not samuku naru or tsumetaku naru: hot food or drink cooling off is sameru; samui is for weather and people.
why: Heard at nearly every meal (samenai uchi ni douzo, koohii sameta, samechau yo). The transitive samasu (let it cool) is the rarer partner and goes in the notes.
freqNote: 冷める #2747 also counts feelings cooling. The verb goes with any hot food or drink (koohii, ocha, ryouri), so gohan is only the headword noun.

trap: Not osake o motenai: low tolerance is 'weak at alcohol' (osake ga/ni yowai).
why: The standard, face-saving way to turn down drinks (osake yowai n desu). Pair it with osake ga tsuyoi.
freqNote: 弱い #970 counts every sense of weak. osake ni yowai is an equally correct variant. How often the phrase itself comes up is my judgement.

trap: Not aji ga yowai or aji ga nai: food short on salt is usui (thin), the same word as weak coffee.
why: The everyday verdict on home and restaurant food (chotto usui ne). Learn it as a pair with aji ga koi.
freqNote: 薄い #2547 also counts thin (paper, walls) and pale (colour).

trap: Not tsuyoi koohii: coffee, tea and flavour are koi (dense) or usui (thin); tsuyoi is for alcohol.
why: The classic 'strong is not tsuyoi' trap. usui koohii is the opposite, and the same koi/usui pair covers koi ocha and koi aji.
freqNote: The rank is for the kanji 濃い (#3669). The kana こい also matches 来い and 恋, so its rank can't be trusted.

trap: Not watashi wa ippai: the stomach is what's full, onaka ippai.
why: The way to turn down more food (mou onaka ippai); it completes the hunger pair with onaka ga suku.
freqNote: おなか #1253; いっぱい #512 counts every sense ('a lot', 'full', 'a cupful'); 一杯 #2892. Ippai is a noun or adverb, not a verb or adjective; it goes in the partner slot. No phrase entry; 満腹 is #18617.

trap: Catching it from a person is kaze ga utsuru, not kaze o hiku (utsuru kara chikazukanaide).
why: What the sick person warns and others fear; the intransitive half of the utsuru/utsusu pair.
freqNote: 風邪 #2666; 移る #2350 (kana うつる #34832; 映る and 写る are separate words). No phrase entry.

trap: Not tsukau or asobu: idly being on your phone is sumaho o ijiru ('fiddle with'); tsukau means using it for a task.
why: Describes what everyone is doing (zutto sumaho ijitteru). Its mild 'idle fiddling' tone lets it double as a complaint.
freqNote: nounRank is スマホ; keitai (#1458) is the older word and still common. verbRank is kana いじる; 弄る barely appears.

trap: 'Be into / hooked on' has no verb to translate, so learners fall back on suki desu. The native way is X ni hamatteru, with ni.
why: The everyday way to say what you are into lately (saikin X ni hamatteru), with any hobby noun. It is informal but fine with desu/masu. It is the plain way to say this, not a body-part or character idiom.
freqNote: はまる #3789 and ハマる #4047 are one word in two spellings. The subtitles count them separately, so real use is higher than either rank.

kana: うんどうしんけいがいい
trap: There is no adjective for 'athletic': say undou shinkei ga ii ('motor nerves are good'), not supootsu ga jouzu.
why: The everyday way to call someone sporty or coordinated. English gives no route to it.
freqNote: 運動神経 #12050 as a whole compound. It occurs almost only in this phrase and in undou shinkei ga nai/warui, so the phrase is commoner than the rank suggests.

trap: Not kanjou o wakeru: splitting the bill is the noun warikan + ni suru, literally 'make it warikan'. Warikan de ii? is the usual question.
why: Comes up almost every time you eat out with friends. English 'split' gives the wrong verb.
freqNote: 割り勘 is low in drama scripts (#12038). Calling it common whenever friends eat out is a judgement, not data.

trap: Not mise ga tojiru: closing time is shimaru, as in mou shimatteru ('it's already closed'). Mise o shimeru is the owner closing up, and mise o tatamu is closing down for good.
why: The other side of mise ga aku. 'It's closed already' and 'it closes at 9' are needed constantly.

trap: Not konbini ni tomaru, which means staying the night there: dropping in on the way is yoru.
why: A daily plan-making line (chotto konbini yotte iku). The pool's densha ga tomaru and hoteru ni tomaru make tomaru the likely mistake.

trap: Not heya ga kitanai for clutter: messy is chirakatteru, and kitanai means dirty.
why: Hosts say it whenever a guest comes in (chirakatte te gomen). It needs to be kept apart from kitanai (dirty).
freqNote: The transitive 部屋を散らかす is a phrase entry at #118129.

trap: Not just mise ga ippai or hito ga ooi: busy restaurants and trains are konderu, and the opposite is suiteru.
why: Used when deciding where to eat (ima konderu kara ato de). The pool's michi ga komu is the traffic use. This is the much more frequent use for places and trains, and it pairs with suku.

trap: English 'skip' pushes toward tobasu. Meals are 'pulled out': asagohan nuita (any meal works).
why: Common in health and diet chat: 'hiru nuite shimatta'.
freqNote: 朝ご飯 #5780; 朝ごはん is #6629.

trap: Not furui (things only) or ookii: 'older than me' is watashi yori toshi ga ue (toshiue), and younger is toshishita.
why: Age comparison comes up when meeting anyone in Japan, and English 'older' leads to furui.
freqNote: ue is a noun, not an adjective. The compound 年上 toshiue is #3068.

english: make yourself understood; speak the same language
trap: Not wakaru: being understood in a language is tsuujiru, usually with the language as the subject (eigo tsuujiru?, nihongo ga tsuujita).
why: This is the learner's own situation: asking whether English works and saying they got through. It also gives hanashi ga tsuujinai (we're not on the same page).

ja: アクセサリーを付ける
kana: アクセサリーをつける
trap: Not akusesarii o kiru: earrings, necklaces and badges take tsukeru, or just suru (piasu shiteru).
why: Completes the wear verbs (kiru/haku/kaburu/kakeru/suru/hameru/tsukeru). It is less frequent than the others.
freqNote: Rank is for 付ける #1452. The 'wear' spelling 着ける is #3726, and kana つける (#393) also counts the turn-on and attach senses. ピアス 'earrings' is #13111.

trap: Not kontakuto o kakeru like glasses: lenses go in with ireru and come out with hazusu or toru.
why: Daily for lens wearers, and it builds on versatility ireru. Narrow outside that group.
freqNote: コンタクト #8030 also counts 'contact (get in touch)'. コンタクトレンズ is #34753. Rank is for 入れる #222.

trap: Not mafuraa o kiru: a scarf takes suru (mafuraa shiteru), or maku 'wrap' for the act of putting it on.
why: A winter item. It repeats the suru rule already taught by masuku and tokei, so it is a reserve.
freqNote: Ranks are for マフラー #11291 and する #15. 巻く 'wrap' is #3104.

trap: English 'put your hair up' doesn't carry over; the verb is musubu 'tie' (casually kami shibaru or matomeru).
why: Everyday for long hair (kami musunde iku?), but mostly guessable, so a reserve. Cutting and washing hair belong to body/home.
freqNote: Rank is for 髪 #1752. Kana かみ is also 紙 'paper' (#2672) and 神 'god' (#1988). Hair kami was left out of the 180 nouns as a homophone of 10-list-nouns #14 (kami 'paper'). 結ぶ #2173.

kana: しゅうでんがなくなる
trap: Not shuuden o misu suru: Japanese says the last train 'is gone', as in shuuden nakunatchau!
why: The everyday excuse for leaving a night out; the train is the subject, not the speaker. Alternatives: shuuden ni maniawanai, shuuden nogashita.
freqNote: Phrase not counted. 397 is the kana spelling なくなる (無くなる #8961), and its rank covers running out of anything.

trap: Not nimotsu o oku or nimotsu o nokosu: handing bags over to be kept (hotel, locker, airport check-in) is azukeru. Leaving them behind by mistake is wasureru.
why: A hotel and airport staple where both 'leave' and 'check' mislead.
freqNote: Phrase not counted.

trap: Not densha ga hanareru or densha ga saru: a train or bus leaving is just deru, as in tsugi no densha nanji ni deru?
why: The everyday way to ask about timetables (shuppatsu suru is the announcement word); built on H-deru.
freqNote: Phrase not counted. deru's rank covers every sense of going out or appearing.

trap: Not uchi o hanareru or nokosu: leaving home for the day is deru, and the place you leave takes o.
why: Every 'what time do you leave?' exchange uses it ('nanji ni uchi deru?'). The trap is the o particle and the many senses of English 'leave'. Overlaps the travel domain.
freqNote: うち #113 also counts 内 'among/while'; 家 read いえ is #152.

trap: English 'vacuum' is a verb, but Japanese says soujiki o kakeru, not soujiki suru or soujiki o tsukau.
why: A routine chore with a verb no one would guess. It belongs to the kakeru family with kagi, mezamashi and airon.
freqNote: かける #244 counts every sense of kakeru.

trap: Not kakeru or tsurusu: laundry put out to dry is hosu, and the noun is sentakumono (the clothes), not sentaku.
why: Everyday in Japan because laundry is line-dried ('sentakumono hoshita?'). Both the noun and the verb are traps.

trap: No English verb leads here: bed hair 'sticks on' (neguse ga tsuku), as in neguse tsuiteru yo.
why: A frequent, friendly morning remark, and both the noun and the verb are unguessable.
freqNote: つく #355 is the kana spelling across senses (付く #1570).

trap: Not sentakuki o hashiraseru or ugokasu: you 'spin' (mawasu) the washer.
why: Everyday household talk ('sentakuki mawashite oite'), and the verb is a pure trap. Plain sentaku suru is the guessable alternative.
freqNote: 回す #1242 counts every sense of mawasu.

trap: Not gohan o ryouri suru or niru: rice has its own verb, taku.
why: A verb nobody could guess, used daily at home (gohan taiteoku, suihanki de taku). Its intransitive half is gohan ga takeru.
freqNote: 炊く #7563 is used almost only for rice, so its rank roughly tracks this phrase. gohan #1225 also counts the 'meal' sense.

trap: There is no 'get' to translate: it is the verb you, and the drink takes ni (not o).
why: Core nights-out talk (chotto yotta, yotteru desho). The same verb with ni gives kuruma ni you (carsick), and yopparau is the casual partner.
freqNote: 酔う #1768 also counts motion sickness (kuruma ni you). The louder synonym 酔っ払う is #3569. In speech the noun is usually dropped (yotta, yotteru).

trap: Not osake o takusan moteru: a heavy drinker is 'strong at alcohol'; with the drink as topic (kono osake wa tsuyoi) it means the drink is strong.
why: Said all the time at drinking parties (osake tsuyoi ne!). It also shows that a drink's strength IS tsuyoi, unlike koi koohii.
freqNote: 強い #310 counts every sense of strong. How often the phrase itself comes up is my judgement.

trap: Not aji ga tsuyoi: heavy salt or sauce flavour is koi.
why: The other half of aji ga usui, and the adjective+noun form koi aji is also common. It largely shares its lesson with koi koohii, so the selector may want only one of the two.
freqNote: The rank is for the kanji 濃い. The kana こい collides with 来い and 恋.

trap: Not shouyu o oku or ireru: sauce poured over food is kakeru (also mayo, dressing, sauce).
why: Table talk (shouyu kakeru?, kakesugi). It uses the same 'cover/hang' kakeru as megane o kakeru, which helps that verb make sense.
freqNote: Ranks are for the kana spellings (しょうゆ #6392, ahead of 醤油 #8743; かける #244). The かける rank counts every sense (call, sit, spend, put on); 掛ける alone is #2742.

trap: The rice cooker finishing is gohan ga taketa; gohan ga dekita means the whole meal is ready.
why: The intransitive half of gohan o taku, included so the pair is complete. A reserve.
freqNote: 炊ける #16178 is rare as a word, and the phrase is heard almost only at home.

trap: Meat being cooked through is yakeru ('it got grilled'), not niku ga dekita.
why: The intransitive half of niku o yaku, heard at every yakiniku (mou yaketeru yo). A reserve, included so the pair is complete.
freqNote: 焼ける #3296 also counts burning down and sunburn (hi ni yakeru).

kana: てんきよほうがはずれる
trap: A forecast doesn't machigaeru (that is a person's mistake) or chigau. It misses, hazureru, or hits, ataru.
why: A classic weather complaint (yohou hazureta jan), and the verb can't be guessed. Its partner yohou ga ataru belongs in the same entry.
freqNote: Rank is for the compound 天気予報. 予報 alone is #13931. Its partner 当たる (hit/be right) is #719.

trap: English 'the weather turns/breaks' points to kawaru or kowareru. Worsening weather 'crumbles': kuzureru.
why: How people pass on the forecast (gogo kara kuzureru rashii yo). The verb can't be guessed at all, but tenki ga waruku naru also works.
freqNote: Both parts rank mid-range. Its frequency as a phrase is a judgement call: it sounds forecast-like but is commonly repeated in speech.

trap: English has no verb for it: the rainy season is 'entered', tsuyu ni hairu, and when it ends it 'opens', tsuyu ga akeru.
why: A seasonal fixture in Japan with no English equivalent. Its partner tsuyu ga akeru belongs in the same entry.
freqNote: 梅雨 is #22408. The compounds 梅雨入り (#55384) and 梅雨明け (#72305) are listed separately, and 明ける is #6605. Low numbers in drama data, but the phrase is a fixture of June–July small talk.

trap: English 'there's a rainbow' points to niji ga aru. A rainbow comes out: niji ga deru (or niji ga kakaru).
why: A rare topic, but it shows deru for anything appearing in the sky (hi ga deru, tsuki ga deru), so it can stand for that whole pattern.
freqNote: Rank is for the kanji 虹, because kana にじ is dominated by 2時 (two o'clock).

trap: Not hakike ga aru: nausea 'does', hakike ga suru; in casual talk people say kimochi warui.
why: Completes the ga suru symptom set and is what you'd tell a doctor.
freqNote: 吐き気 #12206; する #15; phrase entry 吐き気がする #15877.

trap: Guessable; only the tense trips people: tired eyes now is me ga tsukareta / tsukareteru.
why: Screen-age complaint, near-literal and low trap; a reserve.
freqNote: 目 #216; 疲れる #714. No phrase entry.

trap: The ankle isn't named: you sprain the ashi, ashi o kujiku (ashi kujiita), or nenza shita.
why: A common minor injury with an unguessable verb, but narrow; a reserve.
freqNote: 足 #707; kana くじく #13346 (挫く #93027). No phrase entry.

trap: There is no 'turn up' verb: volume up is oto o ookiku suru ('make the sound big') and down is chiisaku suru; oto o ageru / sageru also work.
why: A household request (oto chotto chiisaku shite) built from known words, since ookii already means 'loud' in the versatility list.
freqNote: verbRank is the adjective ookii; suru is not counted. boryuumu is #9893.

trap: Not deru: 'it came out nice' is kirei ni toreta / yoku toreteru (it got taken well).
why: Said over every phone screen after a photo (ii shashin toreta!); the intransitive partner of shashin o toru.
freqNote: verbRank is the 撮れる spelling; kana とれる (#3422) mixes in 'come off'.

trap: Not just insutooru suru: everyday 'get the app' is apuri o ireru ('put in'); deleting it is kesu.
why: Common when setting up or recommending (kono apuri irete); it reuses ireru from the versatility list, where it already means put in and turn on.

trap: Not okuru: okuru sends to a person; putting a photo up online is ageru ('raise') or appu suru, as in insuta ni ageta.
why: Social-media talk (sore insuta ni agete ii?); it sounds the same as ageru 'give', so context does the work.
freqNote: verbRank is 上げる; kana あげる (#668) is mostly 'give'.

trap: Not kowareru: a cracked screen wareru ('splits'); kowareru means the phone stopped working.
why: The common phone mishap (sumaho no gamen wareta); wareru also covers glass and plates, so it carries over to the home list.
freqNote: kowareru is #1363, for comparison.

trap: For a phone or online video the everyday word is douga; bideo suggests a camcorder or tape. The verb is the same toru as for photos.
why: Phone-camera talk (douga totte!); douga o miru is the watching side (clips, YouTube).
freqNote: ビデオ is #5141.

trap: waifai aru? is fine, but natives often ask waifai tonderu? ('is Wi-Fi flying?'), which is opaque if you only know tobu as 'fly'.
why: Heard in cafes and homes (koko waifai tonderu?). Mainly for listening, since waifai aru? is an acceptable thing to say.
freqNote: nounRank is the ＷｉＦｉ spelling (katakana ワイファイ is #78072). Subtitles mostly write it in Latin letters, so the noun is undercounted.

trap: Not shukudai o morau: homework 'comes out', shukudai ga deta (we got homework). It is the intransitive half of shukudai o dasu.
why: Completes the dasu/deru pair on the same noun, so the transitive/intransitive split is learned together.
freqNote: 宿題 #3935, 出る #81. The deru count covers all its senses; this sense rests on judgement.

kana: きゅうりょうがはいる
trap: 'I got paid' is the pay 'coming in', kyuuryou haitta (or kyuuryou ga deta), not a passive of harau.
why: Payday talk (kyuuryou haittara...). It has the same ga-hairu shape as shigoto ga hairu, and English 'get paid' points the wrong way.
freqNote: 給料 #1927, 入る #115. kyuuryou o morau is also fine and guessable. It borders time-money (money in general).

trap: Not 'shiroi hito', which reads as 'a white person': fair skin is iro ga shiroi ('colour is white'). Iro ga kuroi means tanned.
why: A common appearance remark and compliment in Japan. The shape cannot be guessed and the literal alternative misfires.
freqNote: 色 #1136; 白い #1914. The compound irojiro #17583 says the same thing as one word.

english: lay out the futon (make up the bed)
trap: Not futon o tsukuru or futon o oku: you spread bedding out with shiku. Putting it away is futon o tatamu (fold) or shimau.
why: A daily routine in Japanese homes, ryokan and with host families. Nothing in English points to shiku.

trap: Nothing in English 'run a bath' points to wakasu: Japanese heats the bath, the same verb as oyu o wakasu. When it's ready: ofuro waita yo. Ofuro o ireru is also heard.
why: A nightly household exchange in Japan (ofuro waita yo, the bath is ready). The pool can't express it at the moment.

trap: Not okane o kowasu or waru: breaking a note into change is kuzusu, 'crumble'. For example, ichiman en kuzushite moraemasu ka.
why: Needed at shops, ticket machines and buses that need coins. 'Break' would give kowasu.

trap: There's no adjective for 'picky': it's 'many likes and dislikes', sukikirai ga ooi (or ga hageshii). Not picky at all: sukikirai nai.
why: Hosts and new friends ask sukikirai aru? when sharing food. It's built entirely from words the learner already knows.

trap: Not tamago o wakasu: wakasu is for boiling water. Cooking food in boiling water (eggs, pasta, noodles) is yuderu.
why: Completes the 'boil' set with oyu o wakasu and oyu ga waku. Otherwise English 'boil' sends eggs and pasta to wakasu.
freqNote: Kana ゆでる is #9809 and 茹でる is #25651; the higher one is recorded.

trap: Not sumaho ga kooru: kooru is ice. A frozen screen 'hardens' with katamaru. Furiizu suru is also heard.
why: A daily tech complaint. English 'freeze' leads straight to kooru.
freqNote: 固まる #4448 also counts 'harden / set / freeze up (a person)'. The device sense is one use among several.

english: pollen is in the air (hay-fever season)
trap: English 'the pollen count is high' has nothing to translate. Japanese pollen 'flies' with tobu: kafun tonderu ne.
why: Spring small talk in Japan centres on hay fever. It's the same tobu as the pool's waifai ga tobu.
freqNote: 花粉 is #16753 in drama scripts. Calling it common in real spring talk is a judgement, not data.

english: see a doctor, get checked by a doctor
trap: Not isha o miru, which means you look at the doctor. The doctor looks at you: isha ni mite morau.
why: A classic reversal: 'see a doctor' translated word for word gives the wrong sentence. The pool's byouin ni iku names the place and avoids the verb.
freqNote: verbRank is the dictionary form 診る. 医者にかかる is a phrase entry at #47992.

trap: Not wasuremono o oku: leaving something behind is wasuremono o suru, or just wasureta.
why: Comes up on trains, in taxis and in classrooms (wasuremono shinai you ni). A classic noun + suru that can't be guessed.

trap: You don't need a word for 'handwriting': say ji ga kirei or ji ga kitanai (the characters are neat or messy).
why: A common compliment and self-description. Ji ga heta is also used.
freqNote: verbRank is hiragana きれい, the usual spelling.

trap: Not sumaho o kowashita, unless you broke it: 'my phone broke' is intransitive, sumaho kowareta.
why: English 'my phone broke' hides the transitive/intransitive choice. The same frame works for pasokon and terebi.

trap: Not gohan ga junbi da: 'dinner's ready!' is gohan dekita yo (dekiru = come into being).
why: Called out in every household. The pool's gohan ga takeru covers only the rice cooker.
freqNote: verbRank is kana できる (#73); 出来る is #1313.

trap: Not nikibi o morau: spots, rashes and blisters 'form', so nikibi dekichatta.
why: The model for every skin complaint (mame, kuma and aza all take dekiru).
freqNote: ニキビ (katakana) #28682; hiragana にきび #69135.

trap: Dipping is tsukeru, pouring over is kakeru: sushi ni shouyu tsukeru, but toufu ni shouyu kakeru.
why: Teach it with the pool's shouyu o kakeru: the two are a classic table-manners mix-up.
freqNote: Noun is kana しょうゆ (#6392); 醤油 is #8743. Verb is kana つける (#393), all senses; 付ける is #1452.

ja: シートベルトを締める
kana: シートベルトをしめる
trap: Not tsukeru or kiru: belts and ties are shimeru ('tighten'). Casually, shiitoberuto shite.
why: Said every time you get in a car or taxi.
freqNote: 締める #4630; kana しめる (#1764) is mostly 閉める 'close'.

trap: English 'get out' pushes toward deru. Families say ofuro agatta? ('came up out of the bath').
why: The other half of ofuro ni hairu, used every evening at home.

trap: Not uchi ni hairu: you step up into a home, so 'come on in' is douzo agatte.
why: Hosting and visiting: 'agatte agatte' and 'ojama shimasu'.
freqNote: Noun is kana うち (#113), which also counts 'within'; 家 read いえ is #152.

english: take, walk or drive someone home
trap: Not tsurete iku: seeing someone home is okuru ('send'), so okutte iku yo, or eki made okuru.
why: After every evening out: 'okutte iku yo' / 'okutte kurete arigatou'.
freqNote: Noun is kana うち, which also counts 'within'.

trap: Not megusuri o ireru or nomu: eye drops take sasu, the same verb as kasa o sasu.
why: Hay-fever season and screen strain. A doctor or pharmacist will say it to you.
freqNote: 差す #7696; kana さす (#3059) mixes several sasu verbs.

trap: Not gohan o oku: leaving food on your plate is nokosu, as in nokoshite ii? or nokosanaide.
why: Table manners and full-up talk: 'gomen, chotto nokoshichatta'.

trap: Not koe o nakusu: a hoarse voice 'withers', as in karaoke de koe kareta.
why: After karaoke, cheering or a cold.
freqNote: verbRank is 枯れる (#6468), which also covers withering plants; 嗄れる is only listed with the reading しゃがれる.

trap: Not kiru or tsukeru: creams and lotions are spread on, so nuru (the paint verb).
why: Summer routine. Nuru also covers ointment, butter and lip balm.

trap: Not atsui ga dame: 'I can't take heat (or cold)' is atsusa ni yowai / samusa ni yowai. It's the osake ga yowai idea with ni.
why: Weather small talk about yourself. The pool's osake ga yowai gives the model.

trap: Not tsuyu ga owaru: the rainy season 'opens out' (akeru), the same akeru as yo ga akeru (day breaks).
why: The second half of the tsuyu ni hairu / tsuyu ga akeru pair that frames every early-summer weather chat. The verb can't be guessed.
freqNote: 梅雨 is seasonal, so its drama rank understates how much it comes up in June and July.

trap: English has a verb, but in Japanese a sneeze 'comes out' (kushami ga deru); kushami o suru also works.
why: Completes the cold and hay-fever set with seki ga deru and hanamizu ga deru. English offers no noun to start from.

english: get a cramp in one's leg
trap: Not ashi ni kuranpu ga aru: a cramping leg 'tsuru' (pulls tight). It's usually said in the past: ashi tsutta!
why: Used for cramps in sport, swimming and at night. Nothing in English leads to tsuru.
freqNote: 攣る is nearly always written in kana, and kana つる (#2909) is shared with 釣る and 吊る, so the kanji row (#151338) understates it.

trap: Not bansoukou o kiru or kakeru: anything stuck on flat (plasters, compresses, stickers, posters) is haru.
why: The small-injury follow-up to kega o suru. The same haru covers shippu (compresses).
freqNote: nounRank is the kana spelling (#19099); 絆創膏 is #23672. Regional brand-names (kizuban, sabio, bando-eido) vary.

english: turn on the tap / the water
trap: Not mizu o tsukeru: tsukeru is for lights and power, while water is 'let out' (dasu).
why: The water half of the on/off set. English 'turn on' leads to tsukeru, which is wrong here.

kana: せんたくものをとりこむ
trap: Not sentakumono o ireru or motte kuru: laundry is 'taken in' (torikomu). Example: ame futte kita, sentakumono torikonde!
why: The other half of sentakumono o hosu (in the pool), and a daily rush whenever rain starts.

trap: Switches are 'put in' (ireru) to turn on and 'cut' (kiru) to turn off, not tsukeru and kesu.
why: Covers heaters, kotatsu, rice cookers and PCs. dengen o ireru / kiru (power) uses the same frame.

trap: Not osake o ireru: ireru is for making tea and coffee, while pouring into someone's glass is tsugu.
why: Pouring for others is central to drinking etiquette, and it contrasts with ocha o ireru in the pool.
freqNote: 注ぐ is listed only under the reading sosogu (#4243), and kana つぐ (#10827) is mixed with 継ぐ and 次ぐ, so there's no clean rank for tsugu.

trap: Japanese has no verb for 'dump': you get 'shaken off' (furu, passive furareru), as in kanojo ni furareta. Don't confuse it with ame ni furareru.
why: A staple of relationship talk. It works the same with kareshi, and it forms a confusable pair with ame ni furareru.
freqNote: The passive 振られる has its own row (#23700).

trap: Not just yoku kikoenai: the set phrase is 'the phone is far', as in chotto denwa ga tooi n desu ga.
why: The fixed polite phrase for a bad line. It mirrors mimi ga tooi.

trap: English 'turn off' leads to kesu; a ringing alarm is stopped: tomeru.
why: Part of every morning, and the step the alarm set is missing: you set it (kakeru), it goes off (naru), you stop it (tomeru).
freqNote: 目覚まし #15035 (めざまし same entry); アラーム #12854 is the loanword alternative; 止める #545 covers every 'stop' sense.

english: get worn out, tiredness builds up
trap: English 'worn out' gives only tsukareta; built-up tiredness is a noun that tamaru (piles up), like sutoresu ga tamaru.
why: Very common way to say you're run down (tsukare tamatteru), and the opposite of tsukare ga toreru, which is already in the pool.
freqNote: 疲れ #3920; 1650 is kana たまる, which mixes 溜まる and 貯まる (溜まる alone #16850).

trap: English 'yawn' is one verb; Japanese is a noun that deru (comes out), or akubi o suru.
why: An everyday body reflex. It follows the same deru pattern as seki and kushami, so it fits in the same group.
freqNote: Kana あくび #14579 (the kanji 欠伸 is not in the list); 出る #81.

trap: Not shakkuri ga aru: hiccups deru, and 'I can't stop hiccupping' is shakkuri ga tomaranai.
why: An everyday reflex with an unguessable verb. It is one of the weaker additions and can be cut if space is tight.
freqNote: Kana しゃっくり #28750, a low rank, so commonness is set at 2; 出る #81.

trap: Not kasa o shimeru: an umbrella is folded, tatamu; opening it is sasu (or hiraku).
why: The opposite of kasa o sasu, which is in the pool. English 'close' leads straight to shimeru.

kana: せんたくものをたたむ
trap: Not oru: oru is for folding paper (origami) or breaking things; clothes and laundry are tatamu.
why: A daily chore whose verb English sends to the wrong word (fold → oru).

trap: Not butsukaru: a crashing app ochiru (falls); a frozen one katamaru.
why: An everyday phone problem, and English 'crash' leads straight to the wrong verb.

trap: Not ofuro ga dekiru: a bath that is ready waku (heats up). The bath panel announces ofuro ga wakimashita.
why: Heard every evening (ofuro waita yo), and the intransitive half of ofuro o wakasu.

english: get dark circles under one's eyes
trap: Dark circles are a noun, kuma, and they dekiru (form), like nikibi ga dekiru.
why: The standard remark about someone who looks exhausted (kuma sugoi yo).
freqNote: 68268 is 隈. Subtitles usually write クマ (#6292) or くま (#14871), but both are mostly 'bear', so the true rank is unknown and higher than 68268. Commonness rests on judgement.

english: a cockroach shows up, there's a cockroach
trap: Not gokiburi ga iru for one that has just appeared: pests (and ghosts) deru. The usual cry is gokiburi deta!
why: A classic summer moment at home. It teaches the 'appear' sense of deru, which English 'there is' hides.

trap: English 'get food poisoning' gives no verb; Japanese is 'hit by' the food: kaki ni atatta.
why: A high-trap idiom-free phrase for a common travel and eating mishap. It is one of the weaker additions by frequency.
freqNote: 食べ物 #2103; 当たる #719. In real speech the specific food usually replaces tabemono (kaki ni atatta).

trap: Not kinniku o tsukuru: muscle tsuku (attaches); building it on purpose is kinniku o tsukeru.
why: The usual way to talk about the result of gym or sport, with a verb English never suggests.
freqNote: 筋肉 #4421; 1570 is 付く (kana つく #355 is mixed).

trap: Not infuru o hiku (hiku goes with kaze only): named illnesses take ni kakaru (infuru ni kakatta, korona ni kakatta).
why: After kaze o hiku, this is the next illness phrase learners need, and the verb changes. Byouki ni kakaru uses the same frame, and infuru ni natta is a casual alternative.
freqNote: Short form インフル is #38273 and full インフルエンザ is #15539. かかる #385 is the kana spelling shared by every sense (take time, cost, hang); the illness kanji 罹る is #126444.

trap: Not shigoto ga hima ni naru or shizuka ni naru: a busy stretch 'settles' (ochitsuku), the same verb as calming yourself down.
why: The usual polite way to put off plans: shigoto ga ochitsuitara nomi ni ikou. It connects work talk to making plans.

trap: English 'swamped' or 'snowed under' gives no verb: Japanese says you're 'chased by work' (owareru, the passive of ou).
why: A small-talk and excuse staple (saikin shigoto ni owaretete). It says more than isogashii and is the natural way to put it.
freqNote: The passive 追われる has no entry of its own (lemmatised), so verbRank is the base verb 追う (#1006).

english: turn out fine, clear up (the weather)
trap: Not 'become weather': here tenki alone means fine weather (ashita tenki ni naru kana = hope it's nice tomorrow).
why: Small talk about tomorrow's plans and the forecast, and the meaning can't be worked out from the parts. Learn it beside ame ni naru (turn to rain) and tenki ga kuzureru.

trap: Not ireru or tsunagu: plugs go in with sasu and come out with konsento o nuku. Konsento is the wall socket, not 'consent'.
why: Charging your phone at a friend's place or a hotel (juudenki sashite ii?). It's the third sasu after kasa o sasu and megusuri o sasu.
freqNote: Both 差す (#7696) and 挿す (#17730) are written for plugs; the kana さす (#3059) mixes several verbs.

trap: There's no fog word: glasses 'cloud over' with the same verb as the sky (kumoru).
why: A winter and mask complaint in Japan (masuku suru to megane ga kumoru). It belongs in the glasses set with kakeru and hazusu.

trap: English 'it says read' has no noun: on LINE the read mark 'attaches' (kidoku ga tsuku), and reading without replying is kidoku suruu.
why: Messaging in Japan runs on LINE, and kidoku tsuita kedo henji konai is an everyday complaint.
freqNote: kidoku suruu (既読スルー, read and ignored) has its own entry at #25718.

english: air out a room, let fresh air in
trap: English 'air out' has no Japanese match: you 'swap the air' (irekaeru), usually after opening a window.
why: Home routine and cooking smells (mado akete kuuki irekaeyou). Airing rooms became a daily habit after the pandemic.

trap: Not hana ga ochiru: scattering petals (above all sakura) chiru (sakura mou chitchatta).
why: Spring sakura talk and timing hanami before the petals go. It pairs with hana ga saku, already in the pool.
freqNote: hana here is flower (#1169), not the nose homophone in 10-list-nouns #37; sakura (#3953) is the usual subject.

trap: Not just takai: 'pricey but worth it' is ne ga haru, built from ne (price) and haru (stretch), words a learner won't connect.
why: Recommending a shop or restaurant (chotto ne ga haru kedo oishii). It's softer than takai when the price is worth it.
freqNote: 値 read 'ne' has no single-word entry (only あたい and ち readings); the whole phrase 値が張る has its own entry at #38507. 値段 (nedan) is #2953.

english: work a shift, be on the rota
trap: Not shifuto o suru: you 'enter' a shift, shifuto ni hairu (ashita shifuto haitteru).
why: Part-time and shift workers say this every week to explain why they can't come.

trap: Not demae o chuumon suru or kau: you 'take' delivery, demae o toru. Younger people also say uubaa tanomu.
why: The standard way to say you're getting food delivered instead of cooking.

english: be a small eater, not eat much
trap: Not taberu no ga sukunai or chiisai: a small eater's eating is 'thin', shoku ga hosoi.
why: Common when refusing more food or describing kids and older people. It is the plain expression, not a body-part metaphor.

trap: Plugging something in is sasu (insert), and the socket takes ni: konsento ni sasu. Unplugging is nuku.
why: Comes up whenever phones need charging (juudenki sashite oite, konsento ni sasu). English "plug in" has no Japanese verb a learner could guess.
freqNote: Both parts are rare in dramas: 充電器 #21014, 差す #7696 (挿す #17730; kana さす #3059 mixes several meanings). Commonness is judgement.

trap: Not tsukuru for "make a mess". Making a mess is the one verb chirakasu, the transitive partner of chirakaru.
why: The transitive half of heya ga chirakaru, which is in the pool. People say it to kids and roommates (chirakasanaide, mata chirakashita).

trap: Not omoi. Heavy makeup is koi (thick, dense) and light makeup is usui; meiku ga koi works the same way.
why: A common comment on appearance (kyou meiku koi ne). It uses the same koi / usui split the pool teaches for coffee and seasoning.

kana: きゅうきゅうしゃをよぶ
trap: English 'call' pushes to denwa o kakeru; you yobu (summon) an ambulance, as in the shout kyuukyuusha yonde!
why: This is the one emergency phrase a learner must be able to produce. It also teaches that yobu (summon) applies to services, not only to people, alongside takushii o yobu.
freqNote: Both ranks are real lookups. Dramas inflate emergencies, so commonness is judged lower than the noun rank suggests, while speakNeed stays high.

trap: English 'not a morning person' has no calque (asa no hito ja nai is wrong). Say asa ga yowai, and asa ga hayai for an early start or an early riser.
why: People use it all the time to describe their own daily routine. It is the same yowai as osake ga yowai and atsusa ni yowai already in the pool, and it is worth contrasting with asa ga hayai ('I have an early start tomorrow').

trap: Not waruguchi o hanasu. Badmouthing takes iu, like monku o iu and joudan o iu.
why: It comes up constantly in talk about friends, coworkers and family (hito no waruguchi iwanai de). It belongs in the pool's iu set next to monku o iu, joudan o iu and orei o iu.

english: skin gets rough or irritated, break out
trap: English 'my skin is dry / bad' pushes to hada ga kawaku or warui. Skin that flares up from stress, cold or lack of sleep areru (hada areta).
why: This is everyday self-care talk (nebusoku de hada areta, fuyu wa hada ga areru). The partner verb cannot be guessed from English, and the pool's skin item, nikibi ga dekiru, does not cover it.

english: get over a cold (actively), shake off a cold
trap: English 'get well' has no object, but Japanese makes you naosu the cold: hayaku kaze naoshite ne (get well soon).
why: Hayaku (kaze) naoshite ne is the everyday get-well wish. This is the transitive half of kaze ga naoru, which is already in the pool; the two are learned as a pair.

kana: けっこんしきをあげる
english: have a wedding, hold the ceremony
trap: English 'have a wedding' pushes to motsu or aru. A ceremony is held with ageru (shiki o ageru). Casual speech also says kekkonshiki yaru.
why: It is standard in adult talk about friends and family (shiki wa itsu ageru no?). It sounds the same as the stage-2 verb ageru (give) but is a different verb, which a learner must keep apart.

trap: Not futsukayoi ga aru. You become hungover (futsukayoi ni natta), or simply say futsukayoi da.
why: It is the natural follow-on to the drinking set already in the pool (osake ni you, yoi ga sameru, osake ga tsuyoi/yowai), and a frequent Monday-morning line.

english: be treated (to a meal), let someone pay
trap: Not a passive like gochisou sareru: being treated is gochisou ni naru, like osewa ni naru. The person paying says gochisou suru or ogoru.
why: Said every time someone pays for your meal or drinks. The set thanks gochisou ni narimashita goes with gochisousama.
freqNote: ごちそう #2702 (kana) also counts gochisousama; ご馳走 #15229.

trap: Not pointo o morau as the default: points build up, so tamaru. Pointo o tameru is collecting them and pointo o tsukau is spending them.
why: Every checkout in Japan asks about point cards. Pointo tamatteru and tamaru kara kocchi de kau are everyday shopping talk.
freqNote: ポイント #2464 also counts 'point' as in key point. 貯まる #24870 is the money/points spelling. Kana たまる #1650 mostly counts tamaranai ('unbearable'), so it is not used.

english: music is playing (in a shop, at a party, on the radio)
trap: Not ongaku ga hiku or ongaku ga suru: a song that's on is kakatteru (or nagareteru), the intransitive of ongaku o kakeru.
why: How you say a song was on in a shop, at a party or on the radio (kono kyoku, mise de kakatteta).
freqNote: かかる #385 pools all senses (take time, cost, be locked); 掛かる alone is #5316.

trap: Not iyahon o kiru: earphones take suru (or tsukeru), like a watch or a mask, as in iyahon shiteta kara kikoenakatta. Taking them out is hazusu.
why: A daily excuse and request: earphones in on the train, so I didn't hear you; iyahon hazushite.
freqNote: イヤホン #13621; the variant spelling イヤフォン is #123250.

trap: Not kaze ga mawaru: an illness going around is 'in fashion', hayatteru. Infuru ga hayatteru is just as common.
why: Standard winter small talk and warning (ima kaze hayatteru kara ki o tsukete). Hayaru also covers trends.
freqNote: 流行る #7728. Kana はやる #3176 is probably mostly this verb but also counts 逸る, so it is not used.

english: come with a drink (a set includes it)
trap: Not dorinku to kuru: 'comes with' is tsuku (kore, saarada tsuku?). Tsuku 'arrive' is a different verb.
why: Ordering sets and lunch menus (dorinku tsukimasu ka; setto ni suupu ga tsuku). The noun swaps freely (saarada, suupu, omake).
freqNote: 付く #1570; kana つく #355 pools arrive / turn on / stick.

trap: Not mushiba o motsu: cavities, like pimples and bruises, 'come into being', so dekiru.
why: The dentist sentence. The pool has the dekiru-for-body set (nikibi, kuma, aza), and teeth are its commonest case.
freqNote: できる #73 is the kana form.

trap: Not shio o kakeru: salt is shaken on, furu (same sound as ame ga furu). Kakeru is for liquids like shouyu.
why: Cooking together and at the table (shio futta?). It is the third seasoning verb beside shouyu o kakeru and shouyu o tsukeru.
freqNote: 振る #1638 also counts 'wave' and 'dump (a partner)'.

trap: Not iiwake o tsukuru: you 'do' an excuse, iiwake (o) suru.
why: The noun is high-frequency (#1512) and shows up in arguments and apologies: 'iiwake shinaide', 'iiwake ja nai kedo...' ('I'm not making excuses, but...'). It works the same way as kenka o suru and henji o suru, which are already in the pool, where English 'make' pulls a learner toward tsukuru.

trap: There is no single verb for 'waste': Japanese says muda ni suru ('make it useless'), and 'a waste of time' is jikan no muda.
why: 'Jikan no muda da' and 'jikan o muda ni shita' are everyday complaints, and muda ni suru works the same with okane and tabemono. English 'waste' has no single verb a learner could find.
freqNote: verbRank is 無駄 (muda), the content word of muda ni suru. suru is #15, and ムダ is #5230.

english: invite someone over (to your place), have people over
trap: Not shoutai suru, which is for formal invitations such as weddings. Having friends over uses yobu, 'call': tomodachi o uchi ni yobu.
why: This is the everyday way to say you're having people over ('kondo uchi ni yobu ne', 'tomodachi yonde paatii shita'). Dictionaries give shoutai suru for 'invite', which sounds formal. The pool's takushii o yobu teaches yobu only as 'call'. The guest's side is asobi ni kuru, which the versatility pattern -ni kuru already covers.
freqNote: nounRank is the kana form うち (#113). That count includes uchi meaning 'we/our' and -uchi ni ('while'), so it overstates the 'home' sense. 家 read as いえ is #152.

trap: English 'my legs are sore' leads to ashi ga itai. Next-day exercise ache is one noun, kinnikutsuu, with ni naru.
why: Said after any gym session, hike or moving day (kinou hashitte kinnikutsuu ni natta). It fits the same 'illness noun + ni naru' shape as byouki ni naru, but the noun can't be guessed.
freqNote: The list has no phrase counts. nounRank is 筋肉痛 and verbRank is なる.

kana: ねっちゅうしょうになる
trap: Not netchuushou o toru / morau: you 'become' heatstroke, ni naru, usually in the warning netchuushou ni naranai you ni.
why: Every Japanese summer, people say this to each other as a 'stay safe' line (mizu nonde ne, netchuushou ni naranai you ni).
freqNote: The list has no phrase counts. nounRank is 熱中症 and verbRank is なる. The drama corpus undercounts it; it is a staple of summer news and everyday warnings.

english: be wide awake (and can't get to sleep)
trap: Not me ga sameru, which means waking up. Lying in bed wide awake is me ga saeru (koohii nonda kara me ga saete nerarenai).
why: The usual way to explain a sleepless night. It must be learned alongside me ga sameru (in the pool) and okiru.
freqNote: verbRank is the kana entry さえる (#13581); kanji 冴える is #18380.

trap: English 'is it cooked / done?' leads to yaketa? or ryouri sareta. Asking whether meat is cooked through is mou hi tootteru?
why: Said at every yakiniku, BBQ and home cooking session. The transitive form is hi o toosu (chanto hi toshite ne).
freqNote: nounRank is 火 (fire), not 日 (#209). verbRank is 通る.

english: (a dish) makes you eat more rice; goes great with rice
trap: English has no matching phrase. Praising a dish as moreish with rice is gohan ga susumu, 'the rice moves forward', also sake ga susumu.
why: One of the most common ways to compliment home food or a side dish (kore gohan susumu ne). A learner could never build it from English.
freqNote: nounRank is ご飯 and verbRank is 進む. The list has no phrase counts.

trap: Not gohan o ireru / dasu: dishing rice or soup into a bowl is yosou (gohan yosotte kureru?).
why: Said at every family dinner and when dishing up for others. The verb has no other everyday use, so the pairing is the only way to learn it.
freqNote: verbRank is the kana entry よそう (#18376). 予想 (yosou, 'prediction', #2712) is a different word, as is 装う (よそおう).

english: the flavour has soaked in (simmered food)
trap: Not aji ga hairu: flavour soaking into simmered food is shimiru (kono daikon, aji ga shimite oishii).
why: A standard compliment for oden, nimono and curry the next day. It belongs in the same set as the pool's aji ga koi / aji ga usui.
freqNote: verbRank is kanji 染みる (#10142). The kana しみる (#7498) also counts the 'sting' sense, so it isn't used here.

kana: しんごうにひっかかる
english: get caught at a red light
trap: Not shingou de tomaru / matsu alone: getting stopped by lights is hikkakaru, 'get snagged' (shingou zenbu hikkakatta).
why: The stock excuse for running a bit late (gomen, shingou ni hikkakatte). It goes with okureru.
freqNote: verbRank is 引っ掛かる (#3595); the 引っかかる spelling is #3643.

kana: くつのひもがほどける
trap: Not himo ga hazureru / aku: a knot coming loose is hodokeru (himo hodoketeru yo). Tying it is himo o musubu.
why: A line you say to someone else. hodokeru has no other common use, so the pairing is the only way in.
freqNote: nounRank is kanji 紐. The kana ひも (#9283) is inflated by the slang 'kept man' sense. verbRank is the kana entry ほどける, because the 解ける kanji entries are dominated by the とける reading.

english: be offended, take it the wrong way
trap: Not okoru or kizutsuku: 'don't take this the wrong way / no offence' is ki o waruku shinaide (ne).
why: Used to soften frank remarks and in apologies (ki o waruku shitara gomen). It is the plain, literal way to say 'be offended', not a character idiom, so it passes the borderline rule. Keep apart from ki ni shinaide.
freqNote: The list has no entry for 悪くする. verbRank is the adjective 悪い (warui). nounRank is 気.

english: look up (a word) in the dictionary
trap: Not jisho o miru / sagasu: consulting a dictionary is hiku, 'pull' (jisho de hiite mita).
why: A learner talks about looking up words more than most people do. It is the third common use of hiku after kaze o hiku and piano o hiku, which are both in the pool.
freqNote: nounRank is 辞書 and verbRank is 引く (pull). 弾く (play an instrument) is a separate entry.
